metadata.scope: e_arabia (all baronies across k_persia, k_arabia, k_jazira, k_mesopotamia, k_yemen, k_armenia, and k_jerusalem)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.vanilla_ck3_name: Exact English localisation string from CK3 titles_l_english.yml.
schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/standard English display name of the audited settlement or holding (stripped of key prefixes and parenthetical notes).
schema_notes.modern_name_note: Optional administrative parent, alternate designation, or native-script qualifier extracted from modern_name; null if none.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.anachronism_type: Mutually exclusive historicity category: attested_pre_867 | fictional_placeholder | post_867_eponym | renamed_post_867 | modern_anachronism | early_modern_foundation | high_late_medieval_attestation | unattested_indigenous_or_minor.
schema_notes.is_historical_at: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'}: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= that bookmark year.
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation for the audited name (negative values = BCE; null if unattested).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.eponym: Structured eponym object {year, post_867, type, details} when named after a person, saint, ruler, deity, or dynasty/tribe; null otherwise.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.historical_names: List of distinct pre-867 attested names for the same site or immediate predecessor: [{name, native_script, language, attested_from, attested_to, source, relationship, notes}].
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_al-hasa.first_mention_attestation: 899–926 CE (Qarmatian foundation and fortification of al-Ahsa oasis as their capital by Abu Sa'id al-Jannabi and Abu Tahir al-Jannabi)

morphemes.translation: sandy depressions holding groundwater near the surface (plural of ḥisy)

b_al-hasa.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Aḥsāʾ (الأحساء), plural of ḥisy, referring to sandy hollows where groundwater lies close to the surface. The oasis itself was settled in antiquity (pre-Islamic Hajar), but the name al-Aḥsāʾ / al-Ḥasā for the fortified Qarmatian capital dates to 899–926 CE, after 867 CE.

b_al-hajar.first_mention_attestation: c. 325 CE (Sasanian campaign of Shapur II in Eastern Arabia recorded in early Islamic historiography; also 628 CE letter of Muhammad to al-Mundhir ibn Sawa)

morphemes.translation: town, fortified settlement (from South Arabian hgr)

b_al-hajar.etymology_analysis: From Old South Arabian / Hasaitic hgr ('town, city', noted by al-Hamdani as Himyaritic for 'large village'), via Arabic Hajar (هجر). It served as the pre-Islamic and early Islamic capital of al-Bahrayn (Eastern Arabia) until eclipsed by al-Ahsa after 899 CE.

b_al-mushaqqar.first_mention_attestation: c. 550–600 CE (pre-Islamic Arabic poetry of Tarafa ibn al-Abd and al-A'sha; site of the pre-Islamic Battle of al-Mushaqqar / Yawm al-Safqa)

morphemes.translation: reddish / sorrel-colored (from the root sh-q-r, referring to its painted or reddish stone fortress)

b_al-mushaqqar.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Mushaqqar (المشقر), a pre-Islamic fortress and annual market fair near Hajar in Al-Ahsa, famous in 6th-century CE Arabic poetry and the Battle of al-Mushaqqar (Yawm al-Safqa).

b_az-dhafra.first_mention_attestation: 16th century CE (first historical references to the Bani Yas tribe inhabiting the Al Dhafra region)

morphemes.translation: sandy tract / victory or abundance (regional desert choronym)

b_az-dhafra.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Ẓafrah (الظفرة), the historical choronym for the western desert region of Abu Dhabi. Documented in historical sources only from the 16th century CE onward.

b_al-jiwa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; historical name of the Liwa Oasis attested in early modern/modern Bani Yas traditions and 20th-century accounts

morphemes.translation: wide valley, hollow, or depression between sand dunes

b_al-jiwa.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Jiwāʾ (الجواء), meaning a wide depression or valley between dunes, an older/dialectal name for the Liwa Oasis in Abu Dhabi. No written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_al-uqayr.first_mention_attestation: c. 930 CE (described by the 10th-century CE geographer al-Hamdani as a major port of Eastern Arabia)

morphemes.translation: diminutive/altered form, traditionally linked to the ancient Ajaru/Ajeeru tribe or Arabic ʿaqīr

b_al-uqayr.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-ʿUqayr (العقير). Although the surrounding coast was active in antiquity (and sometimes proposed as the site of Hellenistic Gerrha, c. 200 BCE, though archaeological ruins at the fort date to the Islamic period), the name al-ʿUqayr is first attested in writing in the 10th century CE by al-Hamdani, after 867 CE.

b_murwab.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in written sources (early Abbasid archaeological village in northwest Qatar dated archaeologically to c. 750–899 CE)

morphemes.translation: place where milk is churned or curdled (from r-w-b), or local Qatari toponym

b_murwab.etymology_analysis: Modern Arabic name of an early Abbasid archaeological site in northwestern Qatar (occupied c. 8th–9th centuries CE). While the settlement itself dates to the early Abbasid era, the toponym Murwab has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_mashqar.first_mention_attestation: c. 550–600 CE (pre-Islamic Arabic poetry of Tarafa ibn al-Abd and al-A'sha; Battle of al-Mushaqqar)
b_mashqar.etymology_analysis: Syncopated/un-prefixed form of Arabic al-Mushaqqar (المشقر), the pre-Islamic fortress in Eastern Arabia. In-game this holding in c_uqayr duplicates the historical al-Mushaqqar represented by b_al-mushaqqar in c_al-hasa.

b_yabrin.first_mention_attestation: c. 700 CE (Umayyad-era Arabic poetry of Jarir and al-Farazdaq, and early Islamic geographical works)

morphemes.translation: ancient oasis toponym of uncertain pre-Islamic Semitic/Arabic origin

b_yabrin.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Yabrīn (يبرين, also Jabrīn), an ancient oasis on the northern edge of the Rub' al-Khali. Attested archaeologically from the 3rd millennium BCE and in written Arabic poetry by the Umayyad period (c. 700 CE).

b_amman.first_mention_attestation: c. 850 BCE (Amman Citadel Inscription and Neo-Assyrian records of Ammon / Rabbath Ammon)

morphemes.translation: city of Ammon (from Iron Age Rabbath Ammon)

b_amman.etymology_analysis: From Ammonite ʿAmān / Hebrew Rabbath ʿAmmōn (c. 9th century BCE), renamed Philadelphia by Ptolemy II c. 255 BCE, and restored to Arabic ʿAmmān (عمان) following the Islamic conquest in 635 CE.

b_az-zarqa.first_mention_attestation: 1902 CE (modern city of Zarqa founded by Chechen immigrants along the Zarqa River)

morphemes.translation: blue (feminine adjective, referring to the river)

b_az-zarqa.etymology_analysis: Named after the Zarqa River (Nahr az-Zarqāʾ, 'the Blue River', known in biblical antiquity as the Jabbok). The settlement of Zarqa itself was founded in 1902 CE.

b_al-azraq.first_mention_attestation: 1237 CE (Ayyubid renovation of Qasr al-Azraq; medieval Arabic name from the Azraq oasis)
b_al-azraq.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Azraq (الأزرق, 'the blue'), referring to the blue waters of the Azraq Oasis. While the fort was occupied by Nabataeans and Romans (c. 200–333 CE), the Arabic name al-Azraq is post-867 CE.

historical_names.name: Basie
historical_names.source: Roman military inscriptions and Qasr al-Azraq historical record (c. 200–305 CE)
historical_names.notes: Known in Roman antiquity as Basie before the medieval Arabic name al-Azraq.

b_al-jilat.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in written sources (prehistoric Epipalaeolithic/Neolithic sites surveyed in 1982–1989)

morphemes.translation: rock pools / water depressions in a wadi

b_al-jilat.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Wādī al-Jilāt (وادي الجلات), a seasonal desert ravine trapping winter floodwaters. Prehistoric sites exist there, but the Arabic name is unattested in writing <= 867 CE.

b_qasr_at-tuba.first_mention_attestation: 1896 CE (recorded by Alois Musil; the Umayyad brick palace was built c. 743 CE, but its original name is unattested)
b_qasr_at-tuba.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Qaṣr aṭ-Ṭūba (قصر الطوبة, 'Palace of Mudbrick'). Although built under Umayyad Caliph al-Walid II c. 743 CE, its original Umayyad name is lost and the modern descriptive name is first recorded in 1896 CE.

b_maab.first_mention_attestation: c. 840 BCE (Mesha Stele as Moab; later Hellenistic/Roman Areopolis in Ptolemy c. 150 CE and early Islamic Ma'āb in 629–634 CE)

morphemes.translation: Arabicized form of ancient Moab / Rabbath Moab

b_maab.etymology_analysis: From Iron Age Moabite Mōʾāb (مآب in Arabic), capital of the Moabite kingdom (Rabbath Moab), Hellenized as Areopolis in the Roman period and attested as Maʾāb in early Islamic chronicles of the 7th century CE.

b_zaiza.first_mention_attestation: c. 400 CE (Roman Notitia Dignitatum as Ziza; also al-Tabari under 743–744 CE)
b_zaiza.etymology_analysis: Attested in the Notitia Dignitatum (c. 400 CE) as the Roman garrison fort of Ziza (Equites Dalmatici Illyriciani), and in early Islamic sources (al-Tabari, 743–744 CE) as Zīzyāʾ / Zaizāʾ.

b_mujib.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE under the Arabic name al-Mūjib (known in antiquity as the Arnon River)
b_mujib.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Wādī al-Mūjib (وادي الموجب). In antiquity and the Roman period it was known as the Arnon (Mesha Stele c. 840 BCE; Roman fort Apud Arnona); the Arabic name al-Mūjib is post-867 CE.

historical_names.name: Arnon
historical_names.source: Mesha Stele (c. 840 BCE) and Hebrew Bible (Numbers 21:13)
historical_names.notes: Known in Iron Age and Roman sources as the Arnon River (and fort Apud Arnona).

b_aqiq_tamra.first_mention_attestation: c. 800–828 CE (early Abbasid philologists and geographers such as al-Asma'i, d. 828 CE, and pre-Islamic/Umayyad poetry)
b_aqiq_tamra.etymology_analysis: From Arabic ʿAqīq Tamrah (عقيق تمرة, also ʿAqīq Banī ʿUqayl), the classical Arabic name for Wadi al-Dawasir, attested in early Islamic geographical and poetic traditions before 867 CE.

b_dam.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE (Al-Dam / Al-Ladam in Wadi al-Dawasir is attested only in late medieval/early modern sources)
b_dam.etymology_analysis: Refers to al-Dām / al-Laddām (الدام / اللدام), a historical town and former capital of Wadi al-Dawasir, attested only in later medieval and early modern sources (e.g., 19th-century Gazetteer of the Persian Gulf).

b_sarba.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in historical or geographical sources

morphemes.translation: toponym of uncertain origin (possibly from sarb, flock/path)

b_sarba.etymology_analysis: Sub-barony in c_aqiq (Wadi al-Dawasir / Asir) with no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_wadi_tathlith.first_mention_attestation: 552 CE (Sabaean inscription Ry 506 at Jabal Muraighan in Wadi Tathlith recording Abraha's campaign)

morphemes.translation: Tathlith (pre-Islamic valley name attested in Ry 506)

b_wadi_tathlith.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Wādī Tathlīth (وادي تثليث), a major valley in northeastern Asir / southwestern Najd. Attested by name in the 552 CE Sabaean inscription Ry 506 at Jabal Muraighan.

b_wadi_ghamid.first_mention_attestation: c. 630 CE (early Islamic chronicles recording the delegations of the Ghamid tribe to Muhammad, plus pre-Islamic poetry)

eponym.details: Named after the Arab tribe of Ghamid (Banu Ghamid, a branch of Azd), attested in pre-Islamic and early Islamic sources.

morphemes.translation: Ghamid (major Azd tribe of Al-Baha / Asir)

b_wadi_ghamid.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Wādī Ghāmid (وادي غامد), named after the ancient Azd tribe of Ghāmid, attested in pre-Islamic poetry and early Islamic chronicles (c. 630 CE).

b_al-qatif.first_mention_attestation: 899 CE (first prominent under Qarmatian rule and 10th-century CE Arab geographers; pre-899 region was known as al-Khatt)

morphemes.translation: harvested / plucked (from q-ṭ-f, referring to date/fruit harvests)

b_al-qatif.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Qaṭīf (القطيف), related to q-ṭ-f ('harvesting'). Although the oasis has Bronze Age roots, the name al-Qaṭīf enters written records around 899 CE with the Qarmatians, after 867 CE.

b_al-khatt.first_mention_attestation: c. 550–600 CE (pre-Islamic Arabic poetry of Antara ibn Shaddad and Tarafa ibn al-Abd, famous for Khatti spears)
b_al-khatt.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Khaṭṭ (الخط), the pre-Islamic and early Islamic name for the Qatif coastal strip of Eastern Arabia, famous in 6th-century CE Arabic poetry as a landing port for spears (rimāḥ khaṭṭiyyah).

b_al-jubayl.first_mention_attestation: 1911 CE (modern town of Jubail established near the abandoned early Islamic settlement of 'Aynayn)
b_al-jubayl.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Jubayl (الجبيل), diminutive of jabal ('hill, mountain'). The modern town was founded around 1911 CE; in the early Islamic period the site was known as 'Aynayn ('two springs').

historical_names.name: 'Aynayn
historical_names.source: Early Islamic Arabic geographical sources (cited in Wikipedia: Jubail)
historical_names.notes: Known in the early Islamic period as 'Aynayn ('two springs') before being abandoned and refounded as Jubail in 1911 CE.

b_thaj.first_mention_attestation: c. 580 CE (late 6th-century CE castle built by Rashid ibn Shihab al-Yashkuri; also Umayyad poetry and 691 CE events)

morphemes.translation: ancient oasis town name (possibly related to Ptolemy's Phigeia)

b_thaj.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Thāj (ثاج), an ancient walled oasis city in Eastern Arabia (archaeologically active from c. 600 BCE–300 CE). Attested in Arabic historical sources from the late 6th century CE (castle of Rashid ibn Shihab al-Yashkuri) and Umayyad poetry.

b_kazima.first_mention_attestation: 633 CE (Battle of Chains / Dhat al-Salasil near Kazima; also birthplace of Umayyad poet al-Farazdaq c. 641 CE)

morphemes.translation: ancient port and caravan station on Kuwait Bay

b_kazima.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Kāẓimah (كاظمة), an early Islamic and pre-Islamic port and caravan station on Kuwait Bay, famous for the Battle of Chains (633 CE) and as the birthplace of al-Farazdaq.

b_ar-ruqaii.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE (modern Saudi–Kuwaiti border crossing town near Hafar al-Batin)
b_ar-ruqaii.etymology_analysis: Modern border town (Al-Ruqai / Al-Raq'i) between Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_hafar.first_mention_attestation: c. 644–656 CE (wells dug by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari during the caliphate of Uthman along the Basra–Mecca route)

eponym.details: Historically known as Hafar Abi Musa al-Ash'ari, after the Companion and Basran governor Abu Musa al-Ash'ari (d. c. 662 CE), who ordered the wells dug during the reign of Caliph Uthman (644–656 CE).

b_hafar.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Ḥafar (حفر, 'dug well'), referring to the wells excavated by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari in Wadi al-Batin during the caliphate of Uthman (644–656 CE).

b_al-mawiya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in the Samman / Eastern Arabia region

morphemes.translation: watery place / mirror-like well (or personal name Mawiyyah)

b_al-mawiya.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Māwiyyah (الماوية), with no documented written attestation <= 867 CE in the Samman region.

b_as-samman.first_mention_attestation: c. 600 CE (pre-Islamic Arabic poetry, including Antara ibn Shaddad's Mu'allaqah, Amr ibn Ma'di Yakrib, and later al-Farazdaq and Dhu al-Rummah)
b_as-samman.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Ṣammān (الصمان), the vast limestone plateau of eastern Arabia, frequently attested in pre-Islamic and early Islamic poetry (Antara ibn Shaddad, d. c. 608 CE; Dhu al-Rummah, d. 735 CE).

b_uwal.first_mention_attestation: c. 600 CE (pre-Islamic and early Islamic name for Bahrain Island, named after the pre-Islamic deity Awal)

eponym.details: Named after Awāl (Uwāl), a pre-Islamic deity worshipped on Bahrain Island.

morphemes.translation: name of a pre-Islamic deity and historical name of Bahrain Island

b_uwal.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Awāl / Uwāl (أوال), the pre-Islamic and early Islamic name of Bahrain Island, derived from the pre-Islamic deity Awal worshipped there prior to Islam.

b_al_jawf.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE under the name al-Jawf (in antiquity and early Islam known as Adummatu / Dumat al-Jandal)

morphemes.translation: hollow, depression (referring to the Wadi Sirhan basin)

b_al_jawf.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Jawf (الجوف, 'the depression'). While the oasis city is ancient, it was known in antiquity as Adummatu (845 BCE) and in early Islam as Dūmat al-Jandal (626–630 CE); al-Jawf is a later regional/town name.

historical_names.name: Adummatu
historical_names.source: Neo-Assyrian inscriptions (845 BCE) and Esarhaddon Prism (673–672 BCE); early Islamic sources (626–630 CE)
historical_names.notes: Known to the Neo-Assyrians as Adummatu and in early Islamic sources as Dumat al-Jandal.

historical_names.name: Dumat al-Jandal
historical_names.source: Neo-Assyrian inscriptions (845 BCE) and Esarhaddon Prism (673–672 BCE); early Islamic sources (626–630 CE)
historical_names.notes: Known to the Neo-Assyrians as Adummatu and in early Islamic sources as Dumat al-Jandal.

b_sakaka.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in written sources (oasis has Bronze Age/ancient habitation, but the name Sakākā appears in later medieval/early modern sources)
b_sakaka.etymology_analysis: Arabic Sakākā (سكاكا), capital of Al-Jawf Province. Although inhabited since at least the 2nd millennium BCE, the toponym Sakākā has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_al-qara-jawf.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in written sources (modern suburb southeast of Sakaka near the Chalcolithic Columns of Rajajil)
b_al-qara-jawf.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Qārah (القارة, 'isolated hill/mesa'), a suburb southeast of Sakaka. Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.

b_quraqir.first_mention_attestation: 634 CE (early Islamic historiography recording Khalid ibn al-Walid's desert march from Quraqir in Wadi Sirhan to Suwa in Syria)

morphemes.translation: plural/intensive of qarqar (level ground / wells in Wadi Sirhan)

b_quraqir.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Qurāqir (قراقر), a well and watering station in Wadi Sirhan famously used by Khalid ibn al-Walid as the starting point of his 634 CE desert march into Syria.

b_sirhan.first_mention_attestation: c. 1650 CE (Wadi Sirhan named after the Sirhan tribe, which migrated there from the Hauran c. 1650 CE)

eponym.details: Named after the Sirhan tribe (descendants of Banu Kalb), who migrated from the Hauran to Wadi Sirhan c. 1650 CE (post-867 CE).

b_sirhan.etymology_analysis: Named after the Sirḥān tribe, which migrated to the depression from the Hauran around 1650 CE (earlier referred to as Wadi al-Azraq after the Azraq oasis, represented separately by b_al-azraq; no separate pre-867 CE attestation for the name Wadi al-Azraq itself). Note: the input repo state had a placeholder 'Zant-Gebhard' disambiguation.

b_ath-thalabiya.first_mention_attestation: c. 846 CE (early Abbasid road itineraries of Ibn Khordadbeh and al-Ya'qubi for Darb Zubaydah)

morphemes.translation: place of foxes (from thaʿlab) or Banu Tha'labah

b_ath-thalabiya.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Thaʿlabiyyah (الثعلبية), a major walled station and cistern complex on the Kufah–Mecca pilgrimage road (Darb Zubaydah), attested in 9th-century CE Abbasid geographical itineraries.

b_zubala.first_mention_attestation: c. 780–846 CE (pre-Abbasid/early Abbasid station on Darb Zubaydah, documented by Ibn Khordadbeh c. 846 CE)

eponym.details: Attributed in Saudi heritage sources to Zubalah ibn al-Harith.

morphemes.translation: eponymous settlement name (attributed to Zubalah ibn al-Harith)

b_zubala.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Zubālah (زبالة), a major pre-Abbasid and early Abbasid station on the Kufah–Mecca pilgrimage road (Darb Zubaydah), attested in early Abbasid itineraries.

b_lina.first_mention_attestation: c. 828 CE (attested by early Abbasid geographers such as al-Asma'i, d. 828 CE, as a watering place of Banu Asad between Zubalah and al-Tha'labiyyah)
b_lina.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Līnah (لينة), an ancient desert well complex and caravan station near Darb Zubaydah, attested in early Abbasid geographical works (al-Asma'i, d. 828 CE).

b_bitan.first_mention_attestation: c. 846 CE (early Abbasid Darb Zubaydah itineraries of Ibn Khordadbeh and Waki', d. 918 CE)

morphemes.translation: low-lying / inner ground (station on Darb Zubaydah)

b_bitan.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Biṭān / al-Biṭān (بطان), a station between Zubalah and al-Tha'labiyyah on the Kufah–Mecca pilgrimage road (Darb Zubaydah), attested in 9th-century CE Abbasid road books.

b_makka.first_mention_attestation: 628 CE (Quran 48:24 as Makkah and 3:96 as Bakkah; also possibly Ptolemy's Macoraba c. 150 CE)

morphemes.translation: Mecca (ancient sanctuary city in the Hejaz)

b_makka.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Makkah (مكة), attested in the Quran (7th century CE) and early Islamic historiography, and possibly earlier in Ptolemy's Geography (2nd century CE) as Macoraba.

b_rabigh.first_mention_attestation: 623 CE (Expedition of Ubaydah ibn al-Harith to the valley/baṭn of Rabigh in April 623 CE)
b_rabigh.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Rābigh (رابغ), attested in April 623 CE in early Islamic sources (Expedition of Ubaydah ibn al-Harith to baṭn Rābigh); the adjacent coastal settlement was also known as al-Juḥfah until the 17th century CE.

b_khulays.first_mention_attestation: c. 622–630 CE (attested in the Prophetic biography / Sīrah along the Mecca–Medina route)

morphemes.translation: diminutive of khalīṣ (pure/clear water or sanctuary)

b_khulays.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Khulays (خليص), a station and oasis valley north of Mecca on the historic Mecca–Medina route, attested in early Islamic Sīrah and geographical sources.

b_jidda.first_mention_attestation: 647 CE (designated by Caliph Uthman as the main Red Sea port serving Mecca)
b_jidda.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Jiddah / Juddah (جدة), meaning 'seashore/coast'. Designated as the principal port of Mecca by Caliph Uthman in 647 CE.

b_usfain.first_mention_attestation: 628 CE (attested in the Prophetic biography during the Hudaybiyyah campaign at 'Usfan)

morphemes.translation: place name on the Mecca–Medina caravan route

b_usfain.etymology_analysis: From Arabic ʿUsfān (عسفان), an important station between Mecca and Medina attested in 628 CE during the Hudaybiyyah campaign.

b_at-taif.first_mention_attestation: 630 CE (Siege of Ta'if and Destruction of al-Lat in 630 CE; earlier known as Wajj)

morphemes.translation: the encircled/walled (referring to the wall built by Banu Thaqif)

b_at-taif.etymology_analysis: From Arabic aṭ-Ṭāʾif (الطائف, 'the encircled'), named after the defensive wall built by the Banu Thaqif around the older settlement of Wajj. Attested in 630 CE in early Islamic sources.

historical_names.name: Wajj
historical_names.source: Early Islamic sources (Ibn Ishaq / al-Waqidi / al-Tabari, 630 CE, recording Wajj as the older name of the settlement walled by the Banu Thaqif).
historical_names.notes: Wajj was the pre-Islamic name of the settlement and valley before it was walled and called al-Ta'if.

b_turaba.first_mention_attestation: 628 CE (Expedition of Umar ibn al-Khattab to Turabah in 7 AH / 628 CE)
b_turaba.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Turabah (تربة), a valley and oasis settlement southeast of Ta'if on the Hejaz–Najd border, attested in 628 CE in early Islamic sources.

b_tabala-hijaz.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in early Islamic historical accounts (al-Tabari, al-Baladhuri) for 629–630 CE expeditions to Tabalah (home to the pre-Islamic shrine of Dhu'l-Khalasa); '-Hijaz' is a modern regional disambiguator.

morphemes.translation: ancient Arabian oasis/town name (of uncertain pre-Islamic root)

b_tabala-hijaz.etymology_analysis: Tabalah (تبالة) is a pre-Islamic Arabian toponym of uncertain etymology; the suffix '-Hijaz' is an in-game/modern disambiguator.

b_as-sirayn.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Sirrayn (السرين) in al-Azraqi's Akhbar Makkah (d. c. 865 CE) and al-Ya'qubi's Tarikh (late 9th century CE) as a major Red Sea port and mikhlaf in Tihama.

morphemes.translation: dual of sirr (fertile valley/lowland or secret)

b_as-sirayn.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Sirrayn (السرّين), dual form derived from Arabic sirr (سرّ, fertile valley floor or low-lying ground).

b_hali.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Hali (حلي) in al-Azraqi's Akhbar Makkah (d. c. 865 CE) when locating Suq Hubasha between Qanuna and Hali toward Yemen.
b_hali.etymology_analysis: Named after Wadi Hali (وادي حلي), a major Tihama watercourse; later known in the medieval period as Hali ibn Ya'qub.

b_ash-shuqayq.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Ash-Shuqayq (الشقيق) is a coastal town in Jazan Province attested in modern/later sources.

morphemes.translation: cleft / strip of hard ground between dunes

b_ash-shuqayq.etymology_analysis: Arabic ash-Shuqayq (الشقيق), diminutive or topographic term denoting a cleft or hard-ground tract between sand dunes or coastal plain.

b_as-sawariqiya.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Sawariqiyyah (السوارقية) in early Islamic tradition (7th–8th century CE accounts of Khubayb ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr preserved in al-Bakri, and 9th-century geographer Arram al-Sulami).

eponym.details: Traditional local accounts associate the name with Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Atiq al-Sawariqi, though the settlement dates to the pre-Islamic/early Islamic era of Banu Sulaym.

b_as-sawariqiya.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Sawariqiyyah (السوارقية), also colloquially al-Suwayriqiyyah, a nisba-formed settlement name of Banu Sulaym.

b_as-salila.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Salilah (السليلة) on the Kufa–Mecca pilgrimage route (Darb Zubaydah) in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE) and al-Harbi's Kitab al-Manasik (9th century CE).
b_as-salila.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Salilah (السليلة), meaning a shallow watercourse or wadi channel; a major Abbasid-era station on Darb Zubaydah.

b_madinat_sulaym.first_mention_attestation: The title 'Madinat Sulaym' is an adapted form not attested <= 867 CE; the historical site (modern Mahd adh-Dhahab) was known as Ma'din Bani Sulaym ('Mine of Banu Sulaym').

eponym.details: Named after the pre-Islamic Arab tribe of Banu Sulaym (بنو سليم).

b_madinat_sulaym.etymology_analysis: Adapts Arabic Ma'din Bani Sulaym (معدن بني سليم, 'Mine of Banu Sulaym'), replacing Ma'din ('mine') with Madinat ('city').

historical_names.name: Ma'din Bani Sulaym
historical_names.source: Ibn Khordadbeh, Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE)
historical_names.notes: Known in early Islamic and Abbasid sources as Ma'din Bani Sulaym (and earlier as Faran); modern Mahd adh-Dhahab.

historical_names.name: Faran
historical_names.source: Ibn Khordadbeh, Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE)
historical_names.notes: Known in early Islamic and Abbasid sources as Ma'din Bani Sulaym (and earlier as Faran); modern Mahd adh-Dhahab.

b_sufaina.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Sufaynah (صفينة) on the Darb Zubaydah pilgrimage route in 9th-century CE geographical sources (Ibn Khordadbeh c. 846 CE; al-Harbi), and known since the pre-Islamic era.
b_sufaina.etymology_analysis: Arabic Sufaynah (صفينة), a pre-Islamic and early Islamic oasis village on Darb Zubaydah in Mahd adh-Dhahab.

b_khaybar.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 567 CE (Ghassanid campaign of al-Harith ibn Jabalah) and in 628 CE (Battle of Khaybar in early Islamic historiography).

morphemes.translation: fortified place / fortress (often linked to Hebrew/Aramaic ḥever or Arabic kh-b-r)

b_khaybar.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic oasis name Khaybar (خيبر), traditionally associated with ancient Semitic roots meaning 'fortress' or 'cultivated land'.

b_as-suqya.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Suqya (السقيا / سقيا الجزل) on the Syrian Hajj route in Wadi al-Qura in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE).
b_as-suqya.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Suqya (السقيا), from the root s-q-y ('to give water / irrigate'), denoting an irrigated oasis station in Wadi al-Qura.

b_al-ula.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Ula (العلا) in early Islamic historiography (Ibn Hisham, d. 833 CE; al-Waqidi, d. 823 CE; Ibn Khordadbeh, c. 846 CE); the oasis was earlier known as Dedan (552 BCE).
b_al-ula.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-ʿUla (العُلا), meaning 'the high/elevated place', replacing the ancient North Arabian name Dedan.

historical_names.name: Dedan
historical_names.source: Harran Stela of Neo-Babylonian King Nabonidus (c. 552 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient oasis capital of the Dedanite and Lihyanite kingdoms before becoming known as al-Ula in the Islamic era.

b_al-hijr.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Hijr (الحجر) in the Quran (Surah 15, Al-Hijr, early 7th century CE) and in early Islamic accounts of the 630 CE Tabuk expedition.
b_al-hijr.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Hijr (الحِجْر), meaning 'the stony land/enclosure', corresponding to Nabataean/Greco-Roman Hegra.

historical_names.name: Hegra
historical_names.source: Nabataean inscriptions and classical Greco-Roman geographers (1st century BCE–1st century CE)
historical_names.notes: Major Nabataean city of Hegra (modern Mada'in Salih), referred to in Arabic as al-Hijr.

b_dhul-marwa.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Dhu Marwa / Dhu'l-Marwah (ذو المروة) in early Islamic chronicles for 634 CE (13 AH, Khalid ibn Sa'id's encampment) and in al-Waqidi (d. 823 CE).
b_dhul-marwa.etymology_analysis: Arabic Dhu al-Marwah (ذو المروة), literally 'the place of white quartz/flint stone', an oasis station in Wadi al-Qura.

b_al-madina.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Madinah (المدينة) from 622 CE following the Hijrah (Constitution of Medina and Quranic verses 9:101, 9:120, 33:60, 63:8); earlier known as Yathrib (552 BCE).

morphemes.translation: city (short for Madinat al-Nabi, 'City of the Prophet')

b_al-madina.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Madinah (المدينة, 'the City'), shortened from Madinat al-Nabi ('City of the Prophet'), replacing pre-Islamic Yathrib.

historical_names.name: Yathrib
historical_names.source: Harran Stela of Neo-Babylonian King Nabonidus (c. 552 BCE) and Quran 33:13
historical_names.notes: Pre-Islamic name of the oasis until renamed al-Madinah after 622 CE.

b_as-sayaa.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Sayah (ساية) in early Arabic poetry and Umayyad-era accounts (burial place of poetess Layla al-Akhyaliyya, d. c. 704 CE, recorded in al-Bakri's Mu'jam ma Ista'jam).
b_as-sayaa.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Sayah (الساية), a valley and village in the al-Fur' district near Medina; Arabic lexicographers derive it from taswiya ('levelling/path').

b_batn_nakhl.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Batn Nakhl (بطن نخل) in early Islamic Sira works (Ibn Hisham, al-Waqidi) for the Expedition of Dhat al-Riqa' (c. 626 CE / 4–5 AH).
b_batn_nakhl.etymology_analysis: Arabic Batn Nakhl (بطن نخل), meaning 'basin/valley of date palms', an oasis region east of Medina (modern al-Hinakiyah).

b_as-safra.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Wadi al-Safra (وادي الصفراء) in early Islamic Sira accounts (Ibn Hisham, al-Waqidi) of the Badr campaign in 624 CE (2 AH).
b_as-safra.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Safra' (الصفراء, 'the yellow one'), referring to the prominent valley (also called Wadi Yalayl) between Medina and Badr.

b_al-wajh.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Wajh (الوجه) in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE) as a coastal station on the Red Sea route.
b_al-wajh.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Wajh (الوجه), literally 'the face/front', denoting a prominent coastal headland and Red Sea harbor.

b_an-nabak.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Nabak (النبك) in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE) on the coastal Red Sea route north of Duba and al-Wajh.
b_an-nabak.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Nabak (النبك), meaning an elevated hill or pointed ridge; a medieval Red Sea coastal station.

b_al-awnid.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Awnid (عونيد) in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE) on the Red Sea coastal route immediately north of al-Wajh.
b_al-awnid.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-ʿAwnid / ʿUwaynid (العونيد / عويند), a medieval Red Sea port and pilgrimage station between Duba and al-Wajh.

b_bada.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Bada / Bada Ya'qub (بدا / بدا يعقوب) in al-Maqdisi's Ahsan al-Taqasim (985 CE) and al-Bakri (11th century CE); no confirmed written attestation <= 867 CE.

eponym.details: Later medieval sources associate the oasis with the prophet Jacob (Bada Ya'qub).

b_bada.etymology_analysis: Arabic Bada (بدا), an oasis and pilgrimage station northeast of al-Wajh, derived from Arabic bada ('open country/to appear').

b_yanbu.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Yanbu' (ينبع) in early Islamic Sira accounts (622–623 CE, expedition of al-Ushayra in Yanbu); nearby Sharm Yanbu was known as Charmuthas to Diodorus Siculus (1st century BCE).
b_yanbu.etymology_analysis: Arabic Yanbuʿ (ينبع), meaning 'spring of water', referring to the abundant springs of the coastal oasis.

b_al-jar.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Jar (الجار) from 639 CE (18 AH, Year of Famine), when Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab designated it as Medina's Red Sea port for Egyptian grain shipments.
b_al-jar.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Jar (الجار, 'the neighbor/protected one'), the principal early Islamic port of Medina on the Red Sea.

b_al-hawra.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Hawra' (الحوراء) in 10th-century CE geographical works (e.g., al-Maqdisi, 985 CE) and 10th–11th-century CE archaeological strata near Umluj; no confirmed written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: white / bright-eyed (associated with classical Leuke Kome, 'White Village')

b_al-hawra.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Hawra' (الحوراء, 'the white/fair one'), a medieval Red Sea port 10 km north of modern Umluj.

b_hail.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Ha'il (حائل) in 6th-century CE pre-Islamic Arabic poetry (Imru' al-Qays, Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma, Tarafa ibn al-Abd) as a valley between Mounts Aja and Salma.

morphemes.translation: barrier / intervening valley (lying between Aja and Salma)

b_hail.etymology_analysis: Arabic Ha'il (حائل), active participle meaning 'that which intervenes/separates', referring to the valley separating Mount Aja and Mount Salma.

b_jubba-hail.first_mention_attestation: Despite ancient prehistoric/Thamudic rock art at nearby Jebel Umm Sanman, the oasis of Jubbah is not mentioned in early Arab historical chronicles; its earliest modern written description is by Georg August Wallin in 1845 CE.
b_jubba-hail.etymology_analysis: Arabic Jubbah (جُبّة), denoting a depression or basin surrounded by sandstone outcrops in the Nafud desert; '-Hail' is a disambiguator.

b_mawqaq.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Mawqaq (موقق) is a historic town southwest of Ha'il attested in later Najdi sources.

morphemes.translation: local Najdi toponym of uncertain root

b_mawqaq.etymology_analysis: Arabic Mawqaq (موقق), a settlement in the Aja mountains of Ha'il Province without pre-867 written attestation.

b_fadak.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Fadak (فدك) in 628–629 CE (7 AH) when the oasis peacefully submitted to Muhammad.
b_fadak.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic oasis name Fadak (فدك), modern al-Ha'it in Ha'il Province.

b_fayd.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Fayd (فيد) in early Islamic sources for 630 CE (delegation of Zayd al-Khayl of Tayy' in Ibn Hisham) and in Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE) as the midpoint station of Darb Zubaydah.

morphemes.translation: pre-Islamic and early Islamic oasis name

b_fayd.etymology_analysis: Arabic Fayd (فيد), an ancient fortified oasis in Ha'il that served as the principal midpoint station on Darb Zubaydah.

b_tuz.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Tuz (توز) in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE) as a Darb Zubaydah station equipped with cisterns and wells.
b_tuz.etymology_analysis: Arabic Tuz (توز), an Abbasid-era station on Darb Zubaydah south of Fayd in Ha'il.

b_unayza.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Unayzah (عنيزة) in pre-Islamic Arabic poetry of the 6th century CE, including verses by Imru' al-Qays.
b_unayza.etymology_analysis: Arabic ʿUnayzah (عنيزة), diminutive of ʿanz/ʿanza, denoting a small black hillock or rocky outcrop in Al-Qassim.

b_al-qaryatan-qasim.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Qaryatan / al-Qaryatayn (القريتان / القريتين) in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE) on the Basra–Mecca route in Al-Qassim.
b_al-qaryatan-qasim.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Qaryatan (القريتان, 'the Two Villages'), referring to twin early Islamic settlements near Unayzah; '-Qasim' is a regional disambiguator.

b_rama.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Ramah (رامة) in 6th-century CE pre-Islamic poetry of Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma ('li-man talalun bi-Ramata la yarimu') and later in Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE).
b_rama.etymology_analysis: Arabic Ramah (رامة), a famous pre-Islamic and early Islamic watering station on the Basra Hajj route in Al-Qassim.

b_tikhfa.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Tikhfa (طخفة) as the site of the pre-Islamic Battle of Tikhfa (Yawm Tikhfa, 583 CE) between Banu Yarbu' of Tamim and Lakhmid-allied forces.

morphemes.translation: elevated plateau / hill mass in Najd

b_tikhfa.etymology_analysis: Arabic Tikhfa (طخفة), a prominent plateau and watering place in high Najd on the Basra–Mecca route.

b_an-nibaj.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Nibaj (النباج) from the mid-7th century CE (springs restored by Abd Allah ibn Amir ibn Kurayz c. 650–679 CE) and in Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE).
b_an-nibaj.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Nibaj (النباج), denoting springs that well up with water; modern Uyun al-Asyah in Al-Qassim.

b_al-khuzaimiya.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Khuzaimiyyah (الخزيمية) in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE), named after Abbasid commander Khuzayma ibn Khazim (d. 819 CE); previously called Zarud.

eponym.details: Named after the Abbasid general and governor Khuzayma ibn Khazim al-Tamimi (d. 819 CE), who outfitted the station with water-wheels and cisterns.

morphemes.translation: of Khuzayma (nisba to Khuzayma ibn Khazim)

b_al-khuzaimiya.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Khuzaimiyyah (الخزيمية), a nisba place-name honoring Abbasid commander Khuzayma ibn Khazim (d. 819 CE), replacing the older name Zarud.

historical_names.name: Zarud
historical_names.source: Early Umayyad-era accounts cited by al-Harbi and Yaqut ('Zarud al-atiqa')
historical_names.notes: Known as Zarud in the pre-Islamic and Umayyad periods before being renamed after Khuzayma ibn Khazim.

b_as-sumaina.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Sumayna (السمينة) in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE) on the Basra–Mecca Hajj route immediately before al-Nibaj.
b_as-sumaina.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Sumayna (السمينة), an early Islamic watering station on the Basra–Mecca pilgrimage road.

b_dariya.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Dariyah (ضرية) in early Islamic accounts of Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab (r. 634–644 CE) designating Hima Dariyah as a state pasture, and in pre-Islamic Ayyam al-Arab (Yawm Dariyah).
b_dariya.etymology_analysis: Arabic Dariyah (ضرية), a celebrated oasis and protected pasture (Hima Dariyah) in high Najd.

b_hajir.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Hajir (الحاجر) in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE) as a major station on Darb Zubaydah (modern al-Ba'a'ith).

morphemes.translation: retaining bank / depressed ground holding rainwater

b_hajir.etymology_analysis: Arabic Hajir / al-Hajir (حاجر / الحاجر), denoting depressed ground or a natural basin that retains rainwater.

b_rabadha.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Rabadha (الربذة) during the Ridda Wars (632 CE) and as the place of exile and death of Companion Abu Dharr al-Ghifari in 652 CE.
b_rabadha.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Rabadha (الربذة), a major early Islamic settlement and Darb Zubaydah station northeast of Medina.

b_madin-an-naqira.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Ma'din al-Naqira (معدن النقرة) in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE) as a major mining town and junction on Darb Zubaydah.
b_madin-an-naqira.etymology_analysis: Arabic Ma'din al-Naqira (معدن النقرة, 'Mine of the Hollow'), an Abbasid-era copper/gold mining center and pilgrimage junction.

b_jadila.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Jadilah (الجديلة) on the Basra–Mecca route south of Dariyah in al-Hajari's al-Ta'liqat wa'l-Nawadir (early 10th century CE, d. c. 912 CE) and Yaqut al-Hamawi; no confirmed written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_jadila.etymology_analysis: Arabic Jadilah / al-Jadilah (جديلة / الجديلة), a watering station on the Basra Hajj route near Dariyah.

b_fajla.first_mention_attestation: The title 'Fajla' is a metathesis/typo for Falja (فلجة), a Basra–Mecca Hajj route station attested in Qadi Waki' (d. 918 CE) and al-Hajari (early 10th century CE); neither form has a confirmed attestation <= 867 CE.
b_fajla.etymology_analysis: Metathesis of Arabic Falja (فلجة), a watering station on the Basra Hajj route between al-Jadilah and al-Dathinah.

b_nufud-as-surrah.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Nufud as-Surrah (نفود السرة) is a modern geographic name for a sand-dune belt in high Najd.
b_nufud-as-surrah.etymology_analysis: Arabic Nufud as-Surrah (نفود السرة), literally 'sand-desert of the central tract/navel' in high Najd.

b_jibal-al-urd.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-'Urd (العرض) in al-Hamdani's Sifat Jazirat al-Arab (10th century CE, d. 945 CE); no confirmed written attestation of 'Jibal al-Urd' <= 867 CE.
b_jibal-al-urd.etymology_analysis: Arabic Jibal al-ʿUrd (جبال العرض), a mountain range near al-Quway'iyyah in high Najd, historically also associated with Sawad Bahilah.

b_jibala.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Jabala / Shi'b Jabala (جبلة / شعب جبلة) as the site of the celebrated pre-Islamic Battle of Shi'b Jabala (c. 570 CE, 19 years before Muhammad's birth) between Banu Amir and Tamim/Dhubyan.
b_jibala.etymology_analysis: Arabic Jabala (جبلة), from jabal ('mountain'), denoting the prominent granite massif in high Najd.

b_hafit.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation of the name Hafit <= 867 CE; Bronze Age tombs at Jabal Hafit (3200–2600 BCE) are modernly termed the 'Hafit period' after the mountain.
b_hafit.etymology_analysis: Arabic Hafit (حفيت), a prominent mountain on the Oman–UAE border near Al-Buraimi/Al Ain.

b_dhank.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Omani historical literature by al-Awtabi al-Suhari (late 11th–early 12th century CE); no confirmed written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_dhank.etymology_analysis: Arabic Dank (ضنك), meaning 'narrow' or 'strait', referring to the narrow valley/pass in Ad Dhahirah, Oman.

b_sohar.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Ṣuḥār (صحار) in al-Tabari's Ta'rikh al-Rusul wa'l-Muluk in accounts of the Ridda Wars (632–633 CE), and again in 893–894 CE.

morphemes.translation: ancient Omani port city name (pre-Islamic/early Islamic)

b_sohar.etymology_analysis: Ṣuḥār is an ancient Omani coastal settlement and port. It was historically known in Sasanian/Syriac sources as Mazūn and has been argued to correspond to Pliny the Elder's 'Omanah'; the Arabic name Ṣuḥār is attested in early Islamic accounts of the 632–633 CE Ridda Wars.

b_batina-east.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE for the directional compound 'Batina-East' or the regional name al-Bāṭinah.
b_batina-east.etymology_analysis: Derived from Arabic al-bāṭinah ('the interior/lowland', referring to the coastal plain between the Hajar Mountains and the Gulf of Oman) with an English directional suffix '-East'.

b_rustaq-oman.first_mention_attestation: Retrospectively attested in early Islamic historiography (e.g., al-Baladhuri, c. 869 CE) as al-Rustāq, seat of the Sasanian marzban in Oman, with '-Oman' added as a modern/game disambiguator.
b_rustaq-oman.etymology_analysis: Borrowed into Arabic as al-Rustāq from Middle Persian rōstāg ('district'). Although tradition places a Sasanian marzban there in the 6th–7th centuries CE, written attestation in surviving Arabic sources begins after 867 CE (c. 869 CE), and 'Rustaq-Oman' is a modern disambiguated form.

b_duqm.first_mention_attestation: First documented in modern records in February 1954 CE when Petroleum Development Oman geologists and the Muscat and Oman Field Force landed at the fishing village.
b_duqm.etymology_analysis: A small fishing settlement of the Janubah tribe on Oman's Arabian Sea coast, first documented in modern 20th-century CE records and developed into a major port in the 2010s CE.

b_wahiba.first_mention_attestation: The desert region Rimāl Āl Wahībah (Wahiba Sands) entered scientific documentation in 1986 CE via the Royal Geographical Society expedition; no <= 867 CE written attestation.

eponym.details: Named after the Banu Wahiba (Āl Wahībah) Arab tribe.

b_wahiba.etymology_analysis: Named after the Banu Wahiba (Āl Wahībah) tribe inhabiting the eastern desert sands of Oman (Rimāl Wahībah, now officially Sharqiya Sands).

b_julfar.first_mention_attestation: Archaeological and historical evidence dates the foundation of medieval Julfar (at Mataf and Nudud) to the early-to-mid 14th century CE (c. 1300 CE), succeeding the nearby 5th-century port of Kush.
b_julfar.etymology_analysis: Julfar was an Islamic-era trading entrepôt in Ras Al Khaimah founded c. 1300 CE as the lagoon of its predecessor settlement, Kush (5th–13th centuries CE), silted up.

historical_names.name: Kush
historical_names.source: Archaeological and historical records of the fortified port of Kush (5th century CE), predecessor settlement to Julfar.
historical_names.notes: Kush was established in the 5th century CE and gradually abandoned in the 13th century CE as its lagoon silted up, leading to the establishment of Julfar.

b_tawwam.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Tawām / Tuwwam in al-Tabari's account of events in 893–894 CE and in al-Muqaddasi (985 CE).

morphemes.translation: twins (referring to twin oasis channels or settlements)

b_tawwam.etymology_analysis: Arabic Tawām ('twins'), traditionally associated with the twin oases/aflaj of Al Ain and Buraimi (and also linked archaeologically with Tu'am on Siniyah Island). Earliest surviving dated references in al-Tabari concern 893–894 CE.

b_tawwam_west.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; modern/game directional variant of Tawām (Tawwam West / Tawwam al-Gharb).
b_tawwam_west.etymology_analysis: Modern/game directional subdivision of the historical Tawām region.

b_musandam.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE for the toponym Musandam.
b_musandam.etymology_analysis: Toponym of the mountainous peninsula (also known as Ruʾūs al-Jibāl, 'Capes of the Mountains') jutting into the Strait of Hormuz; unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.

b_dabba.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Dibbā (دبّا) in early Islamic historiography (al-Tabari) as the site of the Battle of Dibba in 632–633 CE during the Ridda Wars, and by Ibn Habib as a major pre-Islamic market.
b_dabba.etymology_analysis: Ancient natural harbor and pre-Islamic entrepôt on the Gulf of Oman, attested in early Islamic accounts of the 632–633 CE Ridda Wars.

b_muscat.first_mention_attestation: Attested in classical antiquity (1st–2nd centuries CE) as Moscha / Moscha Portus in Arrian and Ptolemy's Geography.

morphemes.translation: anchorage / place of letting fall the anchor (disputed)

b_muscat.etymology_analysis: Known since the early 1st century CE as Moscha Portus; the Arabic form Masqaṭ is variously explained as 'anchorage' (from saqaṭa, 'to fall/drop anchor') or from Old Persian ('strong-scented').

b_matrah.first_mention_attestation: Documented as a distinct commercial harbor alongside Muscat in the 18th century CE (reign of Sayyid Sultan bin Ahmed, 1792–1804 CE) and in early 19th-century CE accounts.

morphemes.translation: place where something is cast/laid down; anchorage/emporium

b_matrah.etymology_analysis: From Arabic maṭraḥ ('place where goods/anchors are laid down'). Documented as a commercial port adjacent to Muscat from the late 18th century CE.

b_qalhat.first_mention_attestation: First attested in medieval travel literature by Marco Polo in the late 13th century CE (as Calatu) and Ibn Battuta in the 14th century CE.
b_qalhat.etymology_analysis: Medieval Indian Ocean port city in Oman, recorded as Calatu by Marco Polo (c. 1290 CE) and visited by Ibn Battuta in the 14th century CE.

b_sur.first_mention_attestation: Established by the 6th century CE (c. 550 CE) as a maritime trading center with East Africa.
b_sur.etymology_analysis: Ancient Omani port city on the Gulf of Oman, active in East African maritime trade by the 6th century CE.

b_jaalan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Jaʿlān (جعلان) in an official letter from Imam al-Muhanna ibn Jayfar al-Yahmadi (elected 226 AH / 840–841 CE) to the governor (wālī) of Ja'alan.
b_jaalan.etymology_analysis: Omani region in Ash Sharqiyah South; local tradition links the name to Arabic jaʿālah ('reward/grant') promised by Malik ibn Fahm al-Azdi, and it is documented in administrative correspondence of c. 841 CE.

b_nizwa.first_mention_attestation: Capital of Oman in the 6th–7th centuries CE; addressed in a 630 CE letter from the Prophet Muhammad inviting its inhabitants to Islam.

morphemes.translation: ancient oasis city name (disputed: 'solitude' or an old water spring)

b_nizwa.etymology_analysis: Ancient interior capital of Oman. Historians derive Nizwā either from the Arabic verb inzawā ('to be alone/secluded') or from the name of an ancient water spring.

b_bahla.first_mention_attestation: Ancient oasis town (pottery back to 2500 BCE); attested as an early Islamic scholarly center by the 2nd century AH / 8th century CE (e.g., Abu 'Ubayda 'Abdallah ibn al-Qasim).
b_bahla.etymology_analysis: One of the oldest oasis towns of interior Oman, active as an Islamic scholarly center by the 8th century CE.

b_samad.first_mention_attestation: Archaeological site of Samad al-Shan (Late Iron Age, c. 300 BCE–300 CE) first discovered and named in 1976 CE; no <= 867 CE written attestation of the name Samad.
b_samad.etymology_analysis: Modern village and archaeological type-site (Samad al-Shan) in Ash Sharqiyah, Oman, first surveyed in 1976 CE.

b_aqaba.first_mention_attestation: The name al-ʿAqabah (shortened from ʿaqabat ʿAylah, 'mountain-pass of Ayla') is first attested in the 12th century CE by al-Idrisi.
b_aqaba.etymology_analysis: From Arabic ʿaqabah ('mountain road, pass, ascent'), shortened from ʿaqabat ʿAylah as recorded by al-Idrisi in the 12th century CE.

historical_names.name: Elath
historical_names.source: Hebrew Bible (1 Kings 9:26, Eloth/Elath), Roman/Byzantine Aela/Aila (64 BCE), and early Islamic Ayla (629 CE).
historical_names.notes: Known in antiquity as Elath/Eloth and Berenice (and later Aila/Ayla, represented separately by b_aila) before the name al-ʿAqabah emerged in the 12th century CE.

historical_names.name: Berenice
historical_names.source: Hebrew Bible (1 Kings 9:26, Eloth/Elath), Roman/Byzantine Aela/Aila (64 BCE), and early Islamic Ayla (629 CE).
historical_names.notes: Known in antiquity as Elath/Eloth and Berenice (and later Aila/Ayla, represented separately by b_aila) before the name al-ʿAqabah emerged in the 12th century CE.

b_maqna.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Maqnā (مقنا) in 630 CE when the Prophet Muhammad concluded a peace treaty with its inhabitants during the Expedition of Tabuk.
b_maqna.etymology_analysis: Coastal oasis on the Gulf of Aqaba in southern Midian, attested in early Islamic sources from 630 CE.

b_ainun.first_mention_attestation: Attested as ʿAynūna (عينونة) in early Abbasid geographical works (Ibn Khordadbeh, c. 846 CE; al-Harbi) as a station on the coastal route from Ayla.
b_ainun.etymology_analysis: Derived from Arabic ʿayn ('spring/water source'), referring to the fresh-water oasis near the Red Sea coast, often identified with Nabataean Leuke Kome.

b_sharaf_al-bal.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Sharaf al-Baʿl (شرف البعل) in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE) on the coastal route south of Ayla.
b_sharaf_al-bal.etymology_analysis: Arabic compound meaning 'the ridge/high ground of al-Baʿl', recorded by Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE) and Yaqut al-Hamawi as a station/mountain along the Syrian/Egyptian coastal route.

b_madyan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Midian in the Hebrew Bible, Modiana in Ptolemy's Geography (2nd century CE), and Madyan (مدين) in the Quran and 7th-century CE Islamic sources.

morphemes.translation: ancient land and oasis of Midian

b_madyan.etymology_analysis: Ancient Northwest Arabian oasis and region (modern al-Badʿ), attested from Biblical Midian through Greco-Roman Modiana and Quranic/early Islamic Madyan.

b_ziba.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Ḍubāʾ (ضباء) by Abu Ishaq al-Harbi (198–285 AH / 813–898 CE) in Kitab al-Manasik (late 9th century CE, post-867 CE).

morphemes.translation: humid/sultry harbor (from ḍabba, 'to be hot and humid')

b_ziba.etymology_analysis: According to local Arabic tradition, derived from ḍabba ('sultry/humid weather'). First recorded in Muslim geographical literature by al-Harbi in the late 9th century CE.

b_maan.first_mention_attestation: Founded by the Minaeans (Maʿīn) between the 4th and 2nd centuries BCE; attested in early 7th-century CE Byzantine/Islamic accounts (Farwa ibn Amr al-Judhami, c. 630 CE).
b_maan.etymology_analysis: Named after the ancient South Arabian Minaean traders (Maʿīn) who established it as a caravan station between the 4th and 2nd centuries BCE.

b_al-humayma.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Ḥumaymah (الحميمة) in early Islamic history from c. 687 CE when Ali ibn Abdallah ibn al-Abbas settled the Abbasid family there.

morphemes.translation: diminutive of ḥammah ('warm spring') or ḥamām

b_al-humayma.etymology_analysis: Arabic toponym of the early Islamic settlement built on the Nabataean/Roman site of Hawara/Auara (founded c. 90 BCE, from Aramaic 'white').

b_adruh.first_mention_attestation: Nabataean settlement from at least the 1st century BCE; attested as Adrou (Άδρου) in Ptolemy (2nd century CE) and Udhruḥ (أذرح) in its 631 CE treaty with Muhammad.
b_adruh.etymology_analysis: Ancient Nabataean and Roman military station (Adrou) east of Petra, attested in Islamic sources from 631 CE and famous for the 658 CE arbitration.

b_tabuk.first_mention_attestation: Unambiguously attested as Tabūk (تبوك) in 630 CE during the Expedition of Tabuk (and possibly as Ptolemy's Tabawa in the 2nd century CE).
b_tabuk.etymology_analysis: Northwestern Arabian oasis town on the Syrian-Hijaz route, famous from the 630 CE Expedition of Tabuk.

b_sarj.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE for a settlement named Sarj in the Tabuk region.
b_sarj.etymology_analysis: Arabic sarj ('saddle'), unattested as a documented settlement in the Tabuk region <= 867 CE.

b_fajr.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Wādī Fajr is a modern/geographical valley name southeast of Tabuk.
b_fajr.etymology_analysis: Named after Wādī Fajr, a 170 km valley in the Tabuk region; unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.

b_tayma.first_mention_attestation: First attested by name in an Anatolian hieroglyphic inscription c. 800 BCE and in 8th-century BCE Assyrian inscriptions.
b_tayma.etymology_analysis: Major ancient oasis in northwestern Arabia, attested in Taymanitic, Anatolian, Assyrian (8th century BCE), and Neo-Babylonian (Nabonidus, 6th century BCE) records.

b_al-aqra.first_mention_attestation: Jabal al-Aqraʿ (جبل الأقرع) near al-Ula/Tayma bears over 450 early Arabic inscriptions, including the Zuhayr inscription dated 24 AH (644 CE).
b_al-aqra.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-aqraʿ ('the bald/bare one', referring to a vegetationless peak), a landmark mountain on the Syrian Hajj route with early Islamic inscriptions from 644 CE onward.

b_al-muhdatha.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; al-Muḥdathah (المحدثة) appears in later medieval Syrian Hajj route itineraries.
b_al-muhdatha.etymology_analysis: Arabic passive participle meaning 'the newly established/recent one', referring to a post-867 CE station/landmark on the Syrian Hajj route.

b_al-arid.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE with a dated primary citation for al-ʿĀriḍ (العارض) as a regional name in Najd.

morphemes.translation: the transverse ridge / barrier mountain (Tuwaiq escarpment)

b_al-arid.etymology_analysis: From Arabic ʿāriḍ ('that which lies across/blocks the horizon'), historically applied to the Tuwaiq escarpment (ʿĀriḍ al-Yamāmah) and its central Najd oases.

b_ubad.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Ubāḍ (أُبَاض) in early Islamic historical accounts of the Ridda Wars (Battle of Yamama / Day of Ubāḍ, 632 CE) and cited by Yaqut al-Hamawi.

morphemes.translation: historical village in al-ʿĀriḍ of al-Yamāmah

b_ubad.etymology_analysis: Historical village in al-ʿĀriḍ of al-Yamāmah, famous for its tall palm groves and as a battleground during Khalid ibn al-Walid's 632 CE campaign against Musaylima.

b_falaj.first_mention_attestation: First systematically documented as al-Falaj / al-Aflāj in 10th-century CE Arabic geographical works (e.g., al-Hamdani, c. 950 CE); no dated <= 867 CE written attestation.
b_falaj.etymology_analysis: From Arabic falaj ('running water channel / spring-fed oasis'), referring to the oasis network of southern Najd (al-Aflāj).

b_al-haddar.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Usama ibn Munqidh / Usama ibn Murshid al-Kinani's Kitab al-Manazil wa'l-Diyar (d. 584 AH / 1188 CE) as Wādī al-Haddār.
b_al-haddar.etymology_analysis: Named after Wādī al-Haddār in Al-Aflaj, derived from Arabic haddār ('roaring/gushing', referring to seasonal floodwaters); first documented in the 12th century CE.

b_qasr-al-adi.first_mention_attestation: First attested as al-Qaṣr al-ʿĀdī (القصر العادي) by Abu Muhammad al-Hamdani in the 4th century AH / 10th century CE (c. 950 CE).

morphemes.translation: ancient / of the people of ʿĀd

b_qasr-al-adi.etymology_analysis: Arabic 'the ancient fortress' (attributed in tradition to the ancient people of ʿĀd or Ṭasm and Jadīs), first described by al-Hamdani in the 10th century CE.

b_yamama.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Yamāmah (اليمامة) in pre-Islamic and early Islamic sources, notably as the center of the Battle of al-Yamama in December 632 CE.
b_yamama.etymology_analysis: Historical region of southeastern Najd; historian G. Rex Smith derives al-Yamāmah from the singular of Arabic yamām ('wild pigeons').

b_al-khadarim.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Jawn al-Khaḍārim (جون الخضارم) in early Islamic accounts of 684 CE when the Kharijite leader Abu Talut captured the Umayyad estate there.

morphemes.translation: abundant/vast (waters or lush estates, plural of khiḍrim)

b_al-khadarim.etymology_analysis: Arabic toponym for a major Umayyad agricultural estate in al-Yamāmah, attested from 684 CE.

b_al-kharj.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Kharj (الخرج) by Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE) as a way-station in al-Yamāmah, and became the Banu Ukhaidhir capital in 866 CE.
b_al-kharj.etymology_analysis: Historical oasis in al-Yamāmah, recorded by Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE) and made the seat of the Banu Ukhaidhir in 866 CE.

b_ad-dathina.first_mention_attestation: Attested as al-Dathīnah (الدثينة, later al-Dafīnah) in Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE) and al-Bukhari's al-Tarikh al-Kabir as a station on the Basra–Mecca Hajj route.

morphemes.translation: water-station / oasis in Banu Sulaym territory

b_ad-dathina.etymology_analysis: Early Islamic station on the Basra–Mecca pilgrimage route (Darb Zubayda) in Banu Sulaym territory, later known as al-Dafīnah.

b_marran.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Marrān (مرّان) in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE) as a station on the Basra–Mecca Hajj route.

morphemes.translation: station/oasis name (possibly from marra, 'to pass', or murn/spear-wood)

b_marran.etymology_analysis: Historic watering station and settlement in the Kishb area on the Basra–Mecca pilgrimage route, recorded by Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE).

b_subay.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE for the tribal/regional name Subayʿ (سبيع); the tribe traces its lineage to the older Banu ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿah.
b_subay.etymology_analysis: Arabic tribal name (diminutive of sabʿ), emerging in post-classical Najdi genealogy as a branch of Banu ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿah.

b_ranya.first_mention_attestation: First documented with a dated written reference in Yaqut al-Hamawi's Mu'jam al-Buldan (c. 1225 CE) as Ranyah (رنية).

morphemes.translation: oasis/valley name (linked by Yaqut to ranā, 'to gaze/remain')

b_ranya.etymology_analysis: Oasis town in Wādī Ranyah on the Najd–Asir borderlands; first attested in surviving dated sources in Yaqut al-Hamawi (c. 1225 CE).

b_bisha.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Bīshah (بيشة) on Abbasid silver dirhams minted there in 186 AH (802 CE) under Caliph Harun al-Rashid.
b_bisha.etymology_analysis: Major oasis and gold-mining district in southwestern Arabia, attested on Abbasid coinage from 802 CE and in al-Hamdani (10th century CE).

b_jurash.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Jurash (جرش) in 10 AH (631–632 CE) when a delegation from Jurash visited the Prophet Muhammad after the Battle of Jabal Shakr.
b_jurash.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic and early Islamic city in Asir on the Yemeni pilgrimage route, famous for leatherwork and siege engines, attested in 631–632 CE.

b_kuthba.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE for a settlement named Kuthba in the Bisha/Asir region.
b_kuthba.etymology_analysis: Arabic kuthbah ('sandhill/mound'), unattested as a documented settlement in the Bisha region <= 867 CE.

b_valashkert.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 2nd century CE (c. 160 CE) by Arsacid King Vologases I (Vagharsh I) of Armenia as Vagharshakert / Valarshakert on the site of Urartian Anashe.

eponym.details: Named after King Vologases I (Vagharsh I) of Armenia (r. c. 117–144 CE / Arsacid founder).

b_valashkert.etymology_analysis: Armenian Valarshakert / Vagharshakert ('built by Vologases/Vagharsh'), later contracted to Alashkert (modern Eleşkirt).

historical_names.name: Anashe
historical_names.source: Urartian inscriptions (c. 8th century BCE)
historical_names.notes: Built on the site of the earlier Urartian settlement Anashe.

b_bagavan.first_mention_attestation: Pre-Christian Armenian temple town attested in early 4th century CE Christianization accounts (Tiridates III baptized by Gregory the Illuminator) and in 371 CE at the Battle of Bagavan (Ammianus Marcellinus; Faustus of Byzantium).
b_bagavan.etymology_analysis: Old Armenian Bagawan ('town of the gods'), reflecting its role as a major pre-Christian Zoroastrian/Armenian pagan sanctuary.

b_tsalakert.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Tsalakert in Bagrewand.
b_tsalakert.etymology_analysis: Toponym ending in Armenian -kert ('built/founded by'), unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources for Bagrewand.

b_patnos.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the name Patnos (Armenian Badnots); nearby Aznavurtepe bears Urartian inscriptions naming the city Aludiri (late 9th century BCE).
b_patnos.etymology_analysis: Modern Turkish Patnos from Armenian Badnots; the modern toponym has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE, though the plain has Urartian remains from c. 810–786 BCE.

historical_names.name: Aludiri
historical_names.source: Urartian inscription of King Minua at Aznavurtepe (r. c. 810–786 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Aznavurtepe (2 km northwest of Patnos) preserves Urartian cuneiform inscriptions naming the city Aludiri.

b_dvin.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 335 CE by King Khosrov III Kotak of Armenia as the royal capital; later host to the Councils of Dvin (506 CE, 607 CE).
b_dvin.etymology_analysis: Derived from an Iranian/Armenian word meaning 'hill', referring to the mound on which the citadel was built.

b_naxcivan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE) as Naxuana and in Pawstos Buzand (5th century CE) as Naxchawan.
b_naxcivan.etymology_analysis: Old Armenian Naxchawan ('town of Naxch'), Hellenized by Ptolemy as Naxuana.

b_garni.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Tacitus's Annals (for 51 CE events) as Gorneas and in a 1st-century CE Greek inscription of King Tiridates I (77 CE).
b_garni.etymology_analysis: Old Armenian Gaṙni, recorded as Gorneas in Tacitus and linked to Urartian-era fortified settlement.

b_ani.first_mention_attestation: First attested as a fortress in 5th-century CE Armenian historians (Yeghishe and Ghazar Parpetsi).

morphemes.translation: uncertain (possibly connected to deity Anahit or Iranian *ana-)

b_ani.etymology_analysis: Old Armenian Ani, attested from the 5th century CE as a fortress of the Kamsarakan princes before becoming the Bagratid capital in 961 CE.

b_dlim.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Dlim.
b_dlim.etymology_analysis: Unattested in pre-867 CE Armenian or classical historical sources.

b_bagaran.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 200 BCE during the Orontid dynasty (recorded by Movses Khorenatsi as a major religious center).
b_bagaran.etymology_analysis: Old Armenian Bagaran ('place of the gods'), founded as a pagan temple center in the Orontid period.

b_kumayri.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Kumayri in 773 CE Armenian chronicles (Ghevond) and linked to the 8th-century BCE Urartian toponym.

morphemes.translation: settlement name (possibly linked to Cimmerians / Gimirri)

b_kumayri.etymology_analysis: Ancient name of Gyumri, preserved as Kumayri in 8th-century CE Armenian chronicles and traced to the Urartian period.

b_yerevan.first_mention_attestation: Earliest reference to the form Yerevan (Erewan) in Armenian written sources is 607 CE in the Book of Letters (Girk Tghtots).
b_yerevan.etymology_analysis: Evolved from Urartian Erebuni (founded 782 BCE by Argishti I) via *Erevuni to Armenian Erewan (Yerevan).

historical_names.name: Erebuni
historical_names.source: Urartian foundation inscription of Argishti I (782 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Urartian fortress founded in 782 BCE, direct linguistic predecessor of Yerevan.

b_parnes.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Parnes (Kusti Parnes) / Parisos in the 7th-century CE Armenian Geography (Ashkharhatsuyts).
b_parnes.etymology_analysis: Armenian P'aṙnes / Parisos, attested in the 7th-century CE Ashkharhatsuyts as a district and fortress in Gardman/Artsakh.

b_tovuz.first_mention_attestation: Tavush fortress is first mentioned in historical records in the 10th century CE (reign of King Ashot II of Armenia, r. 914–928 CE); Tovuz is the later Turkicized form.
b_tovuz.etymology_analysis: Azerbaijani Tovuz derives from Armenian Tavush, a medieval fortress first attested in 10th-century CE Armenian chronicles.

b_shamkur.first_mention_attestation: Known since the 5th century CE as Shamkor; restored by Abbasid general Bugha al-Kabir in 854–855 CE.
b_shamkur.etymology_analysis: Ancient Caucasian Albanian/Armenian city attested from the 5th century CE, briefly renamed al-Mutawakkiliyya in 854–855 CE.

b_gardman.first_mention_attestation: Canton and fortress of Utik attested in 387 CE when acquired by Caucasian Albania, and in 7th-century Mihranid records.
b_gardman.etymology_analysis: Historical canton and fortress of Utik (Gardman), attested in early medieval Armenian and Caucasian Albanian sources from the 4th century CE.

b_gandzasar.first_mention_attestation: Monastery built between 1216 and 1238 CE by Hasan-Jalal Dawla, prince of Khachen.
b_gandzasar.etymology_analysis: Armenian Gandzasar ('treasure mountain'), referring to the hill overlooking Vank where the 13th-century CE monastery stands.

b_ktis.first_mention_attestation: Fortress of Qtish (Ktish) first attested in Tovma Artsruni's History for the 853 CE siege by Abbasid general Bugha al-Kabir.
b_ktis.etymology_analysis: Armenian fortress name Qtish/Ktish, attested in 9th-century CE sources for the 853 CE defense by Lord Yesayi Abu-Muse.

b_kapan.first_mention_attestation: Area of modern-day Kapan first mentioned in the 5th century CE as a settlement in Syunik.
b_kapan.etymology_analysis: From Armenian kapan ('narrow valley' or 'gorge/pass'), describing its enclosed mountain valley setting.

b_goris.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in an Urartian cuneiform inscription of King Rusa I (r. 735–713 BCE) as Goristsa.
b_goris.etymology_analysis: Linked to Urartian Goristsa (8th century BCE) and Armenian variants Kores/Gorayk meaning a rocky place.

b_jugha.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Jugha in Movses Khorenatsi's History of Armenia (traditionally dated 5th century CE, or 7th–8th century CE) in connection with Tigranes the Great.
b_jugha.etymology_analysis: Old Armenian Jugha (later Persian/Turkicized Julfa), an ancient settlement on the Aras River.

b_kars.first_mention_attestation: Entered Bagratid domains at some point in the 9th century CE, attested at least by 888 CE; no documented written attestation strictly <= 867 CE for the city name Kars.
b_kars.etymology_analysis: Possibly from Georgian kari ('gate') or Armenian Kaṛuts berd ('fortress of Kaṛuts'); the district around Kars was known earlier as Vanand and Chorzene.

historical_names.name: Chorzene
historical_names.source: Strabo, Geography (1st century CE) for Chorzene; Sebeos (7th century CE) for Vanand
historical_names.notes: Regional names attested <= 867 CE for the Kars area prior to the 888 CE attestation of Kars itself.

historical_names.name: Vanand
historical_names.source: Strabo, Geography (1st century CE) for Chorzene; Sebeos (7th century CE) for Vanand
historical_names.notes: Regional names attested <= 867 CE for the Kars area prior to the 888 CE attestation of Kars itself.

b_zariskat.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Zarishat in Pawstos Buzand's 5th-century CE History of the Armenians for 4th-century CE Sasanian campaigns.

eponym.details: Traditionally associated with Orontid king Zariadres (Zareh).

b_zariskat.etymology_analysis: Old Armenian Zarishat ('joy of Zareh/Zariadres'), an ancient city in Vanand.

b_sevuki.first_mention_attestation: Fortress of Sevuk first attested in 978 CE when Bardas Skleros ceded border districts and Sevuk to David III of Tao.
b_sevuki.etymology_analysis: Armenian Sevuk ('little black one'), a medieval fortress first attested in 978 CE.

b_melitene.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Melitene in Strabo's Geography (1st century CE, c. 20 CE) and later Roman/Byzantine sources (Battle of Melitene, 576 CE).

morphemes.translation: city name (possibly linked to 'honey' / Hittite malit-)

b_melitene.etymology_analysis: Greek Melitene continues Hittite Malidiya and Akkadian Meliddu (modern Malatya).

historical_names.name: Malidiya
historical_names.source: Hittite and Neo-Assyrian cuneiform records (2nd–1st millennium BCE)
historical_names.notes: Bronze/Iron Age predecessor forms of classical Melitene.

historical_names.name: Meliddu
historical_names.source: Hittite and Neo-Assyrian cuneiform records (2nd–1st millennium BCE)
historical_names.notes: Bronze/Iron Age predecessor forms of classical Melitene.

b_arguvan.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 844–863 CE as Argaoun by the Paulician leader Karbeas under the protection of Umar al-Aqta of Melitene.
b_arguvan.etymology_analysis: Medieval Greek Argaoun (modern Turkish Arguvan), established as a Paulician stronghold in the mid-9th century CE.

b_arsamosata.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 240 BCE by Orontid King Arsames I of Sophene.

eponym.details: Named after King Arsames I of Sophene (r. c. 240 BCE).

morphemes.language: Old Armenian / Greek adaptation (from Iranian šāti-)

b_arsamosata.etymology_analysis: Greek Arsamosata from Armenian Aršamošat ('joy of Arsames').

b_arca.first_mention_attestation: Roman colonia of Arca attested from the 2nd century CE (under Hadrian/Marcus Aurelius) and as a bishopric at the Council of Ephesus (431 CE).
b_arca.etymology_analysis: Roman/Byzantine Arca (modern Akçadağ / Arga), attested since the 2nd century CE.

b_tzimisca.first_mention_attestation: Named after Byzantine Emperor John I Tzimiskes (c. 925–976 CE, r. 969–976 CE), who was born there (modern Çemişgezek).

eponym.details: Named after Byzantine Emperor John I Tzimiskes (born c. 925 CE, reigned 969–976 CE), whose sobriquet Tzimiskes (Armenian Chmshkik) gave rise to Tzimisca / Çemişgezek.

morphemes.translation: short boot / personal sobriquet of John I Tzimiskes

b_tzimisca.etymology_analysis: Derived from the sobriquet of 10th-century CE Byzantine Emperor John I Tzimiskes (post-867 CE eponym).

b_camacha.first_mention_attestation: Ancient Ani-Kamakh (Kamacha), Arsacid royal necropolis attested in 5th-century CE Armenian histories and 679 CE Muslim conquest records.
b_camacha.etymology_analysis: Old Armenian Kamax (Byzantine Kamacha, modern Kemah), a major frontier fortress on the Upper Euphrates.

b_koloberd.first_mention_attestation: Armenian variant Koghoberd (Keghi / Kiğı) is first documented in 15th-century CE sources (1432 CE Aqquyunlu inscription and 1464 CE Armenian colophon); no attestation <= 867 CE for Koghoberd itself.
b_koloberd.etymology_analysis: Armenian Koghoberd ('fortress of Kogho/Keghi'), an alternate name for Kiğı attested from the 15th century CE.

historical_names.name: Khorzianene
historical_names.source: 6th–7th century CE Byzantine and Armenian sources (Procopius; Ashkharhatsuyts)
historical_names.notes: Historical district name for the Keghi/Kiğı region prior to 867 CE.

historical_names.name: Khortsenk
historical_names.source: 6th–7th century CE Byzantine and Armenian sources (Procopius; Ashkharhatsuyts)
historical_names.notes: Historical district name for the Keghi/Kiğı region prior to 867 CE.

b_balu.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Urartian Palua (9th–8th century BCE) and later as Palios in 7th-century CE George of Cyprus.
b_balu.etymology_analysis: Continues Urartian Palua and Byzantine Palios, capital of medieval Balabitene (modern Palu).

b_theodosiopolis.first_mention_attestation: Founded/renamed Theodosiopolis c. 415–422 CE by the Eastern Roman Empire under Emperor Theodosius II.

eponym.details: Named after Roman Emperor Theodosius II (r. 402–450 CE).

b_theodosiopolis.etymology_analysis: Greek Theodosioupolis ('city of Theodosius'), built at the older Armenian settlement of Karin.

historical_names.name: Karin
historical_names.source: Classical Armenian sources (5th century CE)
historical_names.notes: Native Armenian name of the city prior to and alongside the Roman foundation Theodosiopolis.

b_speri.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Syspiritis in Strabo's Geography (1st century CE, c. 20 CE) and as Sper/Speri in early Armenian and Georgian sources.
b_speri.etymology_analysis: Derived from the ancient ethnonym/choronym Saspeires / Syspiritis (modern İspir).

b_martyropolis.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Martyropolis in the early 5th century CE (c. 410 CE) by Bishop Marutha, who brought relics of Christian martyrs there.
b_martyropolis.etymology_analysis: Greek Martyropolis ('city of martyrs'), replacing/coexisting with Syriac Maipherqat (Armenian Np'rkert, Arabic Mayyafariqin).

historical_names.name: Maipherqat
historical_names.source: Syriac and 5th-century CE Armenian sources
historical_names.notes: Pre-existing Syriac/Armenian name of the settlement (modern Silvan).

historical_names.name: Nprkert
historical_names.source: Syriac and 5th-century CE Armenian sources
historical_names.notes: Pre-existing Syriac/Armenian name of the settlement (modern Silvan).

b_musch.first_mention_attestation: Ancient Armenian capital of Taron attested in 5th-century CE Armenian historiography (Pawstos Buzand, Movses Khorenatsi) and late 8th-century Bagratid records.

morphemes.language: Old Armenian (possibly linked to Mushki / mshush, 'fog')

b_musch.etymology_analysis: Armenian Mush, variously connected by scholars to the ancient Mushki people or Armenian mshush ('fog').

b_tatvan.first_mention_attestation: Earliest documented written mention of Tatvan is 939–940 CE in connection with Hamdanid ruler Sayf al-Dawla.
b_tatvan.etymology_analysis: Toponym on the western shore of Lake Van; although the citadel has Urartian-era remains, the name Tatvan is first documented in 939–940 CE.

b_khlat.first_mention_attestation: The Armenian name Khlat (Խլաթ) is documented since 788 CE (Greek Chalata, Arabic Akhlat).
b_khlat.etymology_analysis: Armenian Khlat (documented 788 CE), adapted into Arabic as Akhlat and modern Turkish as Ahlat.

b_manzikert.first_mention_attestation: Documented as Manazkert / Manzikert from 390 CE (earlier Manavazakert in Movses Khorenatsi).

eponym.details: Tradition attributes foundation to Manavaz (descendant of Hayk), likely reflecting Urartian King Minua (r. c. 810–786 BCE).

b_manzikert.etymology_analysis: Armenian Manazkert ('fortress of Manavaz/Minua'), Hellenized as Manzikert (modern Malazgirt).

b_arjesh.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 775 CE at the Battle of Arjesh during the Armenian rebellion against the Abbasid Caliphate (also classical Arsissa).
b_arjesh.etymology_analysis: Armenian Arčēš (Arabic Arjish, Byzantine Arzes, modern Turkish Erciş), continuing classical Arsissa.

historical_names.name: Arsissa
historical_names.source: Classical Greco-Roman geographers (1st century CE)
historical_names.notes: Classical form of the town and lake name.

b_varto.first_mention_attestation: Earliest documented written mention of Varto is in 1554 CE as Varto kavar ('Vart's district').

eponym.details: Linked to the Armenian personal name Vart / Vartan (no specific post-867 historical figure identified).
