b_varto.etymology_analysis: Armenian Vardo/Varto, recorded in 1554 CE; the town was also known as Gyumgyum / Gimgim.

b_mardali.first_mention_attestation: District of Mardaghi / Mardali attested in the 7th-century CE Armenian Geography (Ashkharhatsuyts) in Turuberan.
b_mardali.etymology_analysis: Armenian Mardaghi/Mardali, named after the ancient Mardoi tribe inhabiting the region (modern Tekman).

b_khinisi.first_mention_attestation: No information reported in ancient Armenian sources; first written mention of Hınıs / Khnus fortress is the testimony of an Italian traveler in 1471–1478 CE.
b_khinisi.etymology_analysis: Modern Hınıs (Armenian Khnus, CK3 Khinisi) derives from Arabic hisn ('castle/fortress') and is first attested in the 15th century CE.

b_van.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned as Van (and Tosp) in Movses Khorenatsi's History of Armenia (c. 480 CE) and in 7th-century CE Sebeos.
b_van.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Urartian endonym Biaina/Biainili (9th century BCE), reshaped in Armenian as Van.

historical_names.name: Tushpa
historical_names.source: Urartian royal inscriptions of Sarduri I (9th century BCE)
historical_names.notes: Tushpa was the Urartian capital on the Rock of Van; Biaina is the phonetic ancestor of Van.

historical_names.name: Biaina
historical_names.source: Urartian royal inscriptions of Sarduri I (9th century BCE)
historical_names.notes: Tushpa was the Urartian capital on the Rock of Van; Biaina is the phonetic ancestor of Van.

b_berkri.first_mention_attestation: First documented in Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus's De Administrando Imperio (948–952 CE) as Perkri (referring to 9th-century Bagratid control).
b_berkri.etymology_analysis: Armenian Berkri (Byzantine Perkri, modern Muradiye), first attested in mid-10th-century CE Byzantine sources.

b_maku.first_mention_attestation: Maku was a region of old Armenia c. 300–800 CE (Artaz), with the Castle of Maku serving as seat of the Amatuni family.
b_maku.etymology_analysis: Of Armenian origin meaning 'pasture', seat of the Amatuni princes in Artaz.

historical_names.name: Shavarshan
historical_names.source: Early Armenian historiography (for Amatuni castle Shavarshan and Artaz district)
historical_names.notes: Original name of the Castle of Maku was Shavarshan in the Artaz district.

historical_names.name: Artaz
historical_names.source: Early Armenian historiography (for Amatuni castle Shavarshan and Artaz district)
historical_names.notes: Original name of the Castle of Maku was Shavarshan in the Artaz district.

b_akhtamar.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 10th-century CE Tovma Artsruni's History of the House of Artsrunik in connection with King Gagik I Artsruni's Cathedral of the Holy Cross (915–921 CE).
b_akhtamar.etymology_analysis: Armenian Aghtamar (possibly of Urartian origin), an island in Lake Van first documented in the 10th century CE.

b_hadamakert.first_mention_attestation: Documented as Adamakert since the 2nd century BCE (from Urartian Adamma) and contested between Parthia and Eastern Rome from 385 CE.

eponym.details: Folk etymology attributed it to Adam; actually from Urartian Adamma.

b_hadamakert.etymology_analysis: Armenian Hadamakert / Adamakert continues Urartian Adamma with Armenian -kert ('fortress', modern Başkale).

historical_names.name: Adamma
historical_names.source: Urartian-era toponym (1st millennium BCE)
historical_names.notes: Urartian town Adamma underlying Armenian Hadamakert.

b_amid.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Amedi/Amida in the annals of Assyrian King Adad-nirari I (c. 1310–1281 BCE); later Roman/Byzantine Amida and Arabic Amid.
b_amid.etymology_analysis: Derived from the ancient Assyrian/Aramaic toponym Amedi (Amida), attested since the late 2nd millennium BCE and adapted into Greek Amida, Syriac Amid, and Arabic Amid.

b_zermion.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; corresponds to Cermik (Armenian Jermuk, 'hot springs'), documented only in later medieval and Ottoman periods.
b_zermion.etymology_analysis: Hellenized/Byzantine adaptation (Zermion) of Armenian Jermuk ('hot springs', from jerm 'warm'), referring to the natural thermal springs of modern Cermik.

b_as-suwaida.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as al-Suwayda by 867 CE; corresponds to Siverek (Armenian Sevaverag, medieval Arabic Hisn al-Ran), first documented in Byzantine/Arabic sources after 956 CE.
b_as-suwaida.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Suwayda' ('the little black one', feminine diminutive of aswad 'black'), reflecting the black basaltic ruins also expressed in Armenian Sevaverag ('black ruins', modern Siverek).

b_tall_mauzan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Syriac Tella de-Mawzelat (direct basis of Arabic Tall Mawzan) in 615–617 CE in the colophon of Paul of Tella's Syro-Hexapla; earlier known as Constantia (349 CE).
b_tall_mauzan.etymology_analysis: Arabic Tall Mawzan renders Syriac Tella de-Mawzelat ('mound of Mawzelat'), the local Semitic name of Roman Constantia (modern Viransehir).

historical_names.name: Constantia
historical_names.source: Roman and Late Antique sources (Constantia, named by Constantius II in 349 CE)
historical_names.notes: Greco-Roman Constantia/Constantina (349 CE) and short Syriac Tella preceded the compound Tella de-Mawzelat / Tall Mawzan.

historical_names.name: Antoninopolis
historical_names.source: Roman and Late Antique sources (Constantia, named by Constantius II in 349 CE)
historical_names.notes: Greco-Roman Constantia/Constantina (349 CE) and short Syriac Tella preceded the compound Tella de-Mawzelat / Tall Mawzan.

historical_names.name: Tella
historical_names.source: Roman and Late Antique sources (Constantia, named by Constantius II in 349 CE)
historical_names.notes: Greco-Roman Constantia/Constantina (349 CE) and short Syriac Tella preceded the compound Tella de-Mawzelat / Tall Mawzan.

b_hani.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Arabic geographical literature by al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE), followed by Ibn Hawqal (c. 977 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE).
b_hani.etymology_analysis: From Kurdish Heni ('fountain, spring'), Arabicized as Hani.

b_hisn_di-l-qarnain.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; medieval Arabic fortress name associated with the Birkleyn Caves / Tigris source north of Amid.

eponym.details: Named after Dhu al-Qarnayn ('He of the Two Horns'), the Quranic figure commonly identified with Alexander the Great (356–323 BCE).

morphemes.translation: of the Two-Horned One (genitive of Dhu al-Qarnayn)

b_hisn_di-l-qarnain.etymology_analysis: Arabic compound Hisn Dhi'l-Qarnayn ('Fortress of the Two-Horned One'), referring to the legendary association of Alexander the Great / Dhu al-Qarnayn with the Upper Tigris caves (Birkleyn).

b_qulb.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; corresponds to Kulp (Armenian Khulp, Ottoman Turkish Qulb), documented only in later medieval and Ottoman periods.
b_qulb.etymology_analysis: Ottoman Turkish Qulb (modern Kulp), corresponding to Armenian Khulp, of uncertain pre-Ottoman etymology.

b_erkne.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Arghana in accounts of the Battle of Arghana (956 CE) between Hamdanid ruler Sayf al-Dawla and Byzantine general John Tzimiskes.
b_erkne.etymology_analysis: Medieval form of Ergani (Armenian Arghn, Arabic Arghana), attested in 10th-century CE Arab-Byzantine campaigns.

b_shimshat.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 240 BCE as Arsamosata (Armenian Aršamašat) by Orontid king Arsames I; attested in Arabic as Shimshat in 9th-century CE accounts (e.g., Siege of Arsamosata, 837 CE).

eponym.details: Named after Arsames I, Orontid king of Sophene and Commagene (r. c. 260–228 BCE); Middle Persian *Aršāmšād* means 'Joy of Arsames'.

b_shimshat.etymology_analysis: Arabic Shimshat derives via Armenian Ashmushat/Aršamašat from Middle Persian *Aršāmšād* ('Joy of Arsames'), founded by Arsames I c. 240 BCE.

b_hakkari.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Hakariyye/al-Hakkariyya as early as 639 CE during the Muslim conquests.

eponym.details: Named after the local Kurdish tribe of Hakkari.

morphemes.translation: ethnonym of the Hakkari Kurdish tribe

b_hakkari.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Kurdish tribal name Hakkari (Syriac Hakkari, Arabic al-Hakkariyya), attested for the mountainous region from 639 CE.

b_baqirda.first_mention_attestation: Attested in al-Baladhuri's Futuh al-Buldan for the 640 CE Muslim conquest under 'Iyad ibn Ghanm and listed by Ibn Khordadbeh (864 CE).
b_baqirda.etymology_analysis: Arabic Baqirda (Bakirda) derives from Aramaic/Syriac Beth Qardu ('territory of Qardu/Corduene'), the ancient district opposite Jazirat Ibn 'Umar.

historical_names.name: Bezabda
historical_names.source: Ammianus Marcellinus (360 CE siege of Bezabda)
historical_names.notes: The Roman fortress of Bezabda stood in the Bakirda district on the west bank of the Tigris.

historical_names.name: Phoenica
historical_names.source: Ammianus Marcellinus (360 CE siege of Bezabda)
historical_names.notes: The Roman fortress of Bezabda stood in the Bakirda district on the west bank of the Tigris.

b_tamanin.first_mention_attestation: First securely attested in contemporary geographical writing by al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE) as Thamanin at the foot of Mount Judi.

morphemes.translation: eighty (from Islamic tradition of eighty companions of Noah)

b_tamanin.etymology_analysis: Arabic Thamanin ('Eighty', short for Qaryat al-Thamanin 'Village of the Eighty'), named after the eighty companions of Noah said to have settled at the foot of Mount Judi.

b_saird.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Saird / Sirte in pre-Islamic Byzantine and Syriac ecclesiastical records (prior to the mid-7th century CE; Chronicle of Seert).
b_saird.etymology_analysis: From pre-Islamic Syriac/Byzantine Saird / Sirte (Arabic Si'ird, Armenian Sgherd, modern Turkish Siirt).

b_juza.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: unidentified local toponym (cf. jawz 'walnut' or 'Ayn Guza)

b_juza.etymology_analysis: Unverified local toponym in the Hakkari/Upper Tigris region; no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_mayyafariqin.first_mention_attestation: Known in Arabic as Mayyafariqin following the 640 CE Muslim conquest (al-Baladhuri); earlier founded as Tigranocerta (1st century BCE) and renamed Martyropolis c. 400 CE.

morphemes.translation: city/place suffix in Arabized Syriac toponym

b_mayyafariqin.etymology_analysis: Arabic Mayyafariqin derives from Syriac Maipherqat/Mepharqeta (itself associated with Byzantine Martyropolis, 'City of the Martyrs').

historical_names.name: Tigranocerta
historical_names.source: Classical Greco-Roman and Armenian sources (Tigranocerta, 1st century BCE; Martyropolis, c. 400 CE)
historical_names.notes: Founded by Tigranes the Great in the 1st century BCE as Tigranocerta (later Martyropolis, represented separately by b_martyropolis).

b_tall_fafan.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Tall Fafan in 10th-century CE Arabic geographical works (Ibn Hawqal, c. 977 CE; al-Muqaddasi, c. 985 CE).

morphemes.translation: Fafan (proper name of the settlement at the Tigris-Botan confluence)

b_tall_fafan.etymology_analysis: Arabic Tall Fafan ('Mound of Fafan'), attested in 10th-century CE geographers for the mound at the confluence of the Botan and Tigris rivers (modern Cattepe).

b_arzan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Arzan in al-Baladhuri's account of its surrender to 'Iyad ibn Ghanm in 640 CE (and earlier as classical Arzanene in the 4th century CE).
b_arzan.etymology_analysis: From ancient Armenian/Syriac Arzn (Greek Arzanene), Arabicized as Arzan after the 640 CE Muslim conquest.

b_nasriye.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 11th century CE (c. 1011–1061 CE) by Marwanid ruler Nasr al-Dawla Ahmad ibn Marwan as al-Madinat al-Nasriyya near Mayyafariqin.

eponym.details: Named after Nasr al-Dawla Ahmad ibn Marwan, Kurdish Marwanid emir of Mayyafariqin and Diyar Bakr (r. 1011–1061 CE).

b_nasriye.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Nasriyya (short for al-Madinat al-Nasriyya, 'the City of Nasr'), founded by and named after the 11th-century Marwanid amir Nasr al-Dawla Ahmad ibn Marwan.

b_tall_basma.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; documented in Syriac ecclesiastical lists as Tell Bashme northwest of Mardin.
b_tall_basma.etymology_analysis: Arabic Tall Basma from Syriac Tell Bashme ('Mound of Incense/Spices'), a settlement in the Tur 'Abdin / Mardin region.

b_hisn_kaifa.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Arabic as Hisn Kayfa following the Arab conquest of 640 CE; earlier known in Roman/Byzantine sources as Cepha/Kiphas (4th century CE).
b_hisn_kaifa.etymology_analysis: Arabic Hisn Kayfa ('Rock Fortress'), combining Arabic hisn ('fortress') with Syriac kefa ('rock'), later Turkified to Hasankeyf.

historical_names.name: Cepha
historical_names.source: Roman and Late Antique sources (4th century CE under Constantius II)
historical_names.notes: Latin/Greek Cepha/Kiphas (from Syriac kefa 'rock') preceded the Arabic compound Hisn Kayfa (640 CE).

historical_names.name: Kiphas
historical_names.source: Roman and Late Antique sources (4th century CE under Constantius II)
historical_names.notes: Latin/Greek Cepha/Kiphas (from Syriac kefa 'rock') preceded the Arabic compound Hisn Kayfa (640 CE).

historical_names.name: Castrum Cepha
historical_names.source: Roman and Late Antique sources (4th century CE under Constantius II)
historical_names.notes: Latin/Greek Cepha/Kiphas (from Syriac kefa 'rock') preceded the Arabic compound Hisn Kayfa (640 CE).

b_dausar.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Arabic historical tradition as Dawsar in pre-Islamic times (prior to the 7th century CE), before its 11th-century renaming to Qal'at Ja'bar.
b_dausar.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic Arabic toponym Dawsar for the Euphrates hilltop fortress later renamed Qal'at Ja'bar in the 11th century CE.

b_tall_ammar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE.
b_tall_ammar.etymology_analysis: Arabic compound Tall 'Ammar ('Mound of 'Ammar'); no pre-867 CE attestation in the Dausar/Euphrates region.

b_harran.first_mention_attestation: Attested since the late 3rd millennium BCE (c. 25th–20th centuries BCE, Ebla and Mari tablets) as Harran/Harranu.
b_harran.etymology_analysis: From Akkadian harranu ('road, caravan route'), reflecting its ancient position at the crossroads of Upper Mesopotamian trade routes; Hellenized as Carrhae and Arabicized as Harran.

b_saruj.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Syriac Srug/Serugh by the early 6th century CE (Bishop Jacob of Serugh, d. 521 CE) and in Arabic as Saruj upon its surrender in 639 CE.
b_saruj.etymology_analysis: From Syriac Srug (Serugh), Arabicized as Saruj after 639 CE (modern Turkish Suruc).

historical_names.name: Batnae
historical_names.source: Roman sources (Emperor Julian visited Tell-Batnan/Batnae in 363 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman and Byzantine sources referred to the settlement as Batnae or Tell-Batnan.

historical_names.name: Tell-Batnan
historical_names.source: Roman sources (Emperor Julian visited Tell-Batnan/Batnae in 363 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman and Byzantine sources referred to the settlement as Batnae or Tell-Batnan.

b_tall_mahra.first_mention_attestation: Attested by 818 CE as the birthplace of Syriac Orthodox Patriarch Dionysius I Telmaharoyo (Dionysius of Tell Mahre, r. 818–845 CE).
b_tall_mahra.etymology_analysis: Arabic Tall Mahra (Syriac Tell Mahre), an Abbasid-era town in the Balikh valley attested by the early 9th century CE.

b_raqqa.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Arabic as al-Raqqah following the 639 CE Muslim conquest (later Harun al-Rashid's Abbasid capital in 796–809 CE).

morphemes.translation: swampy/marshy land beside a river subject to flooding

b_raqqa.etymology_analysis: Descriptive Arabic toponym al-Raqqah ('the marshy riverbank'), applied after the 639 CE conquest to the site of Hellenistic/Roman Callinicum.

historical_names.name: Nikephorion
historical_names.source: Classical Greco-Roman sources (Seleucus II Callinicus, r. 246–225 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Founded in the Hellenistic period as Nikephorion and renamed Kallinikos/Callinicum by Seleucus II.

historical_names.name: Kallinikos
historical_names.source: Classical Greco-Roman sources (Seleucus II Callinicus, r. 246–225 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Founded in the Hellenistic period as Nikephorion and renamed Kallinikos/Callinicum by Seleucus II.

historical_names.name: Callinicum
historical_names.source: Classical Greco-Roman sources (Seleucus II Callinicus, r. 246–225 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Founded in the Hellenistic period as Nikephorion and renamed Kallinikos/Callinicum by Seleucus II.

b_bajarwan.first_mention_attestation: First securely attested in written sources by Ibn Hawqal (c. 977 CE) as a town in the Balikh valley already falling to ruin (though archaeologically/historically peaking in the late 8th/early 9th centuries CE).
b_bajarwan.etymology_analysis: Arabic Bajarwan, a town on the Balikh River between Raqqa and Tall Mahra.

b_ratla.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; modern village south of Raqqa.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name south of Raqqa

b_ratla.etymology_analysis: Modern Syrian village south of Raqqa without documented pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_makisin.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Maksin/Makisin in late 680s CE (c. 688–689 CE) accounts of the Qays–Taghlib feud along the Khabur River.
b_makisin.etymology_analysis: Medieval Khabur town Makisin (Maksin), likely related to Semitic maks ('toll/tax'), succeeded by modern Markada.

b_mijdal.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as Mijdal in written sources by 867 CE; corresponds to Semitic Magdalu/Majdal ('tower') on the lower Khabur (cf. Tell Sheikh Hamad / Dur-Katlimmu).
b_mijdal.etymology_analysis: From Semitic magdal/mijdal ('fortified elevation, tower'), a common toponym in the Khabur basin.

historical_names.name: Dur-Katlimmu
historical_names.source: Middle Assyrian cuneiform archives (13th century BCE)
historical_names.notes: Tell Sheikh Hamad on the lower Khabur was ancient Middle/Neo-Assyrian Dur-Katlimmu before later being known as Magdalu/Majdal.

b_araban.first_mention_attestation: First attested as 'Arban/'Araban in 10th-century CE Arabic geographical works (al-Istakhri c. 951 CE, Ibn Hawqal c. 977 CE, al-Muqaddasi c. 985 CE).
b_araban.etymology_analysis: Arabic 'Araban ('Arban), a walled cotton-producing town on the Khabur attested in 10th-century CE geographers, occupying the tell of ancient Shadikanni (Tell Ajaja).

historical_names.name: Shadikanni
historical_names.source: Neo-Assyrian inscriptions of Shalmaneser III (859–824 BCE) and Roman/Byzantine military records (Horaba)
historical_names.notes: Tell Ajaja was the Neo-Assyrian provincial capital Shadikanni and Roman/Byzantine Horaba.

historical_names.name: Horaba
historical_names.source: Neo-Assyrian inscriptions of Shalmaneser III (859–824 BCE) and Roman/Byzantine military records (Horaba)
historical_names.notes: Tell Ajaja was the Neo-Assyrian provincial capital Shadikanni and Roman/Byzantine Horaba.

b_al-khanuqa.first_mention_attestation: First attested as the city of al-Khanukah in Ibn Hawqal (c. 977 CE).
b_al-khanuqa.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Khanuqa ('the Strangler'), named after the narrow basalt gorge of the Euphrates flanked by Halabiye and Zalabiye.

historical_names.name: Halabit
historical_names.source: Ebla tablets (24th century BCE) and Roman/Palmyrene sources (3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: The Khanuqa gorge was fortified at Halabiye (ancient Halabit, 24th c. BCE; Palmyrene/Roman Zenobia, 3rd c. CE).

historical_names.name: Zenobia
historical_names.source: Ebla tablets (24th century BCE) and Roman/Palmyrene sources (3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: The Khanuqa gorge was fortified at Halabiye (ancient Halabit, 24th c. BCE; Palmyrene/Roman Zenobia, 3rd c. CE).

b_ash-shamsiya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE.
b_ash-shamsiya.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Shamsiyya ('solar / pertaining to the sun'), unattested in pre-867 CE Khabur records.

b_qarqisiya.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 256 CE in Shapur I's Ka'ba-ye Zartosht inscription (Parthian Krksy', Latin Circesium), and in Arabic as al-Qarqisiya from the 7th century CE (640/684 CE).
b_qarqisiya.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Qarqisiya derives via Syriac Qerqesin from Greco-Roman Circesium ('the castle with the circus'), located at the Khabur–Euphrates confluence.

b_mosul.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Arabic as al-Mawsil from the Muslim conquest of Upper Mesopotamia (637–641 CE).
b_mosul.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Mawsil ('the linking point / junction'), referring to its strategic position on the Tigris opposite ancient Nineveh.

historical_names.name: Mepsila
historical_names.source: Xenophon, Anabasis (401 BCE); Nineveh attested since c. 25th century BCE
historical_names.notes: Ancient Nineveh lies on the east bank opposite Mosul, and Xenophon recorded a settlement Mepsila on the Tigris in 401 BCE.

historical_names.name: Nineveh
historical_names.source: Xenophon, Anabasis (401 BCE); Nineveh attested since c. 25th century BCE
historical_names.notes: Ancient Nineveh lies on the east bank opposite Mosul, and Xenophon recorded a settlement Mepsila on the Tigris in 401 BCE.

b_ain_al-qayyara.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Ibn Jubayr's Rihla (1184 CE) as al-Qayyarah.
b_ain_al-qayyara.etymology_analysis: Arabic 'Ayn al-Qayyarah ('Spring of Tar/Bitumen'), named after the natural bitumen/oil springs south of Mosul.

b_al-hadr.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Hatran Aramaic inscriptions (ḥṭrʾ) from the late 1st century CE (c. 98 CE) and in Roman accounts of Trajan's siege in 117 CE; known in Arabic as al-Ḥaḍr.
b_al-hadr.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Ḥaḍr (الحضر) is the direct phonological and semantic continuation of Hatran Aramaic ḥṭrʾ (Ḥaṭrā, 'enclosure, hedge, fence') and Latin/Greek Hatra, attested from the late 1st century CE.

b_juhaina.first_mention_attestation: Described by the Arab geographer al-Muqaddasi (c. 985 CE) as Mar/Marj Juhayna, the first stage south of Mosul on the road to Baghdad, and later by Yaqut al-Hamawi (c. 1225 CE).

eponym.details: Named after the pre-Islamic Arab tribe of Juhayna (a branch of Quda'a) and its eponymous ancestor.

b_juhaina.etymology_analysis: Arabic Juhayna (جهينة) is a diminutive proper noun referring to the Arab tribe of Juhayna; the settlement on the Tigris south of Mosul (Marj Juhayna, 'meadow of Juhayna') is first attested in 10th-century CE Arabic geography.

b_tall_afar.first_mention_attestation: First attested under the Arabic name Tall A'far by 10th-century CE Arab geographers such as Ibn Hawqal (c. 977 CE) as a station on the road from Balad to Sinjar.
b_tall_afar.etymology_analysis: From Arabic tall ('settlement mound, hillock') and a'far ('dust-colored, reddish-white'). While the surrounding area has prehistoric mounds and has been tentatively linked to Assyrian Nemet-Ishtar, the name Tall A'far is first documented in the 10th century CE.

b_balad-mosul.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Akkadian as Balaṭ and in Syriac as Balad/Balaṭ, where a Church of the East diocese was established by 497 CE; later a major Abbasid town on the Tigris (disambiguated as Balad-Mosul).
b_balad-mosul.etymology_analysis: Derived from Akkadian Balaṭ and Syriac Balaṭ/Balad, attested as a bishopric by 497 CE (and known as Shahrābādh in Sasanian times per Yaqut). The hyphenated '-Mosul' suffix is a modern/game disambiguator distinguishing it from other places named Balad (modern Eski Mosul).

b_nasibin.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 901 BCE in Neo-Assyrian records as Naṣibīna, an Aramean kingdom captured by Adad-nirari II in 896 BCE; later classical Nisibis and Arabic Naṣībīn.
b_nasibin.etymology_analysis: Arabic Naṣībīn continues Aramaic Nṣībīn and Akkadian Naṣibīna (first attested 901 BCE), related to the Semitic root n-ṣ-b ('to set up, erect [pillars/posts]').

b_barqaid.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Ibn Serapion (c. 900 CE) and 10th-century CE Arab geographers (al-Istakhri c. 951 CE, Ibn Hawqal c. 977 CE, al-Muqaddasi c. 985 CE) as a major station between Balad and Nasibin.

morphemes.translation: toponym of obscure pre-Islamic or early Islamic origin

b_barqaid.etymology_analysis: Barqa'īd (برقعيد) is a medieval Jaziran toponym on the Mosul–Nisibis caravan road, possibly of Aramaic/Syriac substrate origin, first documented in surviving written sources around 900 CE.

b_gazirat_ibn_umar.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the mid-9th century CE (by c. 865 CE) by al-Hasan ibn 'Umar al-Taghlibi (d. c. 865 CE), Emir of Mosul, as Jazīrat Ibn ʿUmar.

eponym.details: Named after its 9th-century founder, al-Hasan ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khattab al-Taghlibi (d. c. 865 CE), Emir of Mosul.

morphemes.translation: son of Umar (al-Hasan ibn Umar al-Taghlibi)

b_gazirat_ibn_umar.etymology_analysis: Arabic Jazīrat Ibn ʿUmar ('island of the son of Umar'), referring to the manmade island/canal loop on the Tigris created by its founder al-Hasan ibn 'Umar al-Taghlibi (d. c. 865 CE); modern Turkish Cizre.

historical_names.name: Ad flumen Tigrim
historical_names.source: Ammianus Marcellinus (Res Gestae, 360 CE, for Bezabde) and Tabula Peutingeriana (4th/5th century CE, for Ad flumen Tigrim)
historical_names.notes: Roman fortress of Bezabde/Bazabda lay opposite or immediately adjacent to the 9th-century CE foundation on the Tigris.

historical_names.name: Bezabde
historical_names.source: Ammianus Marcellinus (Res Gestae, 360 CE, for Bezabde) and Tabula Peutingeriana (4th/5th century CE, for Ad flumen Tigrim)
historical_names.notes: Roman fortress of Bezabde/Bazabda lay opposite or immediately adjacent to the 9th-century CE foundation on the Tigris.

historical_names.name: Gāzartā d'Beṯ Zabdaï
historical_names.source: Ammianus Marcellinus (Res Gestae, 360 CE, for Bezabde) and Tabula Peutingeriana (4th/5th century CE, for Ad flumen Tigrim)
historical_names.notes: Roman fortress of Bezabde/Bazabda lay opposite or immediately adjacent to the 9th-century CE foundation on the Tigris.

b_dara.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Syriac Chronicle of Zacharias of Mytilene when East Roman Emperor Anastasius I fortified the village of Dara in 505 CE (renaming it Anastasiopolis).
b_dara.etymology_analysis: From Syriac Dārā (Greek Dáras), likely meaning 'court, enclosure, or dwelling'; rebuilt as a major East Roman frontier fortress in 505 CE.

b_ninawa.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Old Akkadian and 3rd–2nd millennium BCE cuneiform inscriptions (c. 2300 BCE; prominently mentioned c. 1800 BCE under Shamshi-Adad I) as Ninua/Ninuwā.

morphemes.translation: Nineveh (ancient city name, possibly linked to goddess Nina)

b_ninawa.etymology_analysis: Arabic Nīnawā (نينوى) directly preserves the ancient Akkadian name Ninua/Ninuwā (Syriac Nīnwē, Greek Nineuḗ), attested from the 3rd millennium BCE.

b_bartulla.first_mention_attestation: Earliest known written mention is by Father Potrus Qasha in 1153 CE regarding Maphrian Ignatius Elia'azar (1143–1164 CE), and later by Yaqut al-Hamawi (c. 1225 CE).

morphemes.translation: son of / place of (or variant of Bēṯ)

b_bartulla.etymology_analysis: Syriac Barṭullā / Barṭillā (Arabic Barṭalla), a Christian town in the Nineveh Plains first documented in written sources in 1153 CE.

b_fishabur.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 4th century CE as a Christian settlement (Syriac Pēšābūr), linked with the Sasanian name Peroz-Shapur.

eponym.details: Traditional etymology links Pēšābūr / Faysh Khabur to Sasanian king Shapur (Peroz-Shapur), later blended with the Khabur River.

morphemes.translation: Shapur (king's name), assimilated to the Khabur River

b_fishabur.etymology_analysis: Medieval Arabic Faysābūr / Faysh Khābūr (Syriac Pēšābūr) derives from Sasanian Peroz-Shapur ('Victorious is Shapur'), attested from the 4th century CE and later folk-etymologically assimilated to the Khabur River.

b_sinjar.first_mention_attestation: First attested in classical sources in the early 2nd century CE as Singara during Emperor Trajan's Parthian campaign (114–115 CE); later Syriac Shiggār (diocese by 563 CE) and Arabic Sinjār.
b_sinjar.etymology_analysis: Arabic Sinjār (سنجار) continues Syriac Shiggār and Greco-Roman Singara, attested as a fortified Roman outpost from the early 2nd century CE.

b_bashazza.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in medieval Arabic geographical itineraries as a station near Barqa'id on the Mosul–Nisibis road (noted by J. M. Fiey); no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_bashazza.etymology_analysis: From Syriac Bēṯ Shazzā > Arabic Bāshazzā, a medieval station in Upper Mesopotamia along the Mosul–Nisibis route; unattested in surviving sources prior to 867 CE.

b_al-hayyal.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation found in historical or medieval geographical sources <= 867 CE.
b_al-hayyal.etymology_analysis: Arabic-form toponym al-Hayyāl in the Sinjar region; no pre-867 CE written attestation or established historical etymology is documented.

b_al-jibal.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation found as a specific settlement in the Sinjar district <= 867 CE (al-Jibāl is a generic Arabic plural meaning 'the mountains').
b_al-jibal.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Jibāl ('the mountains'), a generic oronymic term (historically applied to Media/Zagros, or locally to the Sinjar Mountains); unattested as a barony/settlement name in Sinjar by 867 CE.

b_tunamir.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation found in historical or medieval geographical sources <= 867 CE.
b_tunamir.etymology_analysis: Tunamir is an obscure/unattested toponym assigned to the Sinjar county; no written attestation <= 867 CE has been found.

b_ras_al-ain.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Arabic Ra's al-'Ayn in accounts of the 7th-century CE Muslim conquest (c. 640 CE, al-Baladhuri); the same site was earlier attested as Sikkan (c. 2000 BCE) and Roman Resaina (2nd century CE).
b_ras_al-ain.etymology_analysis: Arabic Ra's al-'Ayn ('head of the spring', paralleling Syriac Rēš 'Aynā and Roman Resaina), referring to the numerous karstic springs feeding the Khabur River.

historical_names.name: Sikkan
historical_names.source: Tell Fekherye / cuneiform records (c. 2000 BCE for Sikkan) and Ptolemy (2nd century CE for Raisena/Resaina)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Aramean/Hurrian Sikkan and Greco-Roman Resaina / Theodosiopolis (380 CE) at the same site.

historical_names.name: Resaina
historical_names.source: Tell Fekherye / cuneiform records (c. 2000 BCE for Sikkan) and Ptolemy (2nd century CE for Raisena/Resaina)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Aramean/Hurrian Sikkan and Greco-Roman Resaina / Theodosiopolis (380 CE) at the same site.

historical_names.name: Theodosiopolis
historical_names.source: Tell Fekherye / cuneiform records (c. 2000 BCE for Sikkan) and Ptolemy (2nd century CE for Raisena/Resaina)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Aramean/Hurrian Sikkan and Greco-Roman Resaina / Theodosiopolis (380 CE) at the same site.

b_mardin.first_mention_attestation: First attested by Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus (Res Gestae, XIX.9.4) in 359 CE as the fortress of Maride/Marida.
b_mardin.etymology_analysis: Arabic Mārdīn (ماردين) derives from Syriac Mardīn / merdā ('fortress'), attested in Latin as Maride/Marida in 359 CE.

b_kafartutha.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 9th-century CE Abbasid historiography and geography, including al-Tabari's History (Vol. 35, events of the 860s CE) and Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846–885 CE).
b_kafartutha.etymology_analysis: Arabic Kafartūthā directly adapts Syriac Kfar Tūṯā ('village of the mulberry tree'), a documented road junction southwest of Mardin in 9th-century CE sources.

b_al-haditha-furat.first_mention_attestation: Founded during the Caliphate of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (634–644 CE) as al-Haditha ('the New Town') on the Euphrates, recorded by al-Baladhuri and Yaqut al-Hamawi.
b_al-haditha-furat.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Ḥadītha ('the new [town]') with the river disambiguator Furāt ('Euphrates') to distinguish it from al-Ḥadītha on the Tigris; founded in the mid-7th century CE.

b_ana.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Ha-na-at in Old Babylonian cuneiform texts (c. 1800 BCE), A-na-at in Neo-Assyrian inscriptions (885 BCE), Anatha in Ammianus Marcellinus (363 CE), and Arabic 'Āna (657 CE).

eponym.details: Connected in scholarship with the ancient Semitic war goddess Anat.

morphemes.translation: ancient city name (linked to goddess Anat)

b_ana.etymology_analysis: Arabic 'Āna (عانة) continues Old Babylonian Ha-na-at and Neo-Assyrian A-na-at (associated with the goddess Anat), continuously attested on the Middle Euphrates since the 2nd millennium BCE.

b_hadithat-ana.first_mention_attestation: Medieval Arabic geographical designation (Ḥadīthat 'Āna, 'Haditha of Ana') for al-Haditha on the Euphrates, founded during the Caliphate of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (634–644 CE).
b_hadithat-ana.etymology_analysis: Arabic Ḥadīthat 'Āna ('the New Town near Ana'), an alternative medieval Arabic name (alongside Ḥadīthat al-Furāt and Ḥadīthat al-Nūra) for Haditha on the Euphrates.

b_sukayr_al-abbas.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 10th-century CE Arabic geographers (Ibn Hawqal c. 977 CE, al-Muqaddasi c. 985 CE) and Yaqut al-Hamawi (c. 1225 CE) as the dam/town of Sukayr al-'Abbās on the Hirmas/Khabur.

eponym.details: Named after an individual called al-'Abbās (likely an Abbasid-era builder or patron of the weir/dam).

b_sukayr_al-abbas.etymology_analysis: Arabic Sukayr al-'Abbās ('the little dam of al-Abbas'), referring to the hydraulic weir diverting the Hirmas toward the Tharthar channel (modern al-Shaddadah, Syria); first attested in 10th-century CE geographical works.

b_al-rahba.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the early-to-mid 9th century CE (reign of Caliph al-Ma'mun, 813–833 CE, or before 867 CE) by Abbasid governor Malik ibn Tawk (d. 873 CE) as al-Raḥba / Raḥbat Mālik ibn Ṭawk.

eponym.details: Also known as Raḥbat Mālik ibn Ṭawk after its 9th-century founder Malik ibn Tawk al-Taghlibi (d. 873 CE).

morphemes.translation: open square, wide plain, flat wadi

b_al-rahba.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Raḥba ('the wide open space / plain'), founded on the Euphrates by Malik ibn Tawk in the 9th century CE prior to 867 CE.

b_ad-daliya.first_mention_attestation: First attested in early 10th-century CE Arabic sources, notably in accounts of the Qarmatian sack of 928 CE and in Qudama ibn Ja'far's Kitab al-Kharaj (early 10th century CE).

eponym.details: Later also called Dāliyat Mālik ibn Ṭawk after Malik ibn Tawk (d. 873 CE).

b_ad-daliya.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Dāliya ('the waterwheel'), a town on the Euphrates near al-Rahba along the Nahr Sa'id canal, first documented in early 10th-century CE sources.

b_irbil.first_mention_attestation: First attested c. 2300 BCE in the Ebla tablets as Irbilum, later Sumerian Urbilum, Akkadian Arba'ilu, Greek Arbela, and Arabic Irbīl/Arbīl.

morphemes.translation: four gods (Akkadian folk/theophoric etymology) or ancient pre-Semitic toponym

b_irbil.etymology_analysis: Arabic Irbīl/Arbīl continues Old Persian Arbairā, Akkadian Arba'ilu ('four gods'), and 3rd-millennium BCE Sumerian Urbilum / Eblaite Irbilum.

b_al-haditha.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 6th century CE as the Syriac bishopric of Ḥdatta (Bishop Titus of Hdatta) at the confluence of the Tigris and Upper Zab, and in early Islamic sources (al-Baladhuri, al-Tabari).

morphemes.language: Arabic (translating Syriac Ḥdatta / Middle Persian Newkart)

b_al-haditha.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Ḥadītha ('the New [Town]') translates Syriac Ḥdatta and Sasanian Middle Persian Newkart ('Newly Founded'), located on the Tigris at the mouth of the Upper Zab.

b_as-sinn.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 576 CE in the acts of the Church of the East Synod of Ezekiel as Shenna d'Beth Ramman, and in early Abbasid Arabic sources (e.g., 836 CE exile of al-Fadl ibn Marwan in al-Tabari; al-Baladhuri) as al-Sinn / Sinn Bārimmā.
b_as-sinn.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Sinn ('the tooth/crag') continues Syriac Shennā (Shennā d'Beṯ Ramman), referring to a tooth-shaped rocky crag or spur at the confluence of the Lesser Zab and Tigris.

b_tall_haftun.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 14th-century CE Arabic/Persian sources (al-'Umari's Masalik al-Absar, c. 1340s CE, and later Sharafnama of 1597 CE) as Tell-Haftun in the Soran region.
b_tall_haftun.etymology_analysis: Arabic tall ('mound') + Haftūn (possibly related to the East Syriac diocese of Hebton); attested as Tell-Haftun only from the 14th century CE.

b_khuftiyan.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Seljuk period (c. 1150 CE, province of Kurdistan under Sultan Sanjar) and later by Yaqut al-Hamawi (c. 1225 CE) and Mustawfi (c. 1340 CE) as a castle on the Zab.

morphemes.translation: medieval fortress name on the Zab

b_khuftiyan.etymology_analysis: Khuftiyān (خفتيان) is a medieval Kurdish fortress on the Zab River; Guy Le Strange notes it is unmentioned by any of the earlier Arab geographers prior to the 12th century CE.

b_shaqlabadh.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written sources in the 12th–13th centuries CE, notably by Yaqut al-Hamawi in Mu'jam al-Buldan (c. 1225 CE) as Shaqlābād (modern Shaqlawa).
b_shaqlabadh.etymology_analysis: Shaqlābādh (شقلاباد), modern Shaqlawa, combines a local root with the Iranian settlement suffix -ābādh ('town/settlement'); not attested in written sources before the 12th–13th centuries CE.

b_bamardani.first_mention_attestation: First attested as an Assyrian Christian village named Beṯ Mūrdānī in the 10th-century CE Syriac Life of Rabban Joseph Busnaya.
b_bamardani.etymology_analysis: Derived from Syriac Beṯ Mūrdānī (modern Bamarni), first attested in the 10th-century CE Life of Rabban Joseph Busnaya.

b_shahrazur.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Sasanian Paikuli inscription of King Narseh (r. 293–302 CE) as Syrazur, and in 4th-century CE Syriac martyrdoms (Bishop Shahdost of Shahrazur) and al-Baladhuri's Futuh al-Buldan.
b_shahrazur.etymology_analysis: Middle Persian Šahrazūr / Syrazur ('royal forest'), attested in the late 3rd-century CE Paikuli inscription and continuously in Sasanian, Syriac, and early Islamic sources.

b_khuftidkan.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation found <= 867 CE (medieval Shahrazur toponym, cognate/variant of Khuftiyān).
b_khuftidkan.etymology_analysis: Medieval Iranian/Kurdish toponym in Shahrazur (likely a variant or cognate of Khuftiyān); unattested in written sources prior to 867 CE.

b_tiranshah.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation found <= 867 CE (medieval Shahrazur toponym).
b_tiranshah.etymology_analysis: Persian/Kurdish compound Tīrānshāh in the Shahrazur district; no written attestation <= 867 CE has been found.

b_kerak.first_mention_attestation: c. 105 CE (Aramaic Kharkhā / Greek Charach and Charachmoba after Roman annexation, continuing Iron Age Moabite Kir-hareseth from the 9th century BCE)
b_kerak.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Karak derives from Aramaic/Syriac kharkhā ('fortified town'), attested in Greek as Charach/Charachmoba and continuing the Iron Age Moabite stronghold Kir-hareseth.

historical_names.name: Kir-hareseth
historical_names.source: Hebrew Bible (2 Kings 3; Isaiah 15–16) and 9th-century BCE Moabite El-Kerak Inscription
historical_names.notes: Iron Age Moabite royal fortress east of the Dead Sea.

historical_names.name: Kir-heres
historical_names.source: Hebrew Bible (2 Kings 3; Isaiah 15–16) and 9th-century BCE Moabite El-Kerak Inscription
historical_names.notes: Iron Age Moabite royal fortress east of the Dead Sea.

historical_names.name: Kir of Moab
historical_names.source: Hebrew Bible (2 Kings 3; Isaiah 15–16) and 9th-century BCE Moabite El-Kerak Inscription
historical_names.notes: Iron Age Moabite royal fortress east of the Dead Sea.

b_shawbak.first_mention_attestation: 1115 CE (Crusader chronicles recording Baldwin I's construction of Montreal / Castrum Saboach at ash-Shawbak)
b_shawbak.etymology_analysis: Arabic ash-Shawbak, attested in Crusader Latin chronicles as Castrum Saboach / Scobach alongside the Crusader name Mons Regalis (Montreal, founded 1115 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_at-tafila.first_mention_attestation: 1156 CE (medieval Arabic/Crusader sources recording a raid on Shawbak and Tafila, and a 1177 CE charter naming Martin, lord of Tafila)
b_at-tafila.etymology_analysis: Arabic aṭ-Ṭafīlah adapts the ancient Edomite toponym Tophel; the Arabic form itself is first documented in 12th-century CE Crusader/Ayyubid sources.

historical_names.name: Tophel
historical_names.source: Hebrew Bible (Deuteronomy 1:1, Edomite town of Tophel)
historical_names.notes: Edomite settlement of Tophel on the site of modern Tafilah.

b_zughar.first_mention_attestation: c. 6th century BCE (Hebrew Bible as Zoar; 6th-century CE Madaba Map as Zoora; Arabic Zughar in early Islamic geographies)
b_zughar.etymology_analysis: Arabic Zughar is the direct Semitic cognate and continuation of Hebrew Zoar ('small, little'), attested in the Hebrew Bible, Eusebius (325 CE), and the 6th-century CE Madaba Map.

historical_names.name: Zoar
historical_names.source: Hebrew Bible (Genesis 14:2, 19:22; Isaiah 15:5) and 6th-century CE Madaba Map
historical_names.notes: Ancient southeastern Dead Sea town of Zoar/Zoara, Arabicized as Zughar.

historical_names.name: Zoara
historical_names.source: Hebrew Bible (Genesis 14:2, 19:22; Isaiah 15:5) and 6th-century CE Madaba Map
historical_names.notes: Ancient southeastern Dead Sea town of Zoar/Zoara, Arabicized as Zughar.

b_baidha-petra.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE (modern Arabic name al-Bayḍā' 'the white one' for the Pre-Pottery Neolithic site near Siq al-Barid / Little Petra)
b_baidha-petra.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Bayḍāʾ ('the white one', referring to pale sandstone), paired with Petra as a modern geographic disambiguator; the Neolithic site (c. 7000 BCE) lacks a pre-867 CE written name.

b_arandal.first_mention_attestation: 431 CE (Byzantine episcopal see of Arindela at the Council of Ephesus; surrendered c. 634 CE to Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan as Arabic Arandal)
b_arandal.etymology_analysis: Arabic ʿArandal (modern Gharandal) directly continues Byzantine Greek Arindela, a bishopric of Palaestina Tertia conquered by Rashidun forces c. 634 CE.

historical_names.name: Arindela
historical_names.source: Acts of the Council of Ephesus (431 CE) and Council of Jerusalem (536 CE)
historical_names.notes: Byzantine Greek name of the city in Palaestina Tertia.

b_aila.first_mention_attestation: 1st century BCE (Strabo and Roman sources as Aila / Aelana; early Islamic port of Ayla founded c. 650 CE under Caliph Uthman)
b_aila.etymology_analysis: Nabataean/Roman Aila (Greek Aelana, Arabic Ayla) continues the older Semitic port name Elath/Eloth at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba.

historical_names.name: Elath
historical_names.source: Hebrew Bible (Deuteronomy 2:8; 1 Kings 9:26)
historical_names.notes: Iron Age Edomite/Israelite Red Sea port preceding Nabataean-Roman Aila.

b_ghazza.first_mention_attestation: 15th century BCE (military records of Thutmose III; 14th-century BCE Amarna Letters as Azzatu; Arabic Ghazzah conquered 635 CE)
b_ghazza.etymology_analysis: Arabic Ghazzah preserves the ancient Canaanite initial voiced velar fricative (*ġ), attested in Egyptian (15th c. BCE), Amarna Akkadian (Azzatu), and Greek (Gaza).

b_ascalon.first_mention_attestation: 19th–18th century BCE (Egyptian Execration Texts; 14th-century BCE Amarna Letters as Ashqaluna; Greek Askalon)

morphemes.translation: weighing, market (from Semitic root sh-q-l 'to weigh')

b_ascalon.etymology_analysis: Greek Askalon (Latin Ascalon, Arabic ʿAsqalān) derives from Canaanite Ashqelon, likely from the Semitic root sh-q-l ('to weigh', referring to a commercial weighing/trading center).

b_yaffa.first_mention_attestation: 15th century BCE (conquest list of Thutmose III; 14th-century BCE Amarna Letters as Yapu; Arabic Yāfā conquered 636 CE)
b_yaffa.etymology_analysis: Arabic Yāfā continues Canaanite Yapu / Hebrew Yafo (Greek Ioppe, English Jaffa), traditionally linked to the Semitic root y-p-h ('beautiful').

b_cesarea.first_mention_attestation: 22–10 BCE (founded by Herod the Great as Caesarea / Caesarea Maritima in honor of Augustus, replacing Straton's Tower)

eponym.details: Named after Roman Emperor Caesar Augustus (63 BCE – 14 CE) by Herod the Great.

b_cesarea.etymology_analysis: Latin Caesarea (Arabic Qaysāriyah), founded by Herod the Great in 22–10 BCE on the site of Hellenistic Straton's Tower and named after Caesar Augustus.

historical_names.name: Straton's Tower
historical_names.source: Hellenistic/Zenon Papyri (3rd century BCE; founded by Sidonian king Straton in the 4th century BCE)
historical_names.notes: Phoenician-Hellenistic port settlement preceding Herod's foundation of Caesarea.

b_jerusalem.first_mention_attestation: 19th–18th century BCE (Egyptian Execration Texts as Rusalimum; 14th-century BCE Amarna Letters as Urusalim)

morphemes.translation: Shalim (Canaanite deity of dusk) or peace

b_jerusalem.etymology_analysis: From West Semitic *Urū-Šalim ('foundation of Shalim'), attested from the Middle Bronze Age in Egyptian Execration Texts and Amarna Letters.

b_ar-ramla.first_mention_attestation: c. 705–715 CE (founded as capital of Jund Filastin by Umayyad governor and later Caliph Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik)
b_ar-ramla.etymology_analysis: From Arabic ar-Ramlah ('the sand'), founded c. 705–715 CE on sandy ground west of Lydda by Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik as the Umayyad capital of Jund Filastin.

b_nablus.first_mention_attestation: 72 CE (founded by Roman Emperor Vespasian as Flavia Neapolis; Arabicized as Nābulus after the 636 CE conquest)
b_nablus.etymology_analysis: Arabic Nābulus is the direct phonetic adaptation of Greek Neápolis ('New City'), founded in 72 CE by Vespasian as Flavia Neapolis.

historical_names.name: Shechem
historical_names.source: Egyptian Execration Texts (19th–18th century BCE) and Amarna Letters (14th century BCE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Canaanite/Israelite city of Shechem (Tell Balata) immediately east of Neapolis.

b_hebron.first_mention_attestation: Iron Age / c. 6th century BCE (Hebrew Bible as Hebron; Josephus 1st century CE; Eusebius 4th century CE)
b_hebron.etymology_analysis: From West Semitic/Hebrew Ḥevrōn (root ḥ-b-r 'to join, ally'), attested in Iron Age/Biblical texts and classical antiquity (later known in Arabic as al-Khalīl).

b_acre.first_mention_attestation: 19th–18th century BCE (Egyptian Execration Texts; 14th-century BCE Amarna Letters as Akka; Hellenistic Ptolemais)

morphemes.translation: ancient port city name (cf. Semitic ʿ-k-k)

b_acre.etymology_analysis: From Bronze Age Canaanite ʿAkkō (Arabic ʿAkkā, Crusader Acre), temporarily renamed Ptolemais in the Hellenistic period.

b_tyre.first_mention_attestation: 14th century BCE (Amarna Letters as Ṣurru; Herodotus 5th century BCE as Tyros)

morphemes.translation: rock (referring to the offshore rocky island)

b_tyre.etymology_analysis: English Tyre comes via Greek Týros / Latin Tyrus from Phoenician Ṣūr ('rock'), attested in the 14th-century BCE Amarna Letters as Ṣurru.

b_irbid.first_mention_attestation: 1596 CE (Ottoman tax registers naming the village Irbid in the Hauran Sanjak; earlier known as Arbela / ʾrbl)
b_irbid.etymology_analysis: Arabic Irbid developed from ancient Arbela / ʾrbl (attested on Decapolis coins and in 1 Maccabees, Josephus, and Nabataean/Safaitic inscriptions), though the Arabic form Irbid is first attested post-867 CE.

historical_names.name: Arbela
historical_names.source: Decapolis civic bronze coins (1st century BCE), 1 Maccabees 9:2, Josephus, and Nabataean/Safaitic inscriptions
historical_names.notes: Hellenistic-Roman Decapolis city of Arbela/Arabella at Tell Irbid.

historical_names.name: ʾrbl
historical_names.source: Decapolis civic bronze coins (1st century BCE), 1 Maccabees 9:2, Josephus, and Nabataean/Safaitic inscriptions
historical_names.notes: Hellenistic-Roman Decapolis city of Arbela/Arabella at Tell Irbid.

b_jarash.first_mention_attestation: 2nd century BCE (Hellenistic Decapolis city of Gerasa; Josephus 1st century CE; Arabic Jarash after 635 CE conquest)
b_jarash.etymology_analysis: Arabic Jarash continues Hellenistic-Roman Gerasa (Semitic Garshu), a major city of the Decapolis and Roman province of Arabia.

b_tiberias.first_mention_attestation: c. 20 CE (founded by Herod Antipas and attested on local coinage from 20 CE and in Josephus)

eponym.details: Named after Roman Emperor Tiberius (r. 14–37 CE) by Herod Antipas.

b_tiberias.etymology_analysis: Greek Tiberiás (Arabic Ṭabariyyah), founded c. 20 CE by Herod Antipas on the Sea of Galilee and named in honor of Emperor Tiberius.

b_baniyas.first_mention_attestation: c. 200 BCE (Polybius, Histories XVI.18, as Paneion / Paneas; Arabicized as Bāniyās after the 7th-century CE Muslim conquest)
b_baniyas.etymology_analysis: Arabic Bāniyās directly adapts Greek Paneás (from the Hellenistic sanctuary of the god Pan at the spring of the Jordan River; temporarily renamed Caesarea Philippi in 2 BCE).

b_al-anbar.first_mention_attestation: 6th century CE (Middle Persian Anbār 'granary', attested prior to the 633 CE Rashidun conquest; later Abbasid capital 752–762 CE)
b_al-anbar.etymology_analysis: From Arabic definite article al- + Middle Persian anbār ('granary, storehouse'), referring to the Sasanian military granaries in the citadel of Peroz-Shapur.

historical_names.name: Misiche
historical_names.source: Sasanian and Roman sources (244 CE Battle of Misiche; renamed Peroz-Shapur by Shapur I)
historical_names.notes: Adjacent to the Tell Aswad mound (c. 3000 BCE); known as Misiche until 244 CE, then Peroz-Shapur (Greek Pirisapora/Bersabora).

historical_names.name: Peroz-Shapur
historical_names.source: Sasanian and Roman sources (244 CE Battle of Misiche; renamed Peroz-Shapur by Shapur I)
historical_names.notes: Adjacent to the Tell Aswad mound (c. 3000 BCE); known as Misiche until 244 CE, then Peroz-Shapur (Greek Pirisapora/Bersabora).

b_ar-rabb.first_mention_attestation: Early 10th century CE (Ibn Serapion / Suhrab, locating Ar-Rabb 12 leagues below Hit as the former intake of the earlier Dujayl canal)
b_ar-rabb.etymology_analysis: From Arabic ar-Rabb ('the Lord/Master'), attested in early 10th-century CE Abbasid geographical itineraries as a village on the Euphrates below Hit.

b_badaraya.first_mention_attestation: c. 846 CE (Ibn Khordadbeh, Kitāb al-Masālik wa'l-Mamālik, listing the Bādarāyā ṭassūj of the Sawad; derived from Aramaic Bēṯ Darāyē)
b_badaraya.etymology_analysis: Arabicized from Aramaic/Syriac Bēṯ Darāyē ('land of Der'), itself continuing Neo-Assyrian Bīt-Derāya (8th century BCE) and Sumerian Der.

historical_names.name: Der
historical_names.source: Neo-Assyrian annals of Tiglath-Pileser III (8th century BCE) and Sasanian-era Syriac sources
historical_names.notes: Ancient Sumerian city of Der at nearby Tell 'Aqar, attested as Bīt-Derāya in the 8th century BCE and Bēṯ Darāyē in Syriac.

historical_names.name: Bīt-Derāya
historical_names.source: Neo-Assyrian annals of Tiglath-Pileser III (8th century BCE) and Sasanian-era Syriac sources
historical_names.notes: Ancient Sumerian city of Der at nearby Tell 'Aqar, attested as Bīt-Derāya in the 8th century BCE and Bēṯ Darāyē in Syriac.

historical_names.name: Bēṯ Darāyē
historical_names.source: Neo-Assyrian annals of Tiglath-Pileser III (8th century BCE) and Sasanian-era Syriac sources
historical_names.notes: Ancient Sumerian city of Der at nearby Tell 'Aqar, attested as Bīt-Derāya in the 8th century BCE and Bēṯ Darāyē in Syriac.

b_bakusaya.first_mention_attestation: c. 846 CE (Ibn Khordadbeh, Kitāb al-Masālik wa'l-Mamālik, listing Bākusāyā as a ṭassūj of Bazijan-Khusraw in the Sawad)
b_bakusaya.etymology_analysis: From an Aramaic/Syriac toponym *Bēṯ Kusāyē ('place of Kus/Kos'), preserved in early Islamic Arabic as Bākusāyā (modern Baksay/Bagsaya in Wasit).

b_tarsukh.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE sources (modern Tursaq valley/locality in the Badra–Mandali borderlands of eastern Iraq)
b_tarsukh.etymology_analysis: Reflects the modern eastern Iraqi borderland toponym Tursaq (Tarsukh) near Badra and Qazaniya; unattested in medieval or pre-867 CE written sources.

b_baghdad.first_mention_attestation: 762 CE (founded as Madīnat al-Salām by Abbasid Caliph al-Mansur on the site of the pre-Islamic village of Baghdād)
b_baghdad.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic toponym generally derived from Middle Persian Bag-dād ('God-given'), with earlier cuneiform antecedents (Bagdadu) in Mesopotamia; adopted as the common name of al-Mansur's 762 CE capital.

b_baquba.first_mention_attestation: c. 846 CE (Ibn Khordadbeh and early Abbasid geographies as Baʿqūbā, capital of Upper Nahrawan; probable Sasanian foundation)
b_baquba.etymology_analysis: From Aramaic Bēṯ ʿAqūbā ('house of the guardian/punishment' or 'house of Jacob'), contracted in Arabic to Bāʿqūbā / Baʿqūbah.

b_ukbara.first_mention_attestation: 865 CE (al-Tabari, History, recording Abu Ahmad's arrival at ʿUkbarā during the Abbasid civil war of 865–866 CE)
b_ukbara.etymology_analysis: Arabicized form (ʿUkbarā) of an older Aramaic/Mesopotamian settlement on the Tigris north of Baghdad, also known in Sasanian sources as Vuzurg-Shapur.

historical_names.name: Vuzurg-Shapur
historical_names.source: Sasanian administrative tradition (preserved by Yaqut al-Hamawi as Buzurj-Sābūr)
historical_names.notes: Middle Persian Vuzurg-Shapur ('Great Shapur') was the Sasanian official name of the settlement.

b_an-nahrawan.first_mention_attestation: 658 CE (Battle of Nahrawan between Ali ibn Abi Talib and the Kharijites, recorded in al-Tabari; canal built in the 6th century CE)
b_an-nahrawan.etymology_analysis: Named after the Sasanian-era Nahrawan Canal (6th century CE), a major artificial irrigation waterway; the town of Jisr al-Nahrawan grew at the Khurasan Road bridge.

b_al-farasa.first_mention_attestation: 1184 CE (Ibn Jubayr, Riḥla, describing al-Farāshah as a fortified caravanserai village halfway between Baghdad and Hillah)
b_al-farasa.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Farāshah, recorded in late 12th-century CE pilgrimage itineraries (Ibn Jubayr, 1184 CE) as a fortified waystation seven leagues south of Sarsar.

b_sarsar.first_mention_attestation: 815 CE (al-Tabari, History, recording Abu'l-Saraya's retreat from Nahr Ṣarṣar in June 815 CE)
b_sarsar.etymology_analysis: Named after the Nahr Ṣarṣar, an artificial Euphrates-to-Tigris irrigation canal south of Baghdad, with the town of Sarsar at its crossing on the Kufah road.

b_iskaf.first_mention_attestation: c. 846 CE (Ibn Khordadbeh, Kitāb al-Masālik wa'l-Mamālik, listing Iskāf as a ṭassūj of Bazijan-Khusraw; mosque excavated from early 8th century CE)
b_iskaf.etymology_analysis: Full medieval name Iskāf Banī Junayd, referring to a town straddling the Lower Nahrawan Canal associated with the Banu Junayd clan.

b_jabbul.first_mention_attestation: 879 CE (al-Tabari, History, recording the Zanj rebels' advance to Jabbul and al-Nu'maniyah; also described by Ibn Rustah c. 903 CE)
b_jabbul.etymology_analysis: Medieval town on the eastern bank of the Tigris opposite al-Nu'maniyah; earliest surviving written attestation is in al-Tabari's account of the Zanj Rebellion in 879 CE.

b_humaniya.first_mention_attestation: 813 CE (al-Tabari, History, recording that Zubaydah and al-Amin's sons were imprisoned at al-Humānīya by al-Ma'mun after 813 CE)
b_humaniya.etymology_analysis: Medieval town on the Tigris southeast of Dayr al-'Aqul of probable Sasanian origin, attested in early 9th-century CE Abbasid chronicles.

b_karbala.first_mention_attestation: 680 CE (Battle of Karbala, 10 October 680 CE / 10 Muharram 61 AH)

morphemes.translation: sanctuary, proximity (or Arabic karbalāt, soft earth)

b_karbala.etymology_analysis: Disputed pre-Islamic Mesopotamian origin, variously derived from Akkadian/Aramaic karb-ilā ('sanctuary of God'), 'Kar Babel', or Arabic al-karbalāt ('soft earth').

b_hit.first_mention_attestation: 636 CE (conquered by Rashidun forces under the Arabic name Hīt; continues ancient Id / Is attested from c. 1800 BCE and Herodotus c. 440 BCE)
b_hit.etymology_analysis: Arabic Hīt continues the ancient Mesopotamian name Id/Itu (Greek Is in Herodotus), famous for its bitumen springs.

historical_names.name: Id
historical_names.source: Old Babylonian / Mari tablets (c. 1800 BCE) and Herodotus's Histories (c. 440 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient bitumen-producing city of Id/Itu on the Euphrates, called Is by Herodotus.

historical_names.name: Is
historical_names.source: Old Babylonian / Mari tablets (c. 1800 BCE) and Herodotus's Histories (c. 440 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient bitumen-producing city of Id/Itu on the Euphrates, called Is by Herodotus.

b_bajlan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in Basra or Iraq (the Bajlan/Bajilan tribe is attested in the Ottoman–Iranian borderlands from the 18th century CE)
b_bajlan.etymology_analysis: Corresponds to the Bajlan/Bajilan tribal name attested in early modern Ottoman-Iranian borderland records; has no pre-867 CE attestation in the Basra region.

b_basra.first_mention_attestation: 636 CE (founded as an Arab military encampment by Utbah ibn Ghazwan under Caliph Umar)
b_basra.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Baṣrah, traditionally explained by Yaqut and medieval Arabic lexicographers as referring to whitish, stony/pebbly ground.

b_hifair.first_mention_attestation: 656 CE (al-Tabari, History, recording Aisha's encampment at al-Ḥufayr near Basra before the Battle of the Camel; also attested before 837 CE in the Bahila migration)

morphemes.translation: small dug well or trench (diminutive of ḥafr)

b_hifair.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Ḥufayr ('the little dug well/excavation'), a watering station and locality in the desert approaches near Basra.

b_ar-rukhail.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in medieval or pre-867 CE sources for southern Iraq
b_ar-rukhail.etymology_analysis: Appears to be an Arabic diminutive toponym (ar-Rukhayl), unattested in classical Arabic geographical works or pre-867 CE chronicles.

b_ar-rusafa-iraq.first_mention_attestation: Early 10th century CE (Ibn Serapion / Suhrab, describing Ar-Ruṣāfah on the Tigris 10 leagues below Wasit)
b_ar-rusafa-iraq.etymology_analysis: From Arabic ar-Ruṣāfah ('the paved causeway'), a medieval town on the left bank of the Tigris ten leagues below Wasit (distinct from Baghdad's Rusafa quarter).

b_al-farut.first_mention_attestation: Early 10th century CE (Ibn Serapion / Suhrab, listing Al-Fārūth on the eastern bank of the Tigris below Wasit)
b_al-farut.etymology_analysis: Medieval settlement (al-Fārūth) on the lower Tigris downstream of Wasit, first attested in early 10th-century CE geographical works (Ibn Serapion / Suhrab).

b_al-qatr.first_mention_attestation: Early 10th century CE (Ibn Rustah and Ibn Serapion / Suhrab, noting Al-Qaṭr where the Tigris divided and entered the Great Swamp)
b_al-qatr.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Qaṭr, a medieval riverine town 12 leagues below Ar-Rusafah marking the northeastern entry of the Tigris into the Bata'ih marshes.

b_nahr_simmara.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in medieval or pre-867 CE geographical sources for lower Iraq
b_nahr_simmara.etymology_analysis: Compound of Arabic nahr ('canal/river') + Simmāra; unattested in classical Arabic geographical works or pre-867 CE sources.

b_al-ubulla.first_mention_attestation: 636 CE (Rashidun conquest by Utbah ibn Ghazwan recorded in al-Baladhuri and al-Tabari; identified with classical Apologos)

morphemes.translation: adapted from ancient port name Apologos

b_al-ubulla.etymology_analysis: Arabicized as al-Ubulla from the pre-Islamic port name Apologos (Greek Ἀπολόγου ἐμπόριον), located at the head of the Persian Gulf.

historical_names.name: Apologos
historical_names.source: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st–2nd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Classical Greek name Apologos for the pre-Islamic port at the site of al-Ubulla.

b_matara-iraq.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in the Basra/Ubulla region

morphemes.translation: obscure (possibly related to maṭar 'rain' or maṭārah 'water-skin')

b_matara-iraq.etymology_analysis: Modern/obscure Iraqi place-name near the Shatt al-Arab/Basra region (distinct from medieval al-Maṭīrah near Samarra); unattested <= 867 CE.

b_ain_said.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE (corresponds to modern desert spring ʿAyn Ṣayd in Al-Muthanna or a minor Basra locality)
b_ain_said.etymology_analysis: From Arabic ʿayn ('spring') + Ṣayd/Saʿīd; refers to a desert water spring (such as ʿAyn Ṣayd on the Khaṭṭ al-ʿUyūn route in southern Iraq), unattested <= 867 CE.

b_as-salman.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE (modern desert oasis/town in Al-Muthanna Governorate, with a fort dating to 1911 CE)
b_as-salman.etymology_analysis: Southern Iraqi desert oasis and town (as-Salmān) in Al-Muthanna Governorate; lacks any documented pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_al-akhadid.first_mention_attestation: 7th century CE (Qur'an 85:4, Aṣḥāb al-Ukhdūd 'People of the Ditch', referring to the 523 CE persecution at Najran; plural al-Akhādīd)
b_al-akhadid.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-akhādīd ('the trenches/ditches', plural of ukhdūd), famously attested in Qur'an 85:4 in reference to the 523 CE Najran martyrdoms (also applied to desert trench sites).

b_niffar.first_mention_attestation: c. 2500 BCE (Early Dynastic Sumerian cuneiform texts as Nibru / Nippur; continuously occupied to c. 800 CE and known in Arabic as Niffār)
b_niffar.etymology_analysis: Medieval Arabic Niffār is the direct phonological continuation of Akkadian Nippur (Sumerian Nibru), a major Mesopotamian religious center inhabited from c. 5000 BCE to c. 800 CE.

historical_names.name: Nibru
historical_names.source: Early Dynastic Sumerian cuneiform tablets (c. 2500 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Sumerian Nibru / Akkadian Nippur, the ancient form of medieval Arabic Niffār.

historical_names.name: Nippur
historical_names.source: Early Dynastic Sumerian cuneiform tablets (c. 2500 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Sumerian Nibru / Akkadian Nippur, the ancient form of medieval Arabic Niffār.

b_as-saliq.first_mention_attestation: c. 985 CE (al-Muqaddasi, Aḥsan al-Taqāsīm, describing Aṣ-Ṣalīq as a large town on a lagoon in the Bata'ih marshes)
b_as-saliq.etymology_analysis: Medieval town in the Bata'ih (Great Swamp) of southern Iraq, first attested in al-Muqaddasi's late 10th-century CE geography (c. 985 CE).

b_an-najaf.first_mention_attestation: 791 CE (Abbasid foundation by Caliph Harun al-Rashid as a shrine to Ali ibn Abi Talib; Arabic toponym al-Najaf)
b_an-najaf.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Najaf (ٱلنَّجَف), referring to a high, rectangular ridge or elevated plateau around which water accumulates without overflowing it (as glossed by Ibn Manzur). The settlement grew around the shrine built by Caliph Harun al-Rashid in 791 CE.

b_al-kufa.first_mention_attestation: 638 CE (17 AH; founded as a garrison city by Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas under Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab)

morphemes.translation: round sandhill / mound of red sand and pebbles

b_al-kufa.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Kufah (ٱلْكُوفَة), meaning a round mound of sand or pebbles. Founded in 638 CE as a Rashidun garrison city (misr) near al-Hirah.

b_al-hila.first_mention_attestation: 1101 CE (495 AH; founded by the Mazyadid emir Sayf al-Dawla Sadaqa ibn Mansur as Hillah al-Sayfiyah)
b_al-hila.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Hillah (ٱلْحِلَّة), meaning 'the encampment' or 'halting place' (also associated with beauty). Founded in 1101 CE near the earlier 10th-century settlement of al-Jami'ayn.

b_al-qadisiya.first_mention_attestation: 636 CE (site of the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah recorded in al-Tabari and al-Baladhuri)

morphemes.translation: holy/sanctified place or place of Qadis

b_al-qadisiya.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Qadisiyyah (ٱلْقَادِسِيَّة), a pre-Islamic Sasanian-frontier village and later Darb Zubaydah waystation southwest of Kufa, attested from the 636 CE battle.

b_al-udhaib.first_mention_attestation: 636 CE (Sasanian-era fortress at al-'Udhayb mentioned in al-Tabari's account of the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah)
b_al-udhaib.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-'Udhayb (ٱلْعُذَيْب), diminutive of 'adhb ('sweet/fresh [water]'), referring to the desert-edge spring and oasis near al-Qadisiyyah.

b_al-qara.first_mention_attestation: 632 CE (mentioned as al-Qar'a' in al-Tabari's account of the Ridda Wars, and in Ibn Khordadbeh c. 846 CE as a Darb Zubaydah station)
b_al-qara.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Qar'a' (ٱلْقَرْعَاء), meaning 'the bare/treeless ground', a major halting station on the Darb Zubaydah pilgrimage road south of Kufa.

b_safata.first_mention_attestation: c. 1226 CE (attested as Shafatha near Ayn al-Tamr in Yaqut al-Hamawi's Mu'jam al-Buldan)

morphemes.translation: oasis locality near Ayn al-Tamr (modern Shathatha)

b_safata.etymology_analysis: Corresponds to Shafatha (شَفَاثَا, modern Shathatha), an oasis settlement in the Ayn al-Tamr district west of Karbala, first documented in Yaqut al-Hamawi's Mu'jam al-Buldan (early 13th century CE).

b_ain_at-tamr.first_mention_attestation: 633 CE (12 AH; conquered by Khalid ibn al-Walid, also a Sasanian tassuj of Bih-Qubadh al-A'la)
b_ain_at-tamr.etymology_analysis: From Arabic 'Ayn al-Tamr (عَيْن ٱلتَّمْر), literally 'Spring of the Date Palm', named for its desert oasis springs.

b_khaffan.first_mention_attestation: c. 634 CE (attested in al-Tabari's account of the Sawad of Kufa and pre-Islamic Sasanian embankment Isba' Khaffan near al-Hirah)
b_khaffan.etymology_analysis: Arabic Khaffan (خَفَّان), a historic locality and Sasanian-era embankment/watchtower site (Isba' Khaffan) in the environs of al-Hirah and Kufa, celebrated in early Arabic poetry and chronicles.

b_waqisa.first_mention_attestation: 680 CE (attested in al-Tabari for Ibn Ziyad's blockade of the Kufa–Mecca road and in al-Baladhuri for 686 CE; major Darb Zubaydah station)

morphemes.translation: pilgrimage station on the Kufa–Mecca road

b_waqisa.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Waqisah (ٱلْوَاقِصَة), an early Islamic desert station on the Kufa–Mecca route (Darb Zubaydah) south of al-Qar'a.

b_as-subia.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE or standard medieval Islamic geographical sources for the Waqisa/Kufa sector.
b_as-subia.etymology_analysis: No verified historical or geographical attestation found in pre-867 CE sources for a settlement named As-Subia in the Waqisa district.

b_hulwan.first_mention_attestation: 640 CE (conquered by Rashidun forces following the Battle of Jalula; Sasanian astan of Shadh-Fayruz / Hulwan)

morphemes.translation: ancient frontier town at the Zagros pass (from Assyrian Halman)

b_hulwan.etymology_analysis: Arabic Hulwan (حُلْوَان), from Aramaic/Akkadian Halman, an ancient town guarding the Paytak Pass into the Zagros Mountains, attested in Sasanian and 7th-century CE Islamic conquest narratives.

b_bandanijan.first_mention_attestation: c. 846 CE (attested as al-Bandanijan, a tassuj of Shadh-Qubadh in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik)

morphemes.translation: chief town of Badaraya and Bakusaya (modern Mandali)

b_bandanijan.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Bandanijan (ٱلْبَنْدَنِيجِين), an early Islamic and Sasanian-era administrative center (tassuj of Shadh-Qubadh) on the Khuzistan–Jibal frontier, corresponding to modern Mandali.

b_jalula-hulwan.first_mention_attestation: 637 CE (Battle of Jalula between Rashidun and Sasanian forces; Sasanian tassuj of Shadh-Qubadh)
b_jalula-hulwan.etymology_analysis: Jalula (جَلُولَاء, modern Jalawla) on the Diyala River and Khurasan Road, attested from the 637 CE Battle of Jalula; '-Hulwan' is a game disambiguator.

b_daskara.first_mention_attestation: 424 CE (attested as Dasqarta d'Malka in the Church of the East Synod of Dadisho'; rebuilt by Hormizd I r. 270–271 CE and sacked by Heraclius in 628 CE)
b_daskara.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Daskarah (ٱلدَّسْكَرَة), borrowed from Middle Persian Dastagird ('royal estate/handiwork', Syriac Dasqarta d'Malka), a major Sasanian winter residence on the Khurasan Road.

b_kirkuk.first_mention_attestation: c. 1425 CE (first attested as Kirkuk/Karkuk in Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi's Persian Zafarnama)
b_kirkuk.etymology_analysis: Modern name Kirkuk (كركوك) derives from Syriac karka ('citadel'), via medieval Karkhini, and is first attested in the 15th-century Zafarnama.

historical_names.name: Arrapha
historical_names.source: Neo-Sumerian / Akkadian records (Arrapha, c. 2100 BCE); Syriac Synod of Isaac 410 CE (Karka d'Beth Slokh)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Arrapha (c. 2100 BCE) and Seleucid/Sasanian Syriac Karka d'Beth Slokh (410 CE) occupied the same citadel tell prior to the 15th-century name Kirkuk.

historical_names.name: Karka d'Beth Slokh
historical_names.source: Neo-Sumerian / Akkadian records (Arrapha, c. 2100 BCE); Syriac Synod of Isaac 410 CE (Karka d'Beth Slokh)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Arrapha (c. 2100 BCE) and Seleucid/Sasanian Syriac Karka d'Beth Slokh (410 CE) occupied the same citadel tell prior to the 15th-century name Kirkuk.

historical_names.name: Karkhini
historical_names.source: Neo-Sumerian / Akkadian records (Arrapha, c. 2100 BCE); Syriac Synod of Isaac 410 CE (Karka d'Beth Slokh)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Arrapha (c. 2100 BCE) and Seleucid/Sasanian Syriac Karka d'Beth Slokh (410 CE) occupied the same citadel tell prior to the 15th-century name Kirkuk.

b_khanijar.first_mention_attestation: 823 CE (East Syriac diocese of Khanijar in the metropolitan province of Beth Garmai)

morphemes.translation: settlement and East Syriac diocese in Beth Garmai

b_khanijar.etymology_analysis: Khanijar (خَانِيجَار), a town and suffragan East Syriac diocese of Beth Garmai attested in 823 CE and in Eliya of Damascus (893 CE).

b_raushanqubad.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources under this specific compound name.

eponym.details: Contains the name of Sasanian King Kavadh I (Arabic Qubadh, r. 488–531 CE), though the specific toponym Raushanqubad lacks a verified pre-867 CE attestation.

b_raushanqubad.etymology_analysis: Compound of Persian raushan ('bright/splendid') and Qubad (Kavadh I, r. 488–531 CE), following Sasanian royal foundation naming patterns, though unattested by 867 CE.

b_daquqa.first_mention_attestation: c. 846 CE (attested in early Abbasid geographical sources including Ibn Khordadbeh and later Eliya of Damascus 893 CE)
b_daquqa.etymology_analysis: Daquqa (دَاقُوقَاء, modern Daquq), an ancient town in Beth Garmai south of Kirkuk attested in 9th-century CE Abbasid geographies and East Syriac ecclesiastical lists.

b_samarra.first_mention_attestation: 836 CE (221 AH; founded as the Abbasid imperial capital by Caliph al-Mu'tasim)

morphemes.translation: he who sees it is delighted (from earlier Sumere)

b_samarra.etymology_analysis: Founded in 836 CE by Caliph al-Mu'tasim as Surra Man Ra'a ('he who sees it is delighted'), adapted from the pre-Islamic toponym Sumere.

historical_names.name: Sumere
historical_names.source: Ammianus Marcellinus (Res Gestae, 363 CE, during Julian's Persian campaign).
historical_names.notes: Pre-Islamic settlement and fortress of Sumere on the Tigris, adapted into Abbasid Surra Man Ra'a (Samarra) in 836 CE.

b_balad.first_mention_attestation: 866 CE (252 AH; recorded as the place where Muhammad ibn Ali al-Hadi died and was buried, south of Samarra)
b_balad.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Balad (بَلَد, 'town/settlement'), a town in the Dujayl district south of Samarra attested by 866 CE.

b_aiwana.first_mention_attestation: c. 400 CE (attested as Awana in the Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 71b, and in 8th-century CE Syriac monastic histories)
b_aiwana.etymology_analysis: From Aramaic/Syriac Awana (אוונא / ܐܘܢܐ, 'inn/halting station'), a Tigris town near Ukbara and Balad attested from the Talmudic and Sasanian periods.

b_hisn_al-mashuq.first_mention_attestation: 877 CE (built 877–882 CE by Abbasid Caliph al-Mu'tamid across the Tigris from Samarra as Qasr al-'Ashiq / Hisn al-Ma'shuq)
b_hisn_al-mashuq.etymology_analysis: Arabic Hisn al-Ma'shuq (حِصْن ٱلْمَعْشُوق, 'Citadel of the Beloved', also Qasr al-'Ashiq), an Abbasid palace-fortress built in 877–882 CE by Caliph al-Mu'tamid.

b_takrit.first_mention_attestation: 615 BCE (mentioned in the Neo-Babylonian Fall of Assyria Chronicle as a refuge on the Tigris)
b_takrit.etymology_analysis: From ancient Mesopotamian/Syriac Tagrit (تَكْرِيت / تِكْرِيت), a fortified Tigris crossing attested since 615 BCE.

b_jabalta.first_mention_attestation: c. 846 CE (attested as Jabilta in Ibn Khordadbeh's Sawad tassuj list and in Syriac sources near Takrit)

morphemes.translation: settlement on the Tigris near Takrit

b_jabalta.etymology_analysis: Jabalta / Jabilta (جَبَلْتَا), a town on the eastern bank of the Tigris near Takrit (and a Sawad tassuj paired with Jalawla), attested in 9th-century CE Arabic and Syriac sources.

b_barimma.first_mention_attestation: 576 CE (attested as Shenna d'Beth Ramman in the East Syriac Synod of Ezekiel; Arabic Sinn Barimma)
b_barimma.etymology_analysis: Arabic Barimma (بَارِمَّا), from Syriac Beth Ramman ('House of Ramman'), paired with Sinn (Shenna d'Beth Ramman) at the Tigris gorge through Jabal Hamrin.

b_at-tib.first_mention_attestation: 860 CE (246 AH; recorded as the place where the Abbasid poet Di'bil al-Khuza'i died, between Wasit and Khuzestan)
b_at-tib.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Tib (ٱلطِّيب), an Abbasid-era town on the road between Wasit and Susa in Khuzestan, attested by 860 CE.

b_karkha.first_mention_attestation: 410 CE (attested as Karka d'Maishan in the East Syriac Synod of Isaac; Aramaic karkha 'citadel')
b_karkha.etymology_analysis: From Aramaic/Syriac karkha (ܟܪܟܐ, 'fortified town/citadel'), corresponding to Karka d'Maishan (Karkh Maysan) in southern Mesopotamia.

b_wasit.first_mention_attestation: 702 CE (83 AH; founded by the Umayyad governor al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf)

morphemes.translation: middle (situated midway between Kufa and Basra)

b_wasit.etymology_analysis: Arabic Wasit (وَاسِط, 'middle'), founded in 702 CE by al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf as a Syrian garrison city midway between Kufa and Basra.

b_kaskar.first_mention_attestation: 410 CE (attested as Kashkar, senior bishopric of Beth Aramaye in the East Syriac Synod of Isaac; also Sasanian astan of Shadh-Sabur/Kaskar)
b_kaskar.etymology_analysis: Kaskar / Kashkar (كَسْكَر, Syriac ܟܫܟܪ), an ancient and Sasanian city across the Tigris from Wasit, attested as a Christian bishopric by 410 CE.

b_an-numaniya.first_mention_attestation: c. 846 CE (attested in early Abbasid geographical works such as Ibn Khordadbeh and later al-Ya'qubi; named after Lakhmid king al-Nu'man III, r. 580–602 CE)

eponym.details: Named after the Lakhmid king al-Nu'man III ibn al-Mundhir (r. 580–602 CE).

b_an-numaniya.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Nu'maniyyah (ٱلنُّعْمَانِيَّة), derived from the Lakhmid king al-Nu'man III ibn al-Mundhir (r. 580–602 CE), capital of the Upper Zab district between Baghdad and Wasit.

b_arrajan.first_mention_attestation: 7th-century CE Arab conquest accounts (c. 644 CE, recorded by al-Baladhuri and al-Tabari) and 9th-century CE Abbasid geographers (Ibn Khordadbeh) attesting the city of Arrajan (Arrajan/Argan), refounded in the early 6th century CE by Kavad I.
b_arrajan.etymology_analysis: Arabicized form of Middle Persian Argan/Arjan (connected with the Neo-Elamite site of Arjan near Behbahan). Refounded by Sasanian emperor Kavad I (r. 488-531 CE) as Weh-az-Amid-Kawad ('Better than Amid [founded by] Kavad'), with the indigenous name Arrajan attested in 7th-century CE Islamic conquest narratives.

historical_names.name: Wēh-az-Āmīd-Kawād
historical_names.source: Early 6th-century CE Sasanian royal foundation by Kavad I (c. 502-506 CE), attested on Sasanian administrative sealings.
historical_names.notes: Kavad I's official Sasanian dynastic name for the refounded city, alongside the local name Argan/Arrajan.

historical_names.name: Veh-az-Amid-Qobad
historical_names.source: Early 6th-century CE Sasanian royal foundation by Kavad I (c. 502-506 CE), attested on Sasanian administrative sealings.
historical_names.notes: Kavad I's official Sasanian dynastic name for the refounded city, alongside the local name Argan/Arrajan.

b_jannaba.first_mention_attestation: 7th-century CE accounts of the Muslim conquest of Fars (al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan) and 9th-century CE biographical records of Abu Sa'id al-Jannabi (born c. 845-855 CE in Jannaba).
b_jannaba.etymology_analysis: Arabicized form (Jannaba) of Middle Persian Gannawag/Ganawa (modern Ganaveh), meaning 'foul/brackish water', referring to the coastal lagoon and water conditions on the Persian Gulf.

b_siniz.first_mention_attestation: c. 640-643 CE Arab conquest of Fars, when Hormoz ibn Hayyan al-'Abdi was sent by Uthman ibn Abi al-As to capture the coastal fortress of Siniz (recorded in al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, p. 388).
b_siniz.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic Iranian coastal settlement name (Arabicized as Siniz) located between Mahruban and Jannaba in Arrajan province, attested from the 7th-century CE Arab conquest.

b_tawwaj.first_mention_attestation: c. 640 CE capture and garrisoning by al-Hakam and Uthman ibn Abi al-As during the Arab conquest of Fars (al-Baladhuri, al-Tabari); also attested as Tuzag in the Middle Persian Sahrestaniha i Eransahr.

morphemes.translation: ancient town of Persis (also associated with fine linen, tawazi)

b_tawwaj.etymology_analysis: Arabicized form (Tawwaj/Tawwaz) of Middle Persian Tuzag, a Sasanian commercial center in southwestern Fars near the Shapur River.

b_khubadan.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographers al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (985 CE) describing Khubdhan (Khubadan) on the Khubdhan River four leagues from Nawbanjan.
b_khubadan.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Khubdhan River (Nahr Khawrawadhan), a tributary of the Shirin River in western Fars; the town on its banks bore the same hydronymic name in 10th-century CE sources.

b_darabjerd.first_mention_attestation: Late 4th-century CE Sasanian coinage bearing the mint signature DA/DAL/DALAPKR (Darabgerd), and al-Tabari's account of Ardashir I serving as argbad (castellan) of Darabgerd in the early 3rd century CE.

eponym.details: Traditionally attributed to a Parthian or legendary ruler named Dara (Darius), after whom the circular fortress-city was named.

b_darabjerd.etymology_analysis: Compound of the royal/personal name Darab (Dara) + Middle Persian -gird ('fortified enclosure/town', Arabicized as -jird), meaning 'Town of Dara'; a Parthian-era circular city and major Sasanian administrative center.

b_fustujan.first_mention_attestation: 7th-century CE Arab conquest of Fars (c. 641-644 CE), recorded by al-Baladhuri (Futuh al-Buldan, p. 389) as one of the major towns of Darabgerd Khurrah.
