b_fustujan.etymology_analysis: Arabicized form of a Middle Persian toponym (*Postagan/*Fostagan) located along the Shiraz-Kerman road between Fasa and Darabgerd, attested in 7th-century CE conquest accounts.

b_nariz.first_mention_attestation: c. 262 CE trilingual inscription of Shapur I at Ka'ba-ye Zardosht (SKZ, line 50), which refers to the sahrab (governor) of Neyriz (Nariz).

morphemes.translation: early Sasanian settlement and district name

b_nariz.etymology_analysis: Ancient Iranian toponym attested in the 3rd-century CE SKZ inscription of Shapur I; situated at the eastern end of Lake Bakhtegan in Fars.

b_istakhbanat.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographers al-Istakhri (p. 108, c. 951 CE), Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE), and al-Muqaddasi (985 CE) as al-Istahbanan / Istahbanat.
b_istakhbanat.etymology_analysis: Toponym of Darabgerd province (also spelled al-Istahbanan or al-Isbahanat in medieval Arabic sources), shortened in modern Persian to Estahban; first attested in 10th-century CE geographical works.

b_abade-darabjerd.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographers al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (985 CE) as Abadah (modern Abadeh Tashk) near Lake Bakhtegan.
b_abade-darabjerd.etymology_analysis: Compound CK3 disambiguation of Abadeh (Abadeh Tashk, from Persian abadah, 'cultivated/inhabited place') with the province name Darabjerd; known in 9th-10th century sources also as Qaryat 'Abd al-Rahman, with the name Abadah attested from the 10th century CE.

b_naband.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographer al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) describing Naband as a harbour on the Zuhayr coast (Sif Zuhayr) of Irahistan.
b_naband.etymology_analysis: Persian coastal toponym (Naband / Nayband) on the Persian Gulf in Irahistan, situated at the head of the Khawr Naband creek; first attested in 10th-century CE Arabic geography.

b_siraf.first_mention_attestation: 650/651 CE Arab conquest of Fars (al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, p. 391), corroborated by archaeological excavations revealing a Sasanian port and fortress.
b_siraf.etymology_analysis: Ancient Sasanian and early Islamic emporium on the Persian Gulf coast of Fars, conquered in 650/651 CE and later the premier maritime port of the Persian Gulf in the 9th-10th centuries CE.

b_kariyan.first_mention_attestation: Sasanian Zoroastrian tradition preserved in the Greater Bundahishn and Wizidagiha i Zadspram (11.9) and al-Mas'udi's account of the division of the Adur Farnbagh sacred fire at Kariyan during the 7th-century CE Arab conquest.
b_kariyan.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Middle Persian district name Kar + -iyan suffix; famous in Sasanian and early Islamic times as the site of Adur Farnbagh, one of the three supreme Zoroastrian fire temples.

b_istakhr.first_mention_attestation: Early 3rd-century CE Sasanian coinage from Ardashir I's coronation in 205/206 CE, Sasanian administrative sealings, Synodicon Orientale (bishopric in 424 CE), and 648-651 CE Arab conquest accounts.
b_istakhr.etymology_analysis: From Middle Persian Staxr (Old Persian *staxra-, 'strong/firm'), Arabicized as Istakhr; capital of Persis/Fars under the Frataraka, Parthians, and early Sasanians.

b_iqlid.first_mention_attestation: 982 CE Hudud al-'Alam (as Kelid, 'key' to Fars) and early 12th-century CE Fars-nama of Ibn al-Balkhi (as Iqlid); a 5th-century CE Middle Persian inscription exists in Eqlid but does not attest the toponym Iqlid itself.
b_iqlid.etymology_analysis: Arabicized form (Iqlid) of Persian Kelid ('key', ultimately from Greek kleis/kleidos or Iranian kil/kilil 'gateway'), referring to its strategic position on the northern approach to Fars; first attested as Kelid in 982 CE.

b_mayin.first_mention_attestation: 985 CE al-Muqaddasi describing Mayin as the populous capital of the Ramjird district in Istakhr province (Le Strange, Lands of the Eastern Caliphate, p. 281).
b_mayin.etymology_analysis: Medieval Persian town in the Ramjird district north of Shiraz on the summer road to Isfahan; first attested in late 10th-century CE Arabic geography (al-Muqaddasi).

b_abraj.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographers al-Istakhri (pp. 102, 136, c. 951 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (985 CE, pp. 457-458) as a town and fortress (Diz Abraj) near the Kur River in Istakhr.
b_abraj.etymology_analysis: Medieval Persian town and mountain fortress (Diz Abraj, modern Shahrak-e Abraj in Marvdasht County), first attested in 10th-century CE geographical works.

b_abada.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; northern Abadeh on the Shiraz-Isfahan road appears only in post-867 medieval and early modern itineraries (distinct from Abadeh Tashk).
b_abada.etymology_analysis: From Persian abadah ('cultivated/inhabited place'); a minor northern Fars station between Isfahan and Shiraz with no attested pre-867 CE history.

b_lar.first_mention_attestation: Early 12th-century CE rise of the Miladian dynasty of Laristan (Larestan) and subsequent 13th-14th century CE accounts (Ibn Battuta, Mustawfi); an earlier coastal village Lar in Kujaran is unidentified.

morphemes.translation: settlement and regional name of Larestan

b_lar.etymology_analysis: Toponym of southern Fars (capital of Larestan), traditionally linked to the legendary hero Gorgin (son of Milad); the inland city is not securely attested before the 12th century CE.

b_gerash.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE local historical references; although Sasanian-era waterworks (Tag-e-Av dam) exist nearby, the settlement name Gerash is not attested <= 867 CE.
b_gerash.etymology_analysis: Southern Fars (Achomi-speaking) town in Larestan; despite Sasanian-era structures in the surrounding canyon, the name Gerash is first attested in the 10th century CE.

b_jahrum.first_mention_attestation: 641 CE (20 AH) Arab conquest of Fars (al-Baladhuri, al-Tabari), naming Jahram as one of the major towns of Darabgerd Khurrah; also associated with the Sasanian mint signature GHL.
b_jahrum.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic Iranian toponym in southern Fars (Jahram/Jahrom), attested in 7th-century CE Arab conquest narratives and medieval geographical texts.

b_mandestan.first_mention_attestation: c. 1110 CE Fars-nama of Ibn al-Balkhi and 1340 CE Nuzhat al-Qulub of Mustawfi for the form Mandistan; the underlying name Mand is attested c. 600 CE in the Middle Persian Karnamag i Ardashir i Pabagan (VIII.7).
b_mandestan.etymology_analysis: Compound of the hydronym Mand (the lower course of the Sakkan/Mond River) + Persian -istan ('country/region of Mand'); the suffixed form Mandistan is attested from c. 1110 CE, while Mand itself appears c. 600 CE.

historical_names.name: Mand
historical_names.source: Middle Persian Karnamag i Ardashir i Pabagan (VIII.7, c. 600 CE), mentioning the village of Mand.
historical_names.notes: Mand is attested in Sasanian Middle Persian literature; the regional suffix -istan was added in Islamic-era Persian geography.

b_bushkanat.first_mention_attestation: c. 1110 CE Fars-nama of Ibn al-Balkhi and 1340 CE Nuzhat al-Qulub of Mustawfi (Le Strange, p. 260).
b_bushkanat.etymology_analysis: Persian district name Bushkan with the collective suffix -at, located between Ghundijan and Mandistan in southern Fars; first attested in early 12th-century CE sources.

b_gundijan.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographers al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (985 CE), as well as Ibn al-Balkhi (c. 1110 CE), describing Ghundijan in the Dasht-i Barin district (Le Strange, pp. 260, 268).
b_gundijan.etymology_analysis: Medieval Persian town in Dasht-i Barin (between Jirrah and Tawwaj), famous for carpets and veils in the 10th century CE; not attested in written sources <= 867 CE.

b_firuzabad.first_mention_attestation: c. 700 CE Umayyad Arab-Sasanian copper fals of al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf bearing the Pahlavi mint name pylwj'b'd (Perozabad), later popularized by Buyid ruler Adud al-Dawla (r. 949-983 CE) to replace Gor.
b_firuzabad.etymology_analysis: From Middle Persian Perozabad ('City of Victory', New Persian Firuzabad); attested as a mint on late 7th/early 8th-century CE Arab-Sasanian coinage and adopted as the city's primary name under the 10th-century Buyids.

historical_names.name: Gōr
historical_names.source: Early 3rd-century CE Sasanian foundation by Ardashir I (r. 224-242 CE), mint signature ART, and 649-650 CE Arab conquest accounts.
historical_names.notes: Original Achaemenid/Sasanian name of the circular city before Perozabad/Firuzabad superseded it.

historical_names.name: Jūr
historical_names.source: Early 3rd-century CE Sasanian foundation by Ardashir I (r. 224-242 CE), mint signature ART, and 649-650 CE Arab conquest accounts.
historical_names.notes: Original Achaemenid/Sasanian name of the circular city before Perozabad/Firuzabad superseded it.

historical_names.name: Ardašīr-Xwarrah
historical_names.source: Early 3rd-century CE Sasanian foundation by Ardashir I (r. 224-242 CE), mint signature ART, and 649-650 CE Arab conquest accounts.
historical_names.notes: Original Achaemenid/Sasanian name of the circular city before Perozabad/Firuzabad superseded it.

b_karzin.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographer al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) describing Karzin as a fortified town on the Sakkan River in the Qubad Khurrah district (Le Strange, p. 254).
b_karzin.etymology_analysis: Medieval Persian town in the Qubad Khurrah district of Fars on the Sakkan River; while Sasanian/Arab-Sasanian coins bear the district signature Qobad Khurrah, the toponym Karzin itself is first attested in 10th-century CE sources.

b_shiraz-farsi.first_mention_attestation: c. 500 BCE Elamite Persepolis Fortification Tablets (mentioning Tirazzis/Sirazzis), Sasanian clay sealings from Qasr-e Abu Nasr (Siraz), and 693 CE Umayyad refoundation.

morphemes.language: New Persian (from Old Persian *Širājiš / Elamite Tirazziš)

b_shiraz-farsi.etymology_analysis: From Elamite Tirazzis/Sirazzis (c. 500 BCE) via Old Persian *Sirajis and Middle Persian Siraz; attested on Sasanian administrative sealings before becoming the Islamic capital of Fars.

b_sarwistan-shirazi-runiz.first_mention_attestation: 985 CE al-Muqaddasi attesting both Sarvistan (Khawristan) and Runij (Runiz); although the Sarvestan monument dates archaeologically to c. 658-683 CE, the settlement names are first attested in 10th-century CE texts.
b_sarwistan-shirazi-runiz.etymology_analysis: Composite CK3 barony key combining Sarvistan ('place of cypresses'), Shirazi ('of Shiraz'), and Runiz (medieval Runij in eastern Fars); neither the compound nor its constituent toponyms have pre-867 CE written attestations.

b_kubanjan.first_mention_attestation: c. 1110 CE Fars-nama of Ibn al-Balkhi and 1340 CE Nuzhat al-Qulub of Mustawfi describing Kubanjan as a small town near Sarvistan (Le Strange, p. 252).
b_kubanjan.etymology_analysis: Medieval Persian town near Sarvistan in Fars, first attested in early 12th-century CE geographical literature.

b_kazarun.first_mention_attestation: c. 620 CE Middle Persian lawbook Madigan i Hazar Dadestan (MHD 5.6-7, mentioning the datwar [judge] of Kazerun) and 650/651 CE Arab conquest accounts.

morphemes.translation: Sasanian town name in Shapur Khurrah

b_kazarun.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic Iranian toponym in western Fars, attested in the late Sasanian legal compilation Madigan i Hazar Dadestan and early Islamic conquest narratives.

b_sabur.first_mention_attestation: 266 CE foundation of Bishapur (Weh-Sabuhr) by Sasanian emperor Shapur I, attested in Sasanian inscriptions, coinage (BYŠ), and 646 CE Arab conquest accounts (Arabic Sabur).

eponym.details: Named after Sasanian emperor Shapur I (r. 240-270 CE).

b_sabur.etymology_analysis: Arabicized form (Sabur) of Middle Persian Sabuhr / Weh-Sabuhr (Bishapur, 'Good [city of] Shapur'), founded by Shapur I in 266 CE.

b_dinawar.first_mention_attestation: Early 6th-century CE Sasanian fortified town mentioned in connection with Khazar incursions (al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, p. 194) and 642 CE Arab conquest (as Mah al-Kufa).
b_dinawar.etymology_analysis: Sasanian and early Islamic city northeast of Kermanshah in Jibal (Media), also an East Syriac bishopric (Madkai) and later known in early Islamic administration as Mah al-Kufa.

b_andarab_d.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; no settlement named Andarab is attested in the Dinawar region of Jibal in pre-867 sources.
b_andarab_d.etymology_analysis: Persian compound andar-ab ('between the waters'); used here as a CK3 sub-barony in Dinawar without pre-867 CE attestation.

b_sad_khaniya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; no pre-867 CE written attestation exists for Sad Khaniya in Dinawar.
b_sad_khaniya.etymology_analysis: Persian/Kurdish compound ('Hundred Houses/Springs'); unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources.

b_sanda.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; no pre-867 CE written attestation exists for Sanda in Dinawar.
b_sanda.etymology_analysis: Unattested sub-barony name assigned to Dinawar in CK3 without pre-867 CE historical documentation.

b_hamadan.first_mention_attestation: c. 520 BCE Behistun Inscription of Darius I (Old Persian Hagmatana) and Classical Greek Ecbatana; Middle Persian and early Islamic Hamadan/Hamadhan (conquered 642-644 CE).
b_hamadan.etymology_analysis: From Old Persian Hagmatana ('place of gathering/assembly'), capital of Media, evolving through Middle Persian to New Persian Hamadan.

b_rudhrawar.first_mention_attestation: c. 903 CE Kitab al-Buldan of Ibn al-Faqih al-Hamadhani, describing Rudhrawar between Hamadan and Nihawand as a fertile saffron-producing district (later in al-Istakhri, Yaqut, and Mustawfi).
b_rudhrawar.etymology_analysis: Persian toponym (Rudhrawar/Rudavar, 'abounding in streams'), denoting the fertile valley between Hamadan and Nihawand; first attested in Ibn al-Faqih (c. 903 CE).

b_aba.first_mention_attestation: Late 9th-century CE letter of Imam Hasan al-Askari (d. 874 CE) to the people of Qom and Aveh (Aba), and later 13th-14th century CE geographers Yaqut and Mustawfi.
b_aba.etymology_analysis: Early Islamic Persian town (Aba/Abah, modern Aveh) near Saveh in Jibal; attested from the late 9th century CE (post-867 CE) and in Yaqut (1220s CE).

b_mazdaqan.first_mention_attestation: Early 13th-century CE Mu'jam al-Buldan of Yaqut al-Hamawi (mentioning the ribat at Muzdaqan) and 1340 CE Nuzhat al-Qulub of Mustawfi (Le Strange, pp. 211-212).
b_mazdaqan.etymology_analysis: Named after the Mazdaqan (Muzdaqan/Mazlaghan) River flowing past Saveh; first attested in 13th-14th century CE geographical works.

b_sharuq.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; no pre-867 CE written attestation exists for Sharuq in Hamadan.
b_sharuq.etymology_analysis: Unattested sub-barony name in Hamadan without pre-867 CE historical documentation.

b_nihawand.first_mention_attestation: 642 CE Battle of Nihawand (al-Baladhuri, al-Tabari), preceded by Sasanian and Seleucid (Laodicea) occupation.
b_nihawand.etymology_analysis: Ancient Iranian city in Media/Jibal (Hellenistic Laodicea, Middle Persian Nihawand), site of the decisive 642 CE Battle of Nihawand.

b_abtaa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; no pre-867 CE written attestation exists for Abtaa in Nihawand.
b_abtaa.etymology_analysis: Unattested sub-barony name in Nihawand without pre-867 CE historical documentation.

b_karaj-abu-dulad.first_mention_attestation: Early 9th-century CE Abbasid sources (al-Tabari, Ibn Khordadbeh) recording the completion of Karaj by Abu Dulaf al-Ijli (d. 840/841 CE) and Khurramite raids on Karaj in 841-847 CE.

eponym.details: Named after Abu Dulaf al-Qasim ibn 'Isa al-'Ijli (d. 840/841 CE), Abbasid general and governor of Jibal who completed the city.

morphemes.translation: personal kunya of Abu Dulaf al-'Ijli

b_karaj-abu-dulad.etymology_analysis: Named Karaj of Abu Dulaf (Karaj-i Abi Dulaf) after the early 9th-century CE Abbasid commander Abu Dulaf al-Ijli (d. 840/841 CE) to distinguish it from Karaj of Rudhrawar.

b_hormuz.first_mention_attestation: 325 BCE voyage of Nearchus (Harmozeia in Arrian's Indica), Ammianus Marcellinus (Harmozia, 4th c. CE), and 650-651 CE Arab conquest (al-Baladhuri, pp. 391-392).
b_hormuz.etymology_analysis: From Old/Middle Persian Ohrmazd (Ahura Mazda), attested in Greek as Harmozeia (325 BCE) for Old Hormuz on the mainland near Minab before the 14th-century CE transfer to Jarun Island.

b_shahru.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographers al-Istakhri (pp. 163, 166-167, c. 951 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (985 CE) describing the coastal port of Suru/Shahru opposite Hormuz (near modern Bandar Abbas).
b_shahru.etymology_analysis: Medieval Persian Gulf port (Suru or Shahru) opposite Hormuz Island, first attested as Shahru in 10th-century CE geographical accounts.

b_laft.first_mention_attestation: Early 13th-century CE Mu'jam al-Buldan of Yaqut al-Hamawi stating that the island of Bani Kawan / Abarkafan (Qeshm) was also known as Laft (Le Strange, p. 261).
b_laft.etymology_analysis: Historic port on the northern shore of Qeshm Island; while Qeshm was inhabited in antiquity, the specific toponym Laft is first attested in Yaqut (13th century CE).

historical_names.name: Banī Kāwān
historical_names.source: 7th-century CE Arab conquest accounts (al-Baladhuri) and early Islamic geographers naming Qeshm Island Bani Kawan / Abarkafan.
historical_names.notes: Earlier medieval Arabic/Persian names for Qeshm Island before Laft became standard in Yaqut.

historical_names.name: Abarkāfān
historical_names.source: 7th-century CE Arab conquest accounts (al-Baladhuri) and early Islamic geographers naming Qeshm Island Bani Kawan / Abarkafan.
historical_names.notes: Earlier medieval Arabic/Persian names for Qeshm Island before Laft became standard in Yaqut.

b_huzu.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century CE Islamic geographer al-Istakhri (pp. 116, 140, c. 951 CE) and Ibn Hawqal (p. 188) describing Huzu as a strong Buyid fortress and port on the Sif 'Umara coast opposite Kish Island.
b_huzu.etymology_analysis: Medieval coastal fortress and port of embarkation for Kish Island in the Sif 'Umara region of Fars; first attested in 10th-century CE Islamic geography.

b_kaurestan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern town (Kahurestan) in Khamir County, Hormozgan Province, without pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_kaurestan.etymology_analysis: From Persian kahur ('Prosopis cineraria tree') + -estan ('place of'); modern settlement in Hormozgan unattested <= 867 CE.

b_beiram.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern town (Beyram) in Larestan County, Fars Province, without pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_beiram.etymology_analysis: Southern Fars settlement in Larestan County (Beyram), unattested in historical sources <= 867 CE.

b_dun.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; no pre-867 CE written attestation exists for Dun in the Sif-i-Umara / Hormuz region.
b_dun.etymology_analysis: Unattested sub-barony name in Sif-i-Umara without pre-867 CE historical documentation.

b_dazuk.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern village (Dazuk) in Qaleh Ganj County, Kerman Province, without pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_dazuk.etymology_analysis: Modern village name in southern Iran (Dazuk in Kerman/Hormozgan borderlands), unattested in historical sources <= 867 CE.

b_qashan.first_mention_attestation: Ibn Khordadbeh, Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 870 CE, as Qashan/Qasan); also al-Ya'qubi (891 CE). No pre-Islamic written references exist.
b_qashan.etymology_analysis: Derived from the ethnonym of the Kasian (Kassite/Kasian) inhabitants of the oasis near prehistoric Tepe Sialk, yielding Middle/New Persian Kashan (Arabized Qasan/Qashan).

b_natanz.first_mention_attestation: Inscribed Buyid octagonal pavilion in Natanz dated 389 AH (998-999 CE); in geographical literature first mentioned by Yaqut al-Hamawi (c. 1225 CE) as Natanz/Natanzah.

morphemes.translation: toponym of uncertain pre-Islamic Iranian origin

b_natanz.etymology_analysis: Central Iranian toponym (Persian Naṭanz) located at the foot of the Karkas Mountains; no pre-867 CE written attestation is recorded.

b_ardistan.first_mention_attestation: Sasanian town attested in early Islamic geographical traditions as the birthplace of Khosrow I Anushirvan (born c. 512-514 CE) and site of a Sasanian fire temple.
b_ardistan.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Persian *ardastāna (attested in Achaemenid inscriptions, meaning 'stone construction' or 'place of order'), rather than the folk etymology from Persian ārd ('flour').

b_uzwara.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written geographical sources as Uzvarah by Yaqut al-Hamawi (Mu'jam al-Buldan, c. 1225 CE), later Zuvarah (Zavareh) in Mustawfi (1340 CE).

eponym.details: Named in Persian tradition after Zavara (Zavareh), brother of the mythical hero Rostam in the Shahnameh.

b_uzwara.etymology_analysis: Arabicized as Uzwāra by Yaqut al-Hamawi from Persian Zavāreh, traditionally linked to the legendary Iranian hero Zavara.

b_isfahan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Aspadana in Ptolemy's Geographia (c. 150 CE) and as Spahān in 3rd-century CE Middle Persian inscriptions of Kartir.
b_isfahan.etymology_analysis: From Old Persian *spādāna- ('place of the army / military gathering'), yielding Middle Persian Spahān and Arabicized Isfahān.

b_julfa.first_mention_attestation: Established in 1605-1606 CE as New Julfa by Shah Abbas I for Armenian deportees from Old Julfa (Nakhchivan).

morphemes.translation: transferred toponym from Old Julfa on the Araxes

b_julfa.etymology_analysis: Named after the older Armenian trading town of Julfa (Jugha) on the Araxes River when Shah Abbas I resettled its inhabitants south of Isfahan in 1605-1606 CE.

b_gulpaygan.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in Islamic geographical works by al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (985 CE) as Jurbādhaqān.
b_gulpaygan.etymology_analysis: Recorded in early Islamic Arabic as Jurbādhaqān (from Middle Persian *Gulpāyagān / *Gorbādagān), meaning 'place of roses' or 'place of the guardians'.

b_wazwan.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found for Vazvan (Wazwan) in Isfahan province.
b_wazwan.etymology_analysis: Central Iranian toponym (Persian Vazvān) northwest of Isfahan, known for its ancient qanat system, but lacking written attestation by 867 CE.

b_asbid-dasht.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found for Asbid-Dasht (Sepid-Dasht / Sefid-Dasht).
b_asbid-dasht.etymology_analysis: Persian compound of asbīd/sepīd ('white') and dasht ('plain'), literally 'White Plain'.

b_juy-e-sard.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found for Juy-e-Sard.
b_juy-e-sard.etymology_analysis: Persian hydronymic compound meaning 'Cold Stream' (jūy-e sard).

b_qumisha.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written sources as Qūmisah / Qūmiša by al-Muqaddasi (985 CE) on the northern frontier of Fars; renamed Shahreza in the 20th century.
b_qumisha.etymology_analysis: Historical Persian toponym Qūmiša (spelled Qūmisah by al-Muqaddasi in 985 CE), later replaced by Shahreza.

b_jarquh.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written geographical literature as Jarqūh by Yaqut al-Hamawi (Mu'jam al-Buldan, II, p. 63, c. 1225 CE).
b_jarquh.etymology_analysis: From Iranian components gar and kūh (both meaning 'mountain'), or from Avestan gufra- ('deep/lower') + kūh ('lower mountain', contrasting with Abarquh 'upper mountain').

b_sarwistan.first_mention_attestation: Sarvestan in Fars is first attested by 10th-century Islamic geographers (al-Istakhri, c. 951 CE); no pre-867 CE written attestation exists for a holding of this name in Qumisha.
b_sarwistan.etymology_analysis: Persian toponym meaning 'cypress grove / place of cypresses' (sarv + -istān).

b_wardana.first_mention_attestation: Varzana/Vardaneh settlements in central Iran (near Isfahan and Qom) are first attested in 10th-century sources such as Tarikh-i Qum (988 CE); no pre-867 CE written attestation exists for Wardana in Qumisha.
b_wardana.etymology_analysis: Related to Old Persian vardana- / vṛdana- ('town, settlement', cognate with Northwest Iranian barzan 'quarter').

b_firuzan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Firuzan, chief town of the Khanlanjan district south of Isfahan, by Ibn Battuta (c. 1330 CE).

eponym.details: Derived from the Persian personal name Firuzan (Middle Persian Pērōzān), though the specific namesake is unattested.

b_firuzan.etymology_analysis: From Middle Persian Pērōzān (New Persian Fīrūzān), based on pērōz ('victorious').

b_kermanshah.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 390 CE by Sasanian King Bahram IV, who bore the title Kirmanshah ('King of Kirman').

eponym.details: Named after Sasanian King Bahram IV (r. 388-399 CE), whose earlier princely title was Kirmanshah ('King of Kirman').

b_kermanshah.etymology_analysis: From Middle Persian Kirmānšāh ('King of Kirman'), the title held by Bahram IV before his accession, applied to the city he founded c. 390 CE.

b_kerend-kermanshah.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Elamite Karintaš in late 2nd millennium BCE (c. 1200 BCE) and as Karina in Isidore of Charax's Parthian Stations (c. 1st century BCE) and Ptolemy's Geographia.
b_kerend-kermanshah.etymology_analysis: Kerend continues Elamite Karintaš and Parthian-Greek Karina (modern Kerend-e Gharb); the compound appends Kermanshah for regional disambiguation.

b_tazar.first_mention_attestation: First attested along the Khurasan Road by Ibn Hawqal (977 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (985 CE) as Tazar (also Qasr Yazid), noting remains of a Sasanian palace.
b_tazar.etymology_analysis: From Persian tazar ('palace/pavilion', cognate with Old Persian tachara), referring to the Sasanian palace ruins along the Khurasan Road.

b_bisutun.first_mention_attestation: Site of Darius I's trilingual Behistun Inscription (c. 520 BCE) and attested as Bagistanon in Ctesias / Diodorus Siculus.
b_bisutun.etymology_analysis: From Old Persian *Bagastāna ('place/stand of the god(s)'), evolving through Middle Persian *Bayistūn to New Persian Bīsotūn/Bīsutūn.

b_siravan.first_mention_attestation: Chief town of Masabadhan (classical Masabatike), attested as al-Sirawan in early Islamic conquest accounts (c. 643 CE, recorded by al-Baladhuri).
b_siravan.etymology_analysis: Sasanian and early Islamic administrative center of Masabadhan (modern Sirvan in Ilam province), written al-Sīrawān in Arabic geographers.

b_alishtar.first_mention_attestation: First reliably attested as Alishtar (Lashtar/Lishtar) in Hamdallah Mustawfi's Nuzhat al-Qulub (1340 CE); earlier 10th-century manuscript readings (al-Bashr) are uncertain.
b_alishtar.etymology_analysis: Toponym in northern Lorestan (modern Aleshtar), recorded as Alīshtar/Lāshtar in Ilkhanid-era sources; no pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_arivajan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Ariyujan (Ariyohan) alongside al-Sirawan as a town of Masabadhan in 10th-century Islamic geographers (Ibn Hawqal 977 CE, al-Muqaddasi 985 CE).
b_arivajan.etymology_analysis: Medieval Iranian toponym in Masabadhan (modern Ilam region), first documented in 10th-century Arabic geographical works.

b_saburkhawasht.first_mention_attestation: Founded under the Sasanian Empire by Shapur I (r. 240-270 CE) or Shapur II (4th century CE) as Shapurkhwast (Arabic Saburkhwast).

eponym.details: Named after Sasanian King Shapur I (or Shapur II), meaning 'Shapur's Desire'.

b_saburkhawasht.etymology_analysis: Middle Persian Šāpūr-xwāst ('Shapur's Desire'), Arabicized as Sābūrkhwāst, predecessor of medieval Khorramabad.

b_as-saimara.first_mention_attestation: Sasanian city in Mihrijanqadhaq (traditionally attributed to Khosrow II, r. 590-628 CE), conquered by Arab forces c. 642 CE and known as al-Saymarah.
b_as-saimara.etymology_analysis: Arabicized form (al-Ṣaymarah / as-Saimara) of Sasanian/Persian Seymareh, located at modern Darreh Shahr.

b_andamish.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written sources as Qantarat al-Andamish ('Bridge of Andamish') by al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (985 CE).

morphemes.translation: medieval name for Dezful / bridge site

b_andamish.etymology_analysis: Medieval Persian toponym Andāmīš (modern Andimeshk), originally applied to the Sasanian bridge and settlement at Dezful in 10th-century Arabic geographies.

b_abbadan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Apphana in Ptolemy (2nd century CE) and Apphadana in Marcian (4th century CE), and as 'Abbadan in al-Baladhuri (recording Umayyad garrison c. 700 CE).

eponym.details: Folk-etymologized by al-Baladhuri as named after Umayyad commander 'Abbad ibn Husayn (c. 700 CE), though Iranian etymology derives it from āb-pā-ān.

b_abbadan.etymology_analysis: Iranian etymology derives Abadan from āb ('water') + pā ('watch/guard'), i.e. 'coastguard station' (cf. Greek Apphadana), Arabicized as 'Abbādān.

b_bayan.first_mention_attestation: First attested in al-Tabari's History for 875 CE (campaigns of Musa ibn Bugha and Ibn Muflih during the Zanj Rebellion) and in Ibn Serapion (c. 900 CE).

morphemes.translation: town at the mouth of Nahr Bayan (modern Khorramshahr)

b_bayan.etymology_analysis: Medieval port town at the mouth of the Nahr Bayan canal connecting the Tigris and Karun estuaries (site of modern Khorramshahr), first documented in 875 CE.

b_basiyan.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 10th-century Islamic geographers al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (985 CE) as a coastal/estuarine town and fortress in Khuzestan.

morphemes.translation: medieval coastal fortress and town in Khuzestan

b_basiyan.etymology_analysis: Medieval town and Abbasid prison-fortress at the mouth of the Dawraq channels in southern Khuzestan, first documented in the 10th century CE.

b_ahvaz.first_mention_attestation: Founded by Sasanian King Hormizd I (r. 270-271 CE) as Hormizd-Ardashir; conquered by Arab Muslims in 638 CE as Suq al-Ahwaz.

morphemes.translation: plural of Hūz/Khūz (the Khuzi / Elamite people)

b_ahvaz.etymology_analysis: Arabic broken plural (al-Ahwāz) of Hūz/Khūz, referring to the Khūzī people (ancient Ouxioi) of Khuzestan, applied to Sasanian Hormizd-Ardashir.

historical_names.name: Hormizd-Ardashir
historical_names.source: Sasanian foundation by Hormizd I (270 CE) as Hormizd-Ardashir, prior to the 638 CE Arab-Islamic name Suq al-Ahwaz / al-Ahwaz.
historical_names.notes: Sasanian Hormizd-Ardashir (270 CE) preceded the Arabicized name Suq al-Ahwaz / al-Ahwaz (638 CE).

b_al-madhar.first_mention_attestation: Site of the Battle of al-Madhar (Battle of the River) in April 633 CE during the Rashidun conquest of Sasanian Mesopotamia/Maysan.
b_al-madhar.etymology_analysis: Early Islamic and Sasanian-era town in Maysan (Lower Tigris/Karun borderlands), attested in April 633 CE.

b_basinna.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 10th-century Islamic geographers (al-Istakhri c. 951 CE, al-Muqaddasi 985 CE) as a textile-producing town south of Susa.
b_basinna.etymology_analysis: Medieval town south of Susa on the Little Tigris canal, famed for curtains and woolens in 10th-century geographical sources.

b_huwaiza.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 980 CE by the Asad Bedouin chief Dubays ibn 'Afif al-Asadi.
b_huwaiza.etymology_analysis: Arabic diminutive al-Ḥuwayza (Persian Hoveyzeh), founded in 980 CE in western Khuzestan.

b_jubba.first_mention_attestation: First attested in al-Tabari's History for 871 CE as a base of operations during the Zanj Rebellion in al-Ahwaz.
b_jubba.etymology_analysis: Medieval sugarcane-producing town in Khuzestan, first documented in 871 CE during the Zanj Rebellion.

b_dawraq.first_mention_attestation: Sasanian city of Dawraq al-Furs, traditionally attributed to Kawad I (r. 488-531 CE) and attested in early Islamic conquest and Zanj narratives.
b_dawraq.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic Sasanian town (Dawraq al-Furs) on the Dawraq River, precursor of modern Shadegan.

b_azam.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found for Azam in the Dawraq district of Khuzestan.
b_azam.etymology_analysis: Unattested in medieval historical sources for Dawraq; Arabic aʿẓam means 'greatest'.

b_ramhurmuz.first_mention_attestation: Founded by Sasanian King Hormizd I (r. 270-271 CE) as Ram-Hormizd-Ardashir; Umayyad silver dirhams minted there by 714-715 CE.

eponym.details: Named after Sasanian King Hormizd I (r. 270-271 CE).

b_ramhurmuz.etymology_analysis: Abbreviation of Middle Persian Rām-Hormozd-Ardašīr ('Ardashir's peace of Hormizd'), founded by Hormizd I in 270-271 CE.

b_asak.first_mention_attestation: Site of a Sasanian domed hall (aywan) built by Kawad I (r. 488-531 CE) and attested in 679-680 CE as the battleground of Kharijite leader Abu Bilal Mirdas.
b_asak.etymology_analysis: Sasanian and early Islamic town between Ramhurmuz and Arrajan, attested in 7th-century Kharijite battles and 10th-century geographies.

b_idhaj.first_mention_attestation: Attested in early Islamic chronicles during the Kurdish rebellion at Idhaj under Caliph Uthman (c. 649-651 CE); modern Izeh.
b_idhaj.etymology_analysis: Arabicized as Īḏaj from Persian Īzeh (modern Izeh, also later called Mal-Amir), attested from the mid-7th century CE.

b_dariyan.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found for Dariyan in the Ramhurmuz district of Khuzestan.
b_dariyan.etymology_analysis: Persian toponym (homonymous with Darian in Fars) without pre-867 CE attestation in Khuzestan.

b_lurijan.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Lurjan (Lurdagan), capital of the Sardan district, in al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE).
b_lurijan.etymology_analysis: Derived from the ethnonym Lur with the Persian toponymic suffix -igān/-ijān (modern Lordegan), first recorded by al-Istakhri in 951 CE.

b_aruj.first_mention_attestation: First attested as 'Aruj (also called Susan) northwest of Idhaj in Hamdallah Mustawfi's Nuzhat al-Qulub (1340 CE).

morphemes.translation: small town on the upper Karun near Idhaj

b_aruj.etymology_analysis: Medieval town on both banks of the upper Karun four leagues northwest of Idhaj, first documented in 14th-century Mustawfi.

b_samshiborid.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found for Samshiborid.
b_samshiborid.etymology_analysis: Appears to reflect Persian šamšīr-borīd ('sword-cut'), a descriptive/legendary toponym with no pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_tustar.first_mention_attestation: Attested under Sasanian King Shapur I (c. 260 CE, construction of Band-e Qaisar) and in the Siege of Shushtar/Tustar (641-642 CE).
b_tustar.etymology_analysis: Arabicized as Tustar from Persian Šūštar, traditionally analyzed as Šūš + -tar ('greater/better than Susa'), a major Sasanian stronghold.

b_gondishapur.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 271 CE by Sasanian King Shapur I as Weh-Andiyok-Shapur (Middle Persian Gundēšāhpūr; Syriac Beth Lapat).

eponym.details: Named after Sasanian King Shapur I (r. 240-270 CE).

b_gondishapur.etymology_analysis: Middle Persian Gondēšāpūr (from Gund-dēz-ī Šāpūr or Weh-Andiyōk-Šāpūr, 'Better-than-Antioch of Shapur'), Arabicized as Jundaysābūr.

b_bazoh.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found for Bazoh in the Tustar district of Khuzestan.
b_bazoh.etymology_analysis: Unattested in medieval historical sources for Tustar/Khuzestan.

b_dizful.first_mention_attestation: Although the Sasanian bridge dates to Shapur II (4th century CE), the name Dezful (Dezh-pol) is first attested in the 12th century CE; in the 10th century it was called Qantarat al-Andamish.
b_dizful.etymology_analysis: From Persian Dež-pol ('fortress bridge'), Arabicized as Dizfūl/Dezfūl in the 12th century CE.

b_as-sus.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 3rd-millennium BCE Elamite and Mesopotamian cuneiform records as Šušan/Šušim, Old Persian Çūšā, and early Islamic al-Sūs.
b_as-sus.etymology_analysis: Arabicized form al-Sūs of ancient Elamite Šušan (Greek Susa, Persian Shush), one of the oldest continuously attested cities of the Near East.

b_bamm.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Middle Persian Kar-Namag i Ardashir i Pabagan (c. 600 CE) in the legend of Haftvad and in the Arab conquest of Kirman (644 CE).
b_bamm.etymology_analysis: Persian Bam, written Bamm in Arabic to conform to triliteral root morphology, attested from Sasanian-era Middle Persian literature.

b_kashid.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned by al-Muqaddasi (985 CE, p. 460) as one of the four towns of the Khabis sub-district in Kirman.
b_kashid.etymology_analysis: Medieval town in the Khabis district of Kirman, known only from al-Muqaddasi (985 CE).

b_dardjiin.first_mention_attestation: Recorded on the Kirman-Makran caravan road by Ibn Khordadbeh (Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik, first recension c. 846 CE) as Darzin/Dayr-e Wazin.

morphemes.translation: early medieval town between Kerman and Bam

b_dardjiin.etymology_analysis: Early medieval town on the road from Sirjan to Bam, recorded by Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE) and al-Muqaddasi (985 CE).

b_nurmashiir.first_mention_attestation: Recorded as Narmasir on the Kirman-Makran caravan road by Ibn Khordadbeh (Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik, first recension c. 846 CE).
b_nurmashiir.etymology_analysis: Medieval Persian Narmāšīr (Arabicized Narmāsīr), major eastern Kirman town attested from Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE) onward.

b_dafariid.first_mention_attestation: 977 CE (Ibn Hawqal, Kitab Surat al-Ard, as Darfarid; al-Muqaddasi, 985 CE, as Darfani; modern Delfard)
b_dafariid.etymology_analysis: Variant of medieval Darfarid (modern Delfard), a fertile mountain valley north of Jiroft first recorded by 10th-century CE Arab geographers Ibn Hawqal and al-Muqaddasi.

b_behabad.first_mention_attestation: 985 CE (al-Muqaddasi, Ahsan al-Taqasim, as Bihavadh; later Yaqut al-Hamawi, c. 1225 CE, as Bihabad)
b_behabad.etymology_analysis: From Persian beh ('good') + ābād ('cultivated settlement'), recorded in 985 CE by al-Muqaddasi as Bihavadh.

b_nayband.first_mention_attestation: 977 CE (Ibn Hawqal, Kitab Surat al-Ard, as Naband, an oasis between Ravar and Khur)
b_nayband.etymology_analysis: From Persian nāy ('reed' or 'pass') + band ('dam/barrier'), referring to the desert oasis settlement recorded by Ibn Hawqal in 977 CE as Naband.

b_khubayan.first_mention_attestation: 985 CE (al-Muqaddasi, Ahsan al-Taqasim, as Kuhbanan / Kubinan; scribal variant Kubayan/Kuhbayan)
b_khubayan.etymology_analysis: From Persian Kūhbanān ('pistachio-tree mountain'), derived from kūh ('mountain') + banān ('wild pistachio'); Khubayan reflects a medieval Arabic scribal mispointing of Kuhbayan/Kuhbanan.

b_rawar.first_mention_attestation: 985 CE (al-Muqaddasi, Ahsan al-Taqasim, as Rawar / Ravar)
b_rawar.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived from Persian rāhvar ('road-guardian'), reflecting its role as a fortified desert-edge station on the Kerman-Khorasan route; first attested by al-Muqaddasi in 985 CE.

b_jiruft.first_mention_attestation: 640 CE (al-Tabari, Tarikh al-Rusul wa'l-Muluk, recording the 20 AH Arab campaign reaching Jiroft)
b_jiruft.etymology_analysis: An ancient Kerman oasis city on the Halil Rud; its name (medieval Arabic Jayruft/Jiruft) is attested in early Islamic conquest accounts of 640 CE (al-Tabari).

b_maghun.first_mention_attestation: 982 CE (Hudud al-'Alam and 10th-century CE geographers, as Mughun in southern Kerman / Jiroft district)
b_maghun.etymology_analysis: From regional Iranian mogh ('date palm', as in Moghestan) + -ūn, referring to a palm-growing town in the Jiroft-Hormuz region attested from the late 10th century CE.

b_ruyan-jirufti.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a historical settlement name in Jiroft in pre-modern geographical sources
b_ruyan-jirufti.etymology_analysis: Compound disambiguated name combining Ruyan with the nisba Jirufti ('of Jiroft'); not documented as a historical settlement in Jiroft.

b_khabis.first_mention_attestation: 652 CE (al-Tabari, Tarikh, recording capture of Khabis by Abdallah ibn Amir in 32 AH; also 789 CE gravestone)
b_khabis.etymology_analysis: Medieval name of modern Shahdad on the western edge of the Lut Desert, attested during the 652 CE Arab conquest in al-Tabari and on a 789 CE (173 AH) tombstone.

b_zarand_PER.first_mention_attestation: 985 CE (al-Muqaddasi, Ahsan al-Taqasim, describing Zarand and its fortress built by Ibn Ilyas)
b_zarand_PER.etymology_analysis: An Iranian toponym in northern Kerman province first attested in writing by al-Muqaddasi in 985 CE.

b_kirman.first_mention_attestation: c. 500 BCE (Darius I Susa inscriptions DSf/DSz as Old Persian Krmana and Elamite Kurmana; Sasanian Middle Persian Kirman)
b_kirman.etymology_analysis: From Old Persian Kṛmānā (c. 500 BCE) and Middle Persian Kirmān; the modern city was founded by Ardashir I as Weh-Ardashir (Bardsir) and adopted the provincial name Kerman in the 10th century CE.

b_anar.first_mention_attestation: c. 1225 CE (Yaqut al-Hamawi, Mu'jam al-Buldan, as Anar; earlier known as Aban in Ibn Khordadbeh, 846 CE)
b_anar.etymology_analysis: Modern Persian Anār ('pomegranate'), first appearing in Yaqut (13th century CE), replacing the earlier medieval name Aban.

historical_names.name: Aban
historical_names.source: Ibn Khordadbeh, Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846 CE)
historical_names.notes: Known in early Islamic itineraries (Ibn Khordadbeh, Istakhri) as Aban before shifting to Anar by Yaqut's time.

b_rudhan.first_mention_attestation: 846 CE (Ibn Khordadbeh, Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik, p. 48, as al-Rudhan)
b_rudhan.etymology_analysis: From Persian rūdhān ('rivers/streams'), designating the district and town between Anar and Rafsanjan attested in Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 CE).

b_mashiz.first_mention_attestation: 12th century CE (Ibn Ibrahim / Afzal al-Din Kermani, Tarikh-e Saljuqiyan-e Kerman, relating 10th-12th century events; absent from 9th-10th century Arab geographers)
b_mashiz.etymology_analysis: Historical name of modern Bardsir city, southwest of Kerman; absent from early Arab geographers and first attested in the Saljuq-era chronicles of Kerman.

b_sirjan.first_mention_attestation: 644 CE (al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, recording the Arab conquest of Sirjan; also Middle Persian Shahrestaniha i Eranshahr)
b_sirjan.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic capital of Kerman, attributed in Sasanian tradition to Bahram IV (r. 388-399 CE) and attested in early Islamic conquest accounts (al-Baladhuri) and 9th-century Pahlavi Epistles of Manushchihr.

b_bimand.first_mention_attestation: 985 CE (al-Muqaddasi, Ahsan al-Taqasim, describing Bimand as an impregnable fortress four leagues west of Sirjan)
b_bimand.etymology_analysis: Medieval fortress town west of Sirjan on the Fars frontier, first attested in writing by al-Muqaddasi in 985 CE.

b_baaft.first_mention_attestation: 982 CE (Hudud al-'Alam, p. 124, as Baft; later Yaqut, c. 1225 CE, as Bafd)
b_baaft.etymology_analysis: Highland town in Kerman south of Mashiz, first attested in the late 10th-century CE Hudud al-'Alam (982 CE).

b_qain.first_mention_attestation: 651 CE (al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, Arab conquest of Quhistan; also Middle Persian Shahrestaniha i Eranshahr as Kayen)
b_qain.etymology_analysis: From Middle Persian Kāyēn (attested in Shahrestaniha i Eranshahr), Arabicized as Qāʾin; capital of medieval Quhistan attested in early Islamic conquest records.

b_birjand.first_mention_attestation: c. 1225 CE (Yaqut al-Hamawi, Mu'jam al-Buldan, describing Birjand as a fine village/town of Quhistan)
b_birjand.etymology_analysis: Contains the Eastern Iranian settlement suffix -jand/-kand ('town'); absent from 9th-10th century Arab geographers and first attested by Yaqut al-Hamawi in the early 13th century CE.

b_khusf.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (al-Istakhri and al-Muqaddasi, 985 CE, as Khawst; modern spelling Khusf first in Mustawfi, 1340 CE)
b_khusf.etymology_analysis: Fortified town in Quhistan attested in 10th-century CE Arabic geographies as Khawst and later normalized as Khusf.

b_barandud.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in medieval historical or geographical sources; modern village in South Khorasan
b_barandud.etymology_analysis: Modern village in Darmian County, South Khorasan province, with no documented pre-modern or pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_junabid.first_mention_attestation: 651 CE (al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, p. 316, as Jonabadh during the Arab conquest of Khorasan)
b_junabid.etymology_analysis: Medieval Arabicized form Junabidh (modern Gonabad) of an Iranian settlement name, attested in al-Baladhuri's account of the 651 CE Arab conquest of Khorasan.

b_tun.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (al-Istakhri and Ibn Hawqal, 977 CE, as Tun; archaeological citadel dates to at least 9th century CE)
b_tun.etymology_analysis: Medieval name of modern Ferdows in Quhistan; first attested in writing by 10th-century CE Arab geographers (Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal).

b_bejestan.first_mention_attestation: c. 1225 CE (Yaqut al-Hamawi, Mu'jam al-Buldan, mentioning Bajistan as a village)
b_bejestan.etymology_analysis: Iranian place-name with the locative suffix -estān, first attested in writing by Yaqut al-Hamawi in the early 13th century CE.

b_tabas.first_mention_attestation: 651 CE (al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan, p. 403, calling Tabas 'the Gate of Khurasan' during the Arab conquest)
b_tabas.etymology_analysis: Desert oasis town on the border of Khorasan and Yazd, attested in al-Baladhuri (651 CE Arab conquest) as Tabas.

b_khur.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (al-Istakhri and Ibn Hawqal, 977 CE, as Khur in Quhistan)
b_khur.etymology_analysis: Medieval town in Quhistan southeast of Tabas, first attested in 10th-century CE Arabic geographical works (Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal).

b_raqe.first_mention_attestation: 985 CE (al-Muqaddasi, Ahsan al-Taqasim, as al-Raqqa / Ar-Rakkah, 12 leagues from Tabas; visited by Nasir-i Khusraw in 1052 CE)
b_raqe.etymology_analysis: Medieval town between Tabas and Tun (modern Raqeh in Boshruyeh), first attested by al-Muqaddasi in 985 CE.

b_khuwar.first_mention_attestation: c. 26 BCE (Isidore of Charax, Parthian Stations 8, as Choara / Choarene; later Ibn Khordadbeh, 846 CE, as al-Khuwar)
b_khuwar.etymology_analysis: From Old Iranian *huwăra- / *xwăra-, transcribed in Greek as Khoara (Choara) by Strabo, Isidore of Charax, Pliny, and Ptolemy, and in Arabic as al-Khuwar (modern Garmsar/Aradan).

b_simnan.first_mention_attestation: 846 CE (Ibn Khordadbeh, Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik, listing Samnan/Simnan as a stage on the Great Khurasan Road)
b_simnan.etymology_analysis: Ancient town in Qumis (modern Semnan) on the Great Khurasan Road, documented in Ibn Khordadbeh's 9th-century CE itinerary.

b_qom.first_mention_attestation: 702 CE (al-Baladhuri and al-Tabari, recording Arab settlement at Qumm in 83 AH; earlier Sasanian Kumandan)

morphemes.translation: hut, mound, or curtailed form of Kumandan

b_qom.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived from Persian kūmeh ('hut') or as an Arabic curtailment of Sasanian Kumandan; attested in early Islamic conquest and settlement accounts (c. 702 CE).

b_aba-qomi.first_mention_attestation: 985 CE (al-Muqaddasi, Ahsan al-Taqasim, as Ava / Avah; later Yaqut, c. 1225 CE, as Abah)
b_aba-qomi.etymology_analysis: Avah near Qom/Saveh (disambiguated as Aba-Qomi from Avah of Hamadan); first attested by al-Muqaddasi in 985 CE.

b_sawa.first_mention_attestation: 977 CE (Ibn Hawqal, Kitab Surat al-Ard, as Sawa; al-Muqaddasi, 985 CE)
b_sawa.etymology_analysis: Arabicized form Sāwa of modern Saveh on the Hamadan-Rayy road, first attested in 10th-century CE geographical works (Ibn Hawqal, al-Muqaddasi).

b_rayy.first_mention_attestation: 520 BCE (Behistun Inscription of Darius I, as Old Persian Raga; also Avestan Ragha and Greek Rhagai)

morphemes.translation: ancient Iranian city name (cf. Avestan Raγā)

b_rayy.etymology_analysis: From Old Persian Ragā (Behistun Inscription, 520 BCE) and Avestan Raγā, Greek Rhágai/Rhages, Middle Persian Ray, Arabic al-Rayy.

b_dumbawand.first_mention_attestation: 651 CE (al-Tabari, Tarikh, recording the Masmughan Mardanshah of Dunbawand during the Arab conquest; also Sasanian Middle Persian Dunbawand)
b_dumbawand.etymology_analysis: From Middle Persian Dunbāwand / Dumbāwand (modern Damavand), named after Mount Damavand; attested in Sasanian texts and al-Tabari (651 CE).

b_waramin.first_mention_attestation: 977 CE (Ibn Hawqal, Kitab Surat al-Ard, listing Waramin as a large village/district near Rayy)
b_waramin.etymology_analysis: Modern Varamin south of Rayy; first attested in writing by Ibn Hawqal in 977 CE, later replacing Rayy as the regional center after the Mongol invasion.

b_mashkuya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a settlement name near Rayy in medieval or classical sources
b_mashkuya.etymology_analysis: Unattested as a geographical settlement in the Rayy region; structurally resembles the Persian personal name Mushkūya (Miskawayh).

b_qasran.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (al-Istakhri, Kitab Masalik al-Mamalik, and Ibn Hawqal, 977 CE, as al-Qasran, 'the Two Palaces')
b_qasran.etymology_analysis: Arabic dual al-Qaṣrān ('the Two Palaces'), referring to Inner and Outer Qasran north of Rayy (modern Shemiranat/Tehran foothills), first attested by al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE).

b_jarmaq.first_mention_attestation: 977 CE (Ibn Hawqal, Kitab Surat al-Ard, as Jarmaq / Sihdih; al-Muqaddasi, 985 CE, as Jarmaq)
b_jarmaq.etymology_analysis: Arabicized form Jarmaq of Persian Garmah, an oasis hamlet in the Biabanak (Jandaq) desert oasis first attested by Ibn Hawqal (977 CE).

b_wandah.first_mention_attestation: 985 CE (al-Muqaddasi, Ahsan al-Taqasim, p. 491, as Wandah, a desert stage 50 leagues north of Jarmaq)
b_wandah.etymology_analysis: A desert caravan station 50 leagues north of Jarmaq on the road to Damghan, first attested by al-Muqaddasi in 985 CE.

b_mihrijan.first_mention_attestation: 977 CE (10th-century CE geographers, as Mihrijan / Mehrajan oasis in Biabanak)
b_mihrijan.etymology_analysis: From Persian Mehragān (an ancient Iranian festival/place-name), designating an oasis in Biabanak known in caravan itineraries since the 10th century CE.

b_biyadaq.first_mention_attestation: 977 CE (Ibn Hawqal, Kitab Surat al-Ard, and Nasir-i Khusraw, 1052 CE, as Biyadaq / Piyadah, modern Bayaza)
b_biyadaq.etymology_analysis: Arabicized form Biyādaqa of Persian Piyādah (modern Bayaza), one of the three main hamlets of the Jarmaq/Biabanak oasis attested in Ibn Hawqal (977 CE).

b_shahr-e-babak.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (al-Istakhri, Kitab Masalik al-Mamalik, and al-Muqaddasi, 985 CE, as Shahr-i Babak)

eponym.details: Named after Babak (Middle Persian Papak, fl. early 3rd century CE), father of the Sasanian founder Ardashir I.

b_shahr-e-babak.etymology_analysis: Persian Shahr-e Bābak ('City of Babak'), traditionally attributed to Babak, father of Ardashir I; first attested in writing by al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE).

b_muralziyan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in medieval or classical historical and geographical sources
b_muralziyan.etymology_analysis: Unattested in medieval Islamic geographies or modern gazetteers for the Shahr-e Babak region.

b_abarquh.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (al-Istakhri and Ibn Hawqal, 977 CE, as Abarquh / Abarquya)
b_abarquh.etymology_analysis: From Middle Persian abar ('on/above') + kūh ('hill/mountain'), a settlement locator explaining its early hilltop site; first attested in 10th-century CE Arab geographers.

b_qaryat-al-asad.first_mention_attestation: Unattested under this Arabicized form in pre-867 CE sources (Arabic translation of Persian Deh-Shir)
b_qaryat-al-asad.etymology_analysis: Arabic translation ('Village of the Lion') of the Persian village name Deh-Shīr (modern Dehshir, Taft County, Yazd); unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

b_yazd.first_mention_attestation: 582 CE (Sasanian silver drachms of Hormizd IV with mintmark YZ for Yazd; also Sasanian seals)

eponym.details: Traditionally linked to Sasanian king Yazdegerd I (r. 399-420 CE) or Middle Persian yazad ('divine, holy').

b_yazd.etymology_analysis: From Middle Persian Yazd (cognate with yazad 'divine/holy'), attested on Sasanian coinage (mintmark YZ, e.g., 582 CE) and seals; earlier known as Kathah.

historical_names.name: Issatis
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder (Naturalis Historia, 77 CE, as Issatis) and pre-Islamic local tradition (Kathah).
historical_names.notes: Classical Issatis and earlier local name Kathah preceded Sasanian/Islamic Yazd.

historical_names.name: Kathah
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder (Naturalis Historia, 77 CE, as Issatis) and pre-Islamic local tradition (Kathah).
historical_names.notes: Classical Issatis and earlier local name Kathah preceded Sasanian/Islamic Yazd.

b_nain.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (al-Istakhri and Ibn Hawqal, 977 CE, as Na'in)
b_nain.etymology_analysis: Ancient desert-border town between Yazd and Isfahan with pre-Islamic remains, though its earliest surviving written attestation is in 10th-century CE Arabic geographies (al-Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal).

b_uqda.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (al-Istakhri and Ibn Hawqal, 977 CE, as 'Uqda)
b_uqda.etymology_analysis: Frontier settlement between Yazd and Na'in first attested in 10th-century CE Arabic geographical works (al-Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal); popular etymology connects it to a Sasanian commander 'Aqdar.

b_maibud.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (al-Istakhri and Ibn Hawqal, 977 CE, as Maybud)
b_maibud.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic oasis town northwest of Yazd (with the Sasanian-era Narin Qal'a fortress), though its first documented written attestation is in 10th-century CE Arabic geographies (al-Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal).

b_fahraj_yazd.first_mention_attestation: c. 951 CE (al-Istakhri and al-Muqaddasi, 985 CE, as Bahra / Fahraj)
b_fahraj_yazd.etymology_analysis: From Middle Persian *pahra ('watchpost/guard-station'), Arabicized as Fahraj; its Jameh Mosque is early Islamic, but the earliest written geographical attestation is al-Istakhri (c. 951 CE).

b_khazana.first_mention_attestation: 977 CE (Ibn Hawqal, Kitab Surat al-Ard, and al-Muqaddasi, 985 CE, as Khazanah north of Yazd)
b_khazana.etymology_analysis: From Arabic/Persian khazāna ('treasury/storehouse'), a fortified village two stages north of Yazd on the Tabas road first attested by Ibn Hawqal (977 CE).

b_shibam.first_mention_attestation: 3rd century CE (first known inscription mentioning Shibam; became capital of the Kingdom of Hadhramaut c. 300 CE)

morphemes.translation: ancient walled oasis city in Wadi Hadhramaut

b_shibam.etymology_analysis: From Old South Arabian / Hadramitic Shibām (شبام), attested in 3rd-century CE inscriptions and serving as capital of the Kingdom of Hadhramaut by 300 CE.

b_barhut.first_mention_attestation: 7th–9th century CE (early Islamic traditions and classical Arabic geographical lore on the Well of Barhut in Hadhramaut)

morphemes.translation: name of the desert sinkhole/well in Wadi Hadhramaut

b_barhut.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Barhūt (برهوت), referring to the famous desert sinkhole (Bi'r Barhūt) in Hadhramaut, attested in early Islamic traditions and medieval Arabic geography.

b_inat.first_mention_attestation: 16th century CE (prominent in Hadhrami Sufi history as the seat of Shaykh Abu Bakr ibn Salim, d. 1584 CE)
b_inat.etymology_analysis: From Arabic ʿInāt (عينات), a town in Wadi Hadhramaut famous from the 16th century CE onward; unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.

b_qabr_salih.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in written sources (regional Hadhrami pilgrimage shrine)
b_qabr_salih.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Qabr Ṣāliḥ (قبر صالح, 'Tomb of Salih'), a regional pilgrimage site in Hadhramaut with no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_qutn.first_mention_attestation: 16th century CE (established as a Yafa'i state center in western Hadhramaut after the 1488 CE Kathiri invasion)

morphemes.translation: cotton / settlement name in Wadi Hadhramaut

b_qutn.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Qaṭn (القطن), a town in western Wadi Hadhramaut that rose to political prominence in the 16th century CE; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_main.first_mention_attestation: c. 6th–5th century BCE (Minaean inscriptions of the Kingdom of Ma'in; also classical Greek/Latin Minaei)

morphemes.translation: spring/source; name of the ancient Minaean kingdom

b_main.etymology_analysis: From Minaic / Old South Arabian mʿn (Arabic Maʿīn, معين), one of the major ancient South Arabian kingdoms centered at Qarnaw in al-Jawf.

b_shabwa.first_mention_attestation: 5th century BCE (Old South Arabian inscriptions as Šbwt; also Pliny's Sabota)
b_shabwa.etymology_analysis: From Hadramitic Šbwt (Arabic Shabwah, شبوة), the ancient capital of the Kingdom of Hadhramaut, attested epigraphically from the 5th century BCE.

b_bayhan.first_mention_attestation: c. 3rd century BCE (Qatabanic and Sabaic inscriptions referencing the Bayhan valley, heartland of Qataban)
b_bayhan.etymology_analysis: From Qatabanic / Arabic Bayḥān (بيحان), the fertile wadi valley that formed the core of the ancient Kingdom of Qataban.

b_baraqish.first_mention_attestation: 10th century CE (medieval Arabic geographical works such as al-Hamdani; known in antiquity as Yathill)

morphemes.translation: medieval Arabic name for ancient Yathill

b_baraqish.etymology_analysis: Arabic Barāqish (براقش), the medieval name of the ancient Minaean city of Yathill (Yṯl, attested c. 6th–5th century BCE). The Arabic name Barāqish is post-867 CE.

historical_names.name: Yathill
historical_names.source: Minaic and Sabaic inscriptions (c. 6th–5th century BCE)
historical_names.notes: Known in ancient South Arabian inscriptions as Yathill (Yṯl) before the medieval Arabic name Baraqish.

b_hurayda.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in written sources (site of a pre-Islamic Moon temple in Wadi Amd excavated in 1937–1938 CE)
b_hurayda.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Ḥurayḍah (حريضة). While an ancient temple stood nearby, the Arabic toponym Ḥurayḍah has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_khurayba.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in written sources (town in Wadi Dawan, Hadhramaut)
b_khurayba.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Khuraybah (خريبة, diminutive of 'ruin'), a town in Wadi Dawan with no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_najran.first_mention_attestation: c. 685 BCE (Sabaean inscription RES 3945 of Karib'il Watar as Ngrn; also 523 CE Christian martyrs of Najran)
b_najran.etymology_analysis: From Sabaic Ngrn (Arabic Najrān, نجران), an ancient oasis city on the incense route attested in 7th-century BCE Sabaean inscriptions and 6th-century CE Christian/Byzantine records.

b_sada.first_mention_attestation: 893–897 CE (foundation of the Zaydi Imamate at Sa'dah by al-Hadi ila'l-Haqq Yahya; 10th-century CE al-Hamdani)
b_sada.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Ṣaʿdah (صعدة), which became the stronghold of the Zaydi Imams in 893–897 CE; no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_wabar.first_mention_attestation: c. 800 CE (pre-Islamic Arabic poetry and early Islamic historiography such as Ibn Hisham and al-Tabari on Wabar)

morphemes.translation: legendary lost land/city in southern Arabia

b_wabar.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Wabār (وبار, also Ūbār), the legendary lost city/region of southern Arabia attested in pre-Islamic poetry and early Islamic historiography.

b_hisn_al-abr.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in written sources (desert fort on the Hadhramaut–Marib caravan route)
b_hisn_al-abr.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Ḥiṣn al-ʿAbr (حصن العبر, 'Fortress of the Crossing'), unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.

b_al-asa.first_mention_attestation: c. 780 CE (early name al-Asʿāʾ for the port of al-Shihr in Hadhramaut)

morphemes.translation: earlier name of the port of al-Shihr

b_al-asa.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Asʿāʾ (الأسعاء), attested as an early historical name for the Hadhrami port of al-Shihr (traceable to c. 780 CE).

b_raysut.first_mention_attestation: 10th century CE (early medieval Islamic maritime/geographical accounts of Dhofar)
b_raysut.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Raysūt (ريسوت), a historic port in Dhofar, Oman, attested in medieval Islamic sources after 867 CE.

b_dhufar.first_mention_attestation: 10th century CE (medieval Arabic geographers such as al-Hamdani and al-Mas'udi; ancient region was Sachalites / Moscha Limen)
b_dhufar.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Ẓufār / Ẓafār (ظفار), attested for the Dhofar coast in 10th-century CE Islamic geography (after 867 CE). In the 1st-century CE Periplus, the nearby port was Moscha Limen (Sumhuram).

historical_names.name: Moscha Limen
historical_names.source: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st century CE) and Hadramitic inscriptions at Sumhuram
historical_names.notes: Ancient frankincense port of Moscha Limen / Sumhuram (Khor Rori) served the Dhofar coast in the 1st century CE.

historical_names.name: Sumhuram
historical_names.source: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st century CE) and Hadramitic inscriptions at Sumhuram
historical_names.notes: Ancient frankincense port of Moscha Limen / Sumhuram (Khor Rori) served the Dhofar coast in the 1st century CE.

b_mirba.first_mention_attestation: c. 1150 CE (attested by al-Idrisi on the sailing route from Aden to Mirbat)
b_mirba.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Mirbāṭ (مرباط), a coastal port in Dhofar attested in medieval Islamic geography (e.g., al-Idrisi c. 1150 CE), after 867 CE.

b_hasik.first_mention_attestation: 14th century CE (attested by Ibn Battuta in connection with Dhofar frankincense)
b_hasik.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Ḥāsik (حاسك), a coastal port in Dhofar attested in medieval travelogues (14th century CE), after 867 CE.

b_ash-shihr.first_mention_attestation: c. 780 CE (attested in early Islamic history and Ibn Khordadbeh's 9th-century CE geography)
b_ash-shihr.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Shiḥr (الشحر), the principal early Islamic frankincense and ambergris port of Hadhramaut, traceable to c. 780 CE.

b_balhaf.first_mention_attestation: 19th century CE (capital of the Sultanate of Wahidi Balhaf in the 1880s CE)
b_balhaf.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Balḥāf (بلحاف), a coastal port in Shabwah documented in the 19th century CE; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_mukalla.first_mention_attestation: 1035 CE (founded as a fishing settlement in 1035 CE)
b_mukalla.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Mukallā (المكلا), derived from kala'a ('to shelter/preserve'). Founded in 1035 CE, after 867 CE.

b_sanaa.first_mention_attestation: 5th century BCE (Sabaean Musnad inscriptions as ṣnʿw)
b_sanaa.etymology_analysis: From Sabaic ṣnʿw (Arabic Ṣanʿāʾ, صنعاء), derived from the Sabaic root ṣnʿ ('well-fortified'), attested in Musnad inscriptions from the 5th century BCE.

b_ash-sharaf.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in written sources (highland district in Hajjah Governorate)
b_ash-sharaf.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Sharaf (الشرف, 'the highland/eminence'), unattested as a settlement/barony title <= 867 CE.

b_huth.first_mention_attestation: 10th century CE (attested in al-Hamdani's Sifat Jazirat al-Arab)
b_huth.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Ḥūth (حوث), a highland town in Amran Governorate attested in 10th-century CE Yemeni geography (al-Hamdani), after 867 CE.

b_ar-rayda.first_mention_attestation: 10th century CE (attested in al-Hamdani's Sifat Jazirat al-Arab)
b_ar-rayda.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Raydah (الريدة), a town north of Sanaa attested in 10th-century CE Yemeni geography, after 867 CE.

b_shibam-sanaa.first_mention_attestation: 847 CE (capital of the Yu'firid dynasty founded in 847 CE; also known as Shibam Aqyan / Shibam Kawkaban)
b_shibam-sanaa.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Shibām (شبام كوكبان / شبام أقيان), seat of the Yu'firid dynasty (founded 847 CE), <= 867 CE.

b_attar.first_mention_attestation: c. 830–900 CE (early Islamic Red Sea port of 'Aththar in southern Tihama)

morphemes.translation: Red Sea port in Tihama (reflecting pre-Islamic deity 'Athtar)

b_attar.etymology_analysis: From Arabic ʿAththar (عثر), a major early Islamic Red Sea port in Tihama active from the 9th century CE.

b_harad.first_mention_attestation: c. 955 CE (attested in al-Hamdani's 10th-century CE description of Tihama valleys)

morphemes.translation: town and valley in northern Tihama

b_harad.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Ḥaraḍ (حرض), a town in northern Tihama attested in 10th-century CE Yemeni geography (al-Hamdani), after 867 CE.

b_al-mahjam.first_mention_attestation: 11th century CE (medieval Tihama city prominent under the Najahid and Rasulid dynasties)
b_al-mahjam.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Mahjam (المهجم), a major medieval city in northern Tihama prominent from the 11th century CE onward; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_kamaran.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in written sources (Red Sea island off Al Hudaydah)
b_kamaran.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Kamarān (كمران), the largest Yemeni island in the Red Sea; unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.

b_zabid.first_mention_attestation: 820 CE (founded in January 820 CE by Muhammad ibn Ziyad, Abbasid governor of Yemen)

morphemes.translation: city in the Tihama coastal plain (named after Wadi Zabid)

b_zabid.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Zabīd (زبيد), founded as the Ziyadid capital in 820 CE by Muhammad ibn Ziyad.

b_fashal.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in written sources (medieval Tihama locality near Zabid)
b_fashal.etymology_analysis: Arabic Fashal (فشل), a Tihama locality near Zabid with no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_ghalafiqa.first_mention_attestation: 10th century CE (attested in 10th-century CE Arabic geographers such as al-Hamdani and al-Muqaddasi as the port of Zabid)
b_ghalafiqa.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Ghalāfiqah (غلافقة), the historic Red Sea port of Zabid, attested in 10th-century CE geographical sources after 867 CE.

b_mawza.first_mention_attestation: 1st century CE (attested in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea as the Red Sea port of Muza)
b_mawza.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Mawzaʿ (موزع), identified with the ancient port of Muza attested in the 1st-century CE Periplus of the Erythraean Sea.

b_suq-socotra.first_mention_attestation: 1507 CE (Suq recorded as the capital of Socotra by the Portuguese in the 16th century CE; island known in antiquity as Dioscorida)
b_suq-socotra.etymology_analysis: Compound of Arabic Sūq ('market') and Socotra (Arabic Suquṭrā). The town of Suq is attested from the 16th century CE; the island was known in the 1st-century CE Periplus as Dioscorida.

historical_names.name: Dioscorida
historical_names.source: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st century CE)
historical_names.notes: Socotra Island was known in antiquity as Dioscorida before the medieval town of Suq.

b_qualnsiyah.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in written sources (town on western Socotra)
b_qualnsiyah.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Qalansiyah (قلنسية, also Qulensya), a town on Socotra with no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_saqra.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in written sources (coastal town in Abyan / Dathina)
b_saqra.etymology_analysis: Arabic Shaqrāʾ / Saqrāʾ (شقراء), a coastal town in Abyan with no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_ahwan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in written sources (locality in Dathina / Abyan)
b_ahwan.etymology_analysis: Sub-barony in c_dathina with no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_azzan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in written sources (town in Shabwah Governorate)
b_azzan.etymology_analysis: From Arabic ʿAzzān (عزان), a town in Shabwah Governorate with no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_nisab.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in written sources (town in Shabwah Governorate)
b_nisab.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Niṣāb (نصاب), a town in Shabwah Governorate with no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_al-mandab.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in written sources (medieval Arabic name for the Bab al-Mandab strait)

morphemes.translation: grief, lamentation (from Bāb al-Mandab, Gate of Grief)

b_al-mandab.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Bāb al-Mandab (باب المندب, 'Gate of Grief'), referring to the hazardous strait at the Red Sea entrance; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_al-maafir.first_mention_attestation: 1st century CE (attested in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea as Mapharitis and in Sabaic/Himyarite inscriptions)

morphemes.translation: ancient Yemeni tribe and region (Greek Mapharitis)

b_al-maafir.etymology_analysis: From Sabaic / Arabic al-Maʿāfir (المعافر), the ancient South Arabian tribe and highland region (modern al-Hujariah), attested as Mapharitis in the 1st-century CE Periplus.

b_musaymir.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in written sources (town in Lahij Governorate)
b_musaymir.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Musaymir (المسيمير), a town in Lahij Governorate with no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_aden.first_mention_attestation: 1st century CE (attested in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea as Eudaemon Arabia and in Sabaic inscriptions as ʿdn)
b_aden.etymology_analysis: From Sabaic ʿdn / Arabic ʿAdan (عدن), an ancient maritime entrepôt attested in the 1st-century CE Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (as Eudaemon Arabia) and Old South Arabian inscriptions.

b_taizz.first_mention_attestation: First half of the 12th century CE (first historical reference when Sulayhid sultan Abdullah ibn Muhammad al-Sulayhi built Al-Qahira Castle)
b_taizz.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Taʿizz (تعز), first attested in historical sources in the first half of the 12th century CE under the Sulayhid dynasty, after 867 CE.

b_al-janad.first_mention_attestation: c. 630 CE (early Islamic city and Great Mosque of al-Janad founded by Mu'adh ibn Jabal)

morphemes.translation: early Islamic administrative center (mikhlaf) near Taiz

b_al-janad.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Janad (الجند), an early Islamic administrative capital (Mikhlaf al-Janad) where Mu'adh ibn Jabal established one of Yemen's oldest mosques c. 630 CE.

b_zafar.first_mention_attestation: 2nd–1st century BCE (Himyarite inscriptions and classical sources such as Pliny and Ptolemy as Sapphar)

morphemes.translation: ancient capital of the Himyarite Kingdom

b_zafar.etymology_analysis: From Himyaritic / Arabic Ẓafār (ظفار), the highland capital of the Himyarite Kingdom, attested from the 2nd–1st century BCE.

b_rada.first_mention_attestation: 15th century CE (power base of the Tahirid dynasty from 1454 CE)
b_rada.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Radāʿ (رداع), prominent as a Tahirid center in the 15th century CE; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_lawdar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE in written sources (town in Abyan Governorate)
b_lawdar.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Lawdar (لودر), a town in Abyan Governorate with no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_al-qhqaf.first_mention_attestation: 7th century CE (Quran, Surah al-Ahqaf 46:21, and Ibn Sa'd c. 845 CE)
b_al-qhqaf.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Aḥqāf (الأحقاف, 'the curved sand dunes'), attested in the Quran (46:21, 7th century CE) for the desert region of southern Arabia.

b_thamud.first_mention_attestation: 715 BCE (Neo-Assyrian inscriptions of Sargon II as Tamudi; also attested in the Quran, 7th century CE)
b_thamud.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Thamūd (ثمود), an ancient Arabian people attested in 715 BCE Neo-Assyrian inscriptions (Tamudi) and the Quran (7th century CE).
